note: From Old English clud, which meant 'rock, hill'. The mass of rain-bearing vapour was likened to a hill in the sky.
hints: It rains from this when it's grey.
A fluffy white one drifts overhead.

definition: A dried flower bud used as a spice; or a segment of garlic.
note: From Old French clou de girofle, 'nail of the clove tree', since the bud looks like a small nail.
hints: A bud used to stud a ham.
One segment of a bulb of garlic.

definition: A performer in baggy clothes and a red nose.
note: From earlier clowne, 'a rustic, a boor', likely from a Scandinavian source. The meaning shifted from a clumsy peasant to a comic performer.
hints: A circus performer with a red nose.
Someone who acts silly to get laughs.

definition: The noise a hen makes.
note: From Old English cloccian, imitative of the hen's sound. It can also describe a sound of disapproval.
hints: A mother hen calls her chicks with it.
What you do with your tongue to show disapproval.

definition: A tight cluster or lump.
note: From Old English clympre, 'lump or mass of metal', from a Germanic root. It describes things bunched together.
hints: Grass growing in a tuft.
Hair stuck together in a wet mass.

definition: Past tense of cling; held on tightly.
note: From Old English clinge, to stick together. Wet clothes, children and hopes all get clung to.
hints: How a wet shirt held to skin.
What a koala did to a tree.

definition: A trainer; or a large carriage or bus.
note: The carriage named for Kocs, a Hungarian town, is a popular theory. It later meant a tutor who carries a student through an exam.
hints: Leads a sports team from the sideline.
A fancy horse-drawn carriage in a fairy tale.

definition: The land along the sea.
note: From Old French coste, 'rib, side, coast'. The word first meant a side of the body.
hints: Where the land meets the ocean.
To glide without effort, as a bicycle down a hill.

definition: A venomous snake that spreads a hood.
note: From Portuguese cobra, from Latin colubra, 'female snake'. It rears up and flattens its neck when threatened.
hints: Snake charmers play to one.
Rudyard Kipling's Rikki-Tikki-Tavi fights one.

definition: A powder made from cacao seeds; a hot chocolate drink.
note: From Spanish cacao, via Nahuatl. Cocoa came from confusing the word with coco, a spelling Johnson's dictionary helped spread.
hints: Hot drink with marshmallows.
Powder used in baking chocolate cake.

definition: The punctuation mark that looks like two dots; also part of the bowel.
note: From Latin colon and Greek kolon, 'limb, clause'. The mark was named for a member of a sentence, the bowel for a different Greek word.
hints: Written before a list.
Two dots stacked on top of each other.

definition: The quality of light that makes red, blue and green different.
note: From Old French color, from Latin color, 'colour, hue'. Spelled colour in British English.
hints: Red or blue, for example.
A crayon box is full of them.

definition: Cosy and comfortable.
note: A shortening of comfortable plus -y, dating to the early 1800s. It is a casual, affectionate word.
hints: How a favourite old sweater feels.
A cosy armchair is described this way.

definition: Funny; or a person or book that's funny.
note: From Latin comicus, from Greek komikos, 'of comedy', from komos, 'carousal'. It once referred to stage comedy only.
hints: A stand-up performer is called one.
A cartoon strip in a newspaper.

definition: A punctuation mark that marks a short pause.
note: From Latin comma, from Greek komma, 'piece cut off'. It cuts a sentence into smaller parts.
hints: Looks like a tiny curved tail.
What separates items in a list.

definition: A large spiral sea shell.
note: From Latin concha, from Greek konkhe, 'shell'. Blowing through one makes a loud horn-like note.
hints: In a famous novel, boys use one to call order.
Hold it to your ear to hear the sea.

definition: An apartment you own in a building.
note: Short for condominium. The full word describes a building where each unit has a separate owner.
hints: Shortened word for a flat that is bought, not rented.
Often has a shared pool and gym.

definition: Shaped like or relating to a cone.
note: Borrowed from Ancient Greek konikos, from konos, 'cone'. It appears mostly in mathematics, in the phrase 'conic section'.
hints: A word from geometry class.
What a slice through a cone can be called.

definition: A small group of trees.
note: From coppice, contracted in the 1500s. It first meant a small wood grown to be cut regularly.
hints: A small patch of woodland.
Smaller than a forest, bigger than a grove.

definition: The hard, stony skeleton of tiny sea animals.
note: From Old French and Latin corallium, from Greek korallion, probably of Semitic origin. Reefs are built by countless tiny animals.
hints: The Great Barrier Reef is made of it.
A pinkish orange shade as well.

definition: A tool for removing the core from fruit.
note: Built from core plus -er, a tool or person that does the action. The same word also names a device for drilling samples out of the earth or ice.
hints: A kitchen gadget for apples.
Pushed through a fruit to remove its middle.

definition: Cheesy and sentimental.
note: Related to corn, the grain. It was slang for something tired and old-fashioned, as in a joke that's past its best.
hints: A dad's pun might get this label.
A joke so old it makes people groan.

definition: A sofa.
note: From Old French couche, 'bed', from the verb coucher, 'to lay down'. It is a cousin of the Welsh word cwtch.
hints: A 'potato' is someone who lounges on one.
Where you sit to watch TV.

definition: To force air out of the lungs with a harsh sound.
note: From Middle English coughen, imitative of the sound. The gh was once pronounced as a throat sound.
hints: A common sign of a cold.
Syrup is meant to soothe it.

definition: Used for what was possible or for polite requests.
note: From Old English cuthe, the past of cunnan, 'to be able'. The letter L crept in later by analogy with 'would' and 'should'.
hints: A helper word that politely asks something.
Past form of can.

definition: To say numbers in order; or a nobleman.
note: From Old French conter and Latin computare, 'to reckon together'. The noble title count comes from a different Latin word, comes, 'companion'.
hints: One, two, three.
Sesame Street's vampire loves to do it.

definition: A two-door car with a sloping roof.
note: Borrowed from French coupe, 'cut', from a carriage that was cut short. A shallow stemmed dish has the same spelling.
hints: A sporty two-door car.
A cut-down version of a sedan.

definition: A gathering of witches.
note: From Middle English covent, from Old French and Latin conventum, 'a coming together'. It is the same word as convent, whose spelling changed to mean the witches' version.
hints: Thirteen witches is the traditional number.
A group of witches gathering.

definition: To put something over another thing.
note: From Old French covrir, from Latin cooperire, 'to cover completely'. It has many senses, from a lid to a song someone else wrote.
hints: A lid or a blanket does it.
A band plays a version of another's song, called a ___ song.

definition: To desire something that belongs to someone else.
note: From Old French coveitier, 'to desire'. The Tenth Commandment warns against it.
hints: The Tenth Commandment warns not to do this to a neighbour's goods.
To long enviously for what another person has.

definition: A small flock of partridges or quail.
note: From Old French covee, 'a brood', from Latin cubare, 'to lie down'. It describes a family group of game birds.
hints: A hunter flushes a group of quail like this.
A small gathering of game birds.

definition: In a shy or playfully evasive way.
note: From coy plus -ly. Coy comes from Old French coi, 'quiet' or 'still', from Latin quietus.
hints: How someone might smile when teased.
Done with a shy, half-hidden look.

definition: To break with a sharp sound without splitting apart.
note: From Old English cracian, 'to resound', imitative of the sound. It is both the break and the noise it makes.
hints: A line that appears in a broken egg.
What a whip does.

definition: A skill, especially one done by hand.
note: From Old English craeft, 'strength, power, skill'. Strength gave way to skill, and then to a trade or an art.
hints: Knitting is a handmade one.
Also a general word for a small boat or a plane.

definition: A painful, sudden tightening of a muscle.
note: From Old French crampe, from a Frankish word meaning bent or hooked. It describes a muscle clenching up.
hints: What swimmers sometimes get in their legs.
A sudden knot in your calf at night.

definition: A tall wading bird, or a machine for lifting.
note: From Old English cran, the bird. The lifting machine was named for its long neck.
hints: A building site has one towering over it.
Origami paper birds are often this.

definition: A handle that turns a shaft; or an odd person.
note: From Old English crencestaef, a weaver's tool, with a Germanic word meaning bent. The grumpy person sense came later.
hints: Turn it to start an old engine.
A grumpy eccentric with strange ideas.

definition: To hit something violently with a loud noise.
note: From Middle English crasshen, 'to break into pieces', of uncertain origin. It seems to combine sounds like crack and smash.
hints: What two cars might do at an intersection.
A computer might do this and freeze.

definition: Crude and insensitive.
note: From Latin crassus, 'thick, dense'. The thickness of a crass person is of manners.
hints: A tasteless remark at a funeral.
Lacking refinement or tact.

definition: A large box for moving goods.
note: From Dutch krat, 'basket, box'. It is used for fruit, bottles and pets.
hints: A box of oranges for shipping.
A dog may be trained in a wire one.

definition: To want something very badly.
note: From Old English crafian, 'to ask, demand'. Cravings have long been spoken of as demands.
hints: What a pregnant person might do for pickles.
To long for chocolate after dinner.

definition: To move along on hands and knees.
note: From Old Norse krafla, 'to claw about, crawl'. A baby does it before walking.
hints: Babies do it before they walk.
A swimming stroke has this name.

definition: A short-lived but intense fashion.
note: From Middle English crasen, 'to shatter', from Old Norse. The meaning moved from smash to a mind that's cracked, then a passing mania.
hints: Fidget spinners were one.
A passing fad that everyone follows.

definition: Mad or wildly irrational.
note: Built from craze, 'to crush', plus -y. Like cracked, it refers to a mind that has broken.
hints: Way to say something is wild or nuts.
What you might call a plan that makes no sense.

definition: To make a long, squeaky sound.
note: From Middle English creken, from an Old English word meaning to chatter or crash. It is imitative.
hints: Old stairs do it when stepped on.
A rusty hinge on a door.

definition: The rich fat that rises to the top of milk.
note: From Old French creme, a blend of Late Latin chrisma, 'ointment', and an older word for the dairy fat. The best of something is the 'cream of the crop'.
hints: Whipped and put on desserts.
Poured into coffee.

definition: A statement of beliefs.
note: From Latin credo, 'I believe'. It is the same word as creed, and the opening word of a famous Latin prayer.
hints: A personal motto or guiding belief.
Latin for 'I believe'.

definition: A set of beliefs.
note: From Old English creda, from Latin credo, 'I believe'. It names a statement of faith recited in church.
hints: A formal statement of what a faith holds.
Not a political one but a religious one.

definition: A small stream.
note: From Middle English crike, from Old Norse kriki, 'bend, nook'. In Britain it means a narrow inlet; in America a stream.
hints: Kids splash and catch tadpoles in it.
Proverbially, you are up one without a paddle.

definition: A very thin pancake.
note: Borrowed from French crepe, from Latin crispus, 'curled'. The word also names a crinkled fabric.
hints: Filled with Nutella and folded.
A French thin pancake.

definition: A peppery plant used in salads and sandwiches.
note: From Old English cressa, a Germanic word. Egg and ___ sandwiches are a British classic.
hints: Grows quickly on damp cotton wool.
A peppery green in a sandwich.

definition: A sharp stiffness in the neck or back.
note: From Middle English crike, 'muscular spasm', possibly from Old Norse kriki, 'bend'. It appears in English from the 1400s.
hints: Sleeping badly may give you one in your neck.
A painful kink in your neck.

definition: A person who shouts out public announcements.
note: From Old French crieor, built on the verb crier, 'to cry out'. A town crier once shouted news and proclamations to the public.
hints: Once announced news in the marketplace.
Often rang a bell and shouted 'Oyez'.

definition: An act that breaks the law.
note: From Old French crime, from Latin crimen, 'charge, accusation, offence'. It has stood for lawbreaking for centuries.
hints: What a detective investigates.
Theft or arson, for example.

definition: To press into small folds or ridges.
note: From Middle English crimpen and Middle Dutch crimpen, 'to wrinkle'. It is related to the shrinking verbs.
hints: Pinching the edge of a pie crust.
A hairdresser's tool gives hair a wavy texture.

definition: Firm, dry and brittle.
note: From Old English crisp, from Latin crispus, 'curly'. The word first described curled hair, and later things that snap.
hints: Fresh celery is this.
Describes autumn air or a fried potato slice.

definition: A low, hoarse noise like a frog's.
note: From Middle English, back-formed from an Old English word meaning to croak. It imitates the sound.
hints: A frog's call.
A hoarse voice with a sore throat.

definition: An earthenware pot.
note: From Old English crocc, 'pot, jar'. A slow cooker is named for it.
hints: A slow cooker has this word in its name.
A big pottery pot.

definition: An old woman, often an unkind picture of one.
note: From Anglo-Norman carogne, related to carrion. It started as an insult meaning an old ewe or worn-out thing.
hints: A hag in a fairy tale.
An old woman who might stir a cauldron.

definition: A close friend or associate, often in questionable dealings.
note: Coined in the 1660s from Greek khronios, 'long-lasting', as Cambridge student slang for an old friend. Politicians' friends get this label.
hints: '___ capitalism' favours friends of the powerful.
A buddy who gets favours from you.

definition: A criminal; or a bend or hook.
note: From Old Norse krokr, 'hook'. The criminal sense is from the bent, not straight, character. A shepherd's staff has one too.
hints: A dishonest person.
What a shepherd's staff is curved into.

definition: Angry; or the shape of two lines meeting.
note: From Latin crux, 'cross', through Old Irish and Old English. The angry sense came from 'crossing' someone's wishes.
hints: Annoyed or ill-tempered.
A plus sign is a small one.

definition: A children's illness with a barking cough.
note: The name probably imitates the sound of the cough. A horse's rump has the same spelling from a different word.
hints: A child's cough that sounds like a seal.
A childhood illness with a barking cough.

definition: A large group of people together.
note: From Old English crudan, 'to press, drive'. It first meant to push before it meant a mass of people.
hints: Gathers at a football match.
To squeeze together in a small space.

definition: A ring worn on a monarch's head.
note: From Anglo-Norman corone, from Latin corona, 'wreath', from Greek. It also names the top of the head or a tooth cap.
hints: A queen wears it.
The top of your head.

definition: Rough and unrefined.
note: From Latin crudus, 'raw, rough'. It is related to cruel. It names oil in its raw state.
hints: Petroleum before refining.
A rough joke in poor taste.

definition: Willing to cause pain or suffering.
note: From Old French cruel and Latin crudelis, 'hard, severe', related to crudus, 'raw'. A cruel person is raw, not softened.
hints: Describes someone who takes pleasure in others' pain.
The opposite of kind.

definition: A tiny piece of bread or cake.
note: From Old English cruma, from a Germanic root. The b was added to the spelling later, as in thumb.
hints: What toast leaves on the table.
A little piece a bird might peck.

definition: The hard outer layer of bread or pie.
note: From Latin crusta, 'rind, shell', through Old French. It also names the Earth's outer layer.
hints: The hard part of a loaf.
The outer layer of the planet.

definition: An underground room, often beneath a church, used for burials.
note: From Latin crypta, from Greek kryptos, 'hidden'. The word is related to cryptic.
hints: Beneath a cathedral, with tombs inside.
Dracula sleeps in one.

definition: Relating to the shape or measure of a cube.
note: From Middle French cubique, from cube plus -ic. Volumes are measured in these units.
hints: A measure of volume, as in 'a ___ metre'.
Shaped like dice.

definition: A spice used in curries and chilli.
note: From Old English cymen and Old French cumin, from Latin cuminum, ultimately from a Semitic source. It has been used in cooking for thousands of years.
hints: A warm brown spice in Indian and Mexican dishes.
Seeds from a plant in the parsley family.

definition: A small unusual object that people collect.
note: A clipping of curiosity, dated 1851. Collectors displayed them in cabinets of curiosities.
hints: A small, odd collectable in a shop.
An antique trinket on a shelf.

definition: Having curls.
note: From curl plus -y. It describes hair or things that twist into spirals.
hints: Hair that's not straight.
A pig's tail is this.

definition: A spiced dish, popular across India and the UK.
note: From Tamil kari, 'sauce', influenced by an older English word cury, 'cooking'. The first English recipe printed was in 1747.
hints: Served with rice or naan.
A fragrant dish with a spicy sauce.

definition: A wish that harm will fall on someone; or a swear word.
note: From Old English curs, of unknown origin. It names both a spell of misfortune and rude language.
hints: A witch casts one on a prince in a tale.
To swear angrily when you stub your toe.

definition: A smooth bend without corners.
note: From Latin curvus, 'bent', with a root meaning to turn or bend. It has been in English since the 1690s.
hints: A road bends in one.
What a baseball pitcher throws to fool the batter.

definition: Having many smooth bends.
note: From curve plus -y. It describes roads, shapes and figures.
hints: A mountain road with many bends is this.
Winding, with no straight lines.

definition: An attractive or adorable person; also a small, easy-peel orange.
note: From cute plus the -ie ending. Cute itself is a shortening of acute, once meaning 'sharp' and 'clever'.
hints: A friendly pet name.
Also the brand name of a small, easy-peel orange.

definition: Relating to computers, networks or the internet.
note: Taken from cybernetics, which came from Greek kybernetes, 'steersman'. It is now a stand-alone word.
hints: A prefix-like word about being online.
Often paired with 'security' or 'space'.

definition: A series of events that repeat; or a bicycle.
note: From Late Latin cyclus and Greek kyklos, 'circle'. A cycle is a sequence that goes around and returns to its start.
hints: The washing machine has several settings of this kind.
Water goes through one of evaporation and rain.

definition: A person who assumes the worst about people's motives.
note: From Greek kynikos, 'dog-like'. It named a school of ancient Greek philosophers who rejected comforts and conventions.
hints: Expects everyone to be selfish.
Opposite of an optimist.

definition: A child's word for father.
note: From dad plus the -y ending. It is also used for the biggest or best of something.
hints: What a small child calls their father.
Informal word for dad.

definition: Happening every day.
note: From Old English daeglic, from day plus -ly. It is also the name for newspapers that come out every day.
hints: A newspaper that comes out each morning.
Done once every twenty-four hours.

definition: Milk and foods made from it.
note: From Middle English deyerie, from deye, 'dairymaid', plus -erie. The dairymaid made butter and cheese.
hints: Cheese and butter belong in this food group.
A farm or shop section for milk and yoghurt.

definition: A small flower with white petals and a yellow centre.
note: From Old English daeges eage, 'day's eye', because the flower closes at night and opens at dawn.
hints: Children make chains of them.
'She loves me, she loves me not' is played with one.

definition: To waste time or move slowly.
note: From Middle English dalien, from Anglo-Norman. It is a cousin of the word delay.
hints: Don't linger on the way home.
To dawdle instead of getting on with things.

definition: To move your body to music.
note: From Old French dancier, of uncertain earlier origin. It has been in English since the 1300s.
hints: What you do at a party.
Ballet and the tango are forms of it.

definition: A man who takes great care over his clothes.
note: Borrowed from Scots, of uncertain origin. It may be a pet form of the name Andrew. It also means excellent, as in 'fine and ___'.
hints: A sharply dressed man of fashion.
'Yankee Doodle' called himself one.

definition: A single piece of information.
note: From Latin datum, 'given'. The plural, data, is far more familiar.
hints: The singular of a word usually in the plural.
One fact among many.

definition: To make someone feel afraid or discouraged.
note: From Old French danter, from Latin domitare, 'to tame'. To be daunted was first to be tamed.
hints: A steep mountain might do this to a new climber.
'Nothing ___ed' means unafraid.

definition: The end of life.
note: From Old English death, from a Germanic root. It has been the most solemn word for the end for over a thousand years.
hints: The Grim Reaper is its figure.
What a funeral marks.

definition: To officially shut someone out or forbid them.
note: From Anglo-Norman debarrer, from de- plus barre, 'bar'. To be debarred is to have a barrier placed against you.
hints: What a rule might do to a rule-breaker.
Keeping someone out of a profession or a place.

definition: An amount of money taken from an account.
note: From Latin debitum, 'what is owed', from debere, 'to owe'. It is a cousin of the word debt.
hints: What a purchase makes to your bank balance.
Opposite of credit in bookkeeping.

definition: To find and fix faults in software.
note: From de- plus bug. Admiral Grace Hopper's team supposedly found a real moth in a computer in 1947, though the word bug was older.
hints: A programmer does it to fix errors in code.
To remove glitches from a program.

definition: A first public appearance.
note: From French debut, from debuter, 'to begin'. It comes from a word meaning 'goal', as in the first shot at a target.
hints: A singer's first album.
An actor's first film.

definition: A sticker that can be transferred to a surface.
note: A clipping of decalcomania, a French craft of transferring pictures. It names a transfer sticker.
hints: A sticker on a car's rear window.
A transfer you rub onto a model plane.

definition: To rot or break down.
note: From Anglo-Norman decaeir, 'to fall away'. It originally meant simply to decrease.
hints: What happens to a tooth with too much sugar.
Slow breakdown of dead plants into soil.

definition: The style in which a room is decorated.
note: From French decor, from Latin decor, 'beauty, grace'. It is a shortened word for decoration.
hints: A designer chooses it for a house.
The look of a room, from curtains to cushions.

definition: To publicly criticise something as bad.
note: Dating from about 1600, from Old French descrier, 'to shout down'. It is a cousin of descry.
hints: An activist might do this at a rally.
To denounce loudly.

definition: To put off until later.
note: From Middle English differren, 'to postpone', from Latin differre. It is a doublet of differ.
hints: What a student might do with a university place.
To delay, as with a payment.

definition: To do something as if it's beneath you.
note: From Old French deignier, 'to think worthy', from Latin dignare. It is related to dignity.
hints: A snob won't ___ to speak to servants.
To condescend.

definition: A god or goddess.
note: From Middle French deite, from Latin deitas, 'divine nature'. It is a formal word for a god.
hints: Zeus was one.
A divine being that is worshipped.

definition: A triangular landform where a river meets the sea; or a Greek letter.
note: From Greek delta, borrowed from a Phoenician word for 'door'. The Nile mouth looked like the capital letter triangle.
hints: The Nile ends in one.
A letter of the Greek alphabet shaped like a triangle.

definition: To dig deeply, or to search thoroughly.
note: From Old English delfan, 'to dig, burrow'. It is the same root as a ditch dug with a spade, and now it is used for digging into information.
hints: What a researcher does into old records.
To dig into a topic.

definition: An evil spirit.
note: From Medieval Latin daemon, from Greek daimon, 'spirit, divine power'. In Greek a daimon wasn't evil; Christianity changed that.
hints: An evil spirit from hell.
Exorcists try to drive them out.

definition: To raise doubts or politely object.
note: From Anglo-Norman demorer and Old French, 'to linger, delay'. To demur was first to hold back.
hints: Said of someone who politely declines.
To hesitate before agreeing.

definition: Packed closely together.
note: From French dense and Latin densus, 'thick'. It is used of fog, forests and slow-witted people.
hints: A jungle full of thick trees.
Fog that's hard to see through.

definition: A storage place, or a bus or railway station.
note: From French depot, from Latin depositum, 'something put down'. It is a doublet of deposit.
hints: Where buses are parked overnight.
A warehouse for supplies.

definition: How deep something is.
note: From Old English dieph, from deep plus -th. It forms a noun like width or length.
hints: What a diver measures.
The opposite of height.

definition: A horse race, or a local sports rivalry.
note: The race is named for Edward Smith-Stanley, 12th Earl of Derby. The Epsom race began in 1780.
hints: The Kentucky one is a famous horse race.
A match between two teams of the same city.

definition: To discourage someone from doing something.
note: From Latin deterrere, 'to frighten from', from de- and terrere, 'to frighten'. It is a cousin of terror.
hints: A guard dog might do this to burglars.
The aim of a 'no entry' sign.

definition: A process of ridding the body of toxins.
note: A clipping of detoxification. It's used for diets and for rehab from addiction.
hints: A juice diet, supposedly.
Treatment for someone giving up drink.

definition: A score of forty all in tennis; or a two.
note: From Old French deus, 'two', from Latin duo. It also mildly names the devil, as in 'what the ___!'
hints: A tennis score where either side needs two points to win.
A playing card with two pips.

definition: A fiend; the king of evil.
note: From Greek diabolos, 'slanderer', through Latin and Old English. It names Satan and any very wicked or mischievous person.
hints: Said to wear red with a pitchfork.
A cheeky person might be called a little one.

definition: Risky or uncertain.
note: From dice plus -y. A throw of the dice is a gamble.
hints: A risky plan with an uncertain outcome.
Crossing a stormy sea in a small boat.

definition: A single numeral, or a finger or toe.
note: From Latin digitus, 'finger, toe'. People counted on their fingers.
hints: The number 7 is one.
A thumb counts as one.

definition: Something remarkable of its kind.
note: It survives in 'dilly-dally' and in the phrase 'a real dilly', meaning a standout example. Dictionaries give it only a thin history.
hints: A word that sounds old-fashioned and cheerful.
A pickle might be said to be this.

definition: In a faint or unclear way.
note: Built from dim plus -ly. Dim comes from Old English dimm, 'dark' or 'gloomy'.
hints: How you recall something half forgotten.
The way a poor bulb lights a room.

definition: A small restaurant serving casual meals; or a person eating.
note: From dine plus -er. In America the word was borrowed for cheap restaurants shaped like railway dining cars.
hints: Serves all-day breakfast and milkshakes.
A person sitting at a table in a restaurant.

definition: A wild dog of Australia.
note: Borrowed from Dharug dingu, 'tame dingo'. It was the name the Sydney Aboriginal people gave to it.
hints: A wild dog Down Under.
A baby was famously said to have been taken by one.

definition: Dirty, dull and shabby.
note: From a Kentish dialect word for dirty, of unknown origin. It rhymes with stingy.
hints: A poorly lit and grubby room.
A cheap hotel might be called this.

definition: A device that lets current flow one way only.
note: From di-, 'two', and -ode, coined in 1919 by William Eccles, after Greek diodos, 'passage through'. LEDs are a type.
hints: A one-way valve for electricity.
LED stands for light-emitting one.

definition: Not clean.
note: From Middle English dirti, from dirt plus -y. It once was dritti, from drit, an old word for excrement.
hints: Describes laundry that needs washing.
Covered in mud.

definition: Dance music of the 1970s, or a club that plays it.
note: A shortening of the French discotheque. A mirrored ball and flares are classic symbols of it.
hints: Gloria Gaynor sang 'I Will Survive' in this style.
A glittering ball hangs over the floor.

definition: A long narrow channel dug in the ground.
note: From Old English dic, a Germanic word. It is the same word as dyke, and as a verb it means to get rid of something.
hints: A shallow trench beside a road.
To abandon, as in dumping a plan.

definition: The same again.
note: From Italian detto, 'said', from Latin dicere, 'to say'. It first appeared in English in 1625, in bookkeeping and lists.
hints: Two small marks in a list mean this.
What you say when you agree with the thing just said.

definition: A short, simple song or poem.
note: From Old French dite, from Latin dictare, 'to dictate'. It first meant a composed poem.
hints: A little tune you might hum.
A catchy little rhyme.

definition: A person who goes underwater or jumps head first into water.
note: Built from dive plus -er. It also names water birds that plunge after fish, such as the loon.
hints: Wears a wetsuit and a tank.
Might leap from a high board.

definition: Feeling as if everything is spinning.
note: From Old English dysig, 'foolish, stupid'. It started with foolish and moved to giddy.
hints: What a fairground ride might make you.
How you feel after spinning around.

definition: To move quickly out of the way.
note: Perhaps from a dialect word meaning to jerk or jog about, of uncertain origin. It also means to evade, as in a question.
hints: A boxer ducks to do this to a punch.
A game of this involves throwing balls at players.

definition: Unreliable or suspicious.
note: From dodge plus -y, first used in the mid 1800s in England. It describes things that seem to be evading honesty.
hints: An unreliable seller of used cars.
Something that looks risky, as with a questionable alibi.

definition: A belief that is held to be undoubtedly true.
note: From Greek dogma, 'opinion, tenet', from dokein, 'to seem good, think'. It once meant any set opinion before it became rigid.
hints: A rigid set of beliefs not open to question.
A church's official teaching.

definition: The act of carrying something out; also a deed.
note: From do plus -ing, from Old English don. 'Doing' as a noun can also mean someone's responsibility, as in 'it was his own doing'.
hints: Somebody's own deeds are said to be theirs.
A word that ends in -ing and names an action.

definition: A person who gives something, such as blood or money.
note: From Anglo-Norman donour, from Old French doneur. It names someone who gives for a cause.
hints: Gives blood at a clinic.
One who gives an organ or funds.

definition: A small, round, fried sweet cake, often with a hole.
note: An American spelling of doughnut, which first meant a small ball of fried dough. Dough comes from Old English dah.
hints: Often found in a box at the office.
A ring of fried dough.

definition: Silly or slow-witted.
note: From dope plus -y. It is an informal word for a foolish person, also the name of one of the seven dwarfs.
hints: One of the seven dwarfs.
Acting stupid or confused.

definition: To feel unsure about something.
note: From Old French douter and Latin dubitare, 'to hesitate'. The b was added in spelling to match the Latin.
hints: What you feel when you aren't sure it's true.
'Beyond a reasonable one' is the standard for a guilty verdict.

definition: A thick mix of flour and water that is baked.
note: From Old English dag, a Germanic word related to the word for 'to knead'. It is also slang for money.
hints: Bread begins as this.
A pizza chef tosses it in the air.

definition: Plain, dull and unfashionable.
note: First appearing around 1581, likely from an earlier word for a poorly dressed woman. It suggests drab or shabby clothing.
hints: A frumpy outfit.
Dressed in old-fashioned, shapeless clothes.

definition: A short wooden peg used to join pieces.
note: From Middle English dowle, of uncertain origin. Carpenters use it to join two boards.
hints: A woodworker uses it to join two boards.
A round wooden rod.

definition: Soft and covered with fine feathers or fluff.
note: From down, from Old Norse dunn, 'soft feathers'. It describes a baby bird or a peach's skin.
hints: A newborn chick's coat.
As soft as a duckling.

definition: Money or property given when a couple marry.
note: From Anglo-Norman douarie, from Medieval Latin dotarium and Latin dos, 'dowry'. It is related to the word dower.
hints: Property a bride's family gives at a wedding.
Jane Austen's characters worry about them.

definition: Twelve.
note: From Old French dozaine, 'a group of twelve', from doze, 'twelve'. Eggs are often sold this way.
hints: How many eggs in a carton.
A baker's thirteen is one more than it.

definition: A first rough version; or a current of cold air.
note: A phonetic spelling of draught, from Middle English draght, 'that which is drawn'. It also means a military call-up.
hints: A first version of an essay.
A cold breeze from an open window.

definition: To let liquid flow out.
note: From Old English dreahnian, 'to strain out'. It names both a pipe and the act of emptying.
hints: What the plug hole does to bath water.
Where the water goes when you pull the plug.

definition: A male duck.
note: From Middle English, from an old word for duck. A dragon was once also called this.
hints: The male of a mallard.
A male duck.

definition: Past tense of drink; also slang for a drink.
note: From Old English dranc, past of drincan. The slang noun spelling began as a pronunciation spelling of drink.
hints: What you did when the glass was emptied.
A form of a word about glasses and sips.

definition: To hang cloth loosely.
note: From Old French draper, 'to weave or make cloth', from drap, 'cloth'. It also names a curtain.
hints: To hang fabric over a chair.
How a gown falls from the shoulders.

definition: Pulled or sketched; also looking tired and thin.
note: The past participle of draw, from Old English dragan, 'to drag or pull'. A drawn face looks as if pulled thin by worry.
hints: Describes a face after sleepless nights.
What a curtain or a sketch may be.

definition: A one-piece outfit; or to put clothes on.
note: From Old French dresser, 'to arrange, put in order'. It meant to set straight before it meant to clothe.
hints: A one-piece garment often worn to a wedding.
Salad ___ing goes on lettuce.

definition: Having had its moisture removed.
note: The past tense of dry, from Old English drygan. Preserving food by drying is among the oldest methods known.
hints: Fruit may be preserved this way.
What the laundry was after hours in the sun.

definition: More dry; less wet.
note: The comparative of dry, from Old English dryge. It is also a spelling of a device that dries clothes or hair.
hints: Comparing a desert with a meadow.
A word that follows 'wetter' in a pair.

definition: To be carried slowly by a current.
note: From Middle English drift, 'act of driving', from Old English. Snow banks and slow movement share the name.
hints: What a boat does when its engine is off.
Snow piles up in these in the winter.

definition: A tool for making holes; or a repeated practice.
note: From Middle Dutch drillen, 'to bore, move in a circle'. The practising sense came from soldiers' repeated exercises.
hints: A dentist uses a small one.
A fire practice at school.

definition: To swallow a liquid.
note: From Old English drincan, from a Germanic verb. It is also the name for the liquid itself.
hints: What you do with a glass of water.
Water or a soda.

definition: To operate a car.
note: From Old English drifan, 'to push, force'. The word first meant to push cattle, not vehicles.
hints: What you do with a steering wheel.
A strong motivation inside a person.

definition: Amusing in an odd, dry way.
note: From French drole, 'comical', from a Middle French word for a merry rascal. It carries a quirky tone.
hints: A dry, understated sense of humour.
Funny in a quietly peculiar way.

definition: A low humming noise; or a remote-controlled flying machine.
note: From Old English dran, the male bee. The buzzing sound gave us the sound, and a lazy person was compared to the non-working bee.
hints: A male honeybee that doesn't work.
A small flying camera with spinning blades.

definition: To let saliva run from the mouth.
note: From earlier drule, probably an alteration of drivel. It comes from a word meaning to dribble.
hints: What a hungry dog does at dinner time.
A baby does it when teething.

definition: To hang or sag downward.
note: From Old Norse drupa, 'to droop', related to drip and drop. Plants do it when thirsty.
hints: A flower does it without water.
Eyelids do it when you are sleepy.

definition: Worthless waste material.
note: From Old English dros, 'dregs, sediment'. Metalworkers skim it from molten metal.
hints: What's skimmed off melted metal.
Rubbish left behind after the good part is taken.

definition: Past tense of drive; also a large moving herd.
note: The past tense comes from Old English drifan. The noun comes from Old English draf, a herd driven along, and survives in 'droves of people'.
hints: What a driver did on the road.
Cattle moved in one of these.

definition: To die from being under water.
note: From Middle English drownen, of obscure origin. It is a verb with a long history of uncertain roots.
hints: What a lifeguard prevents.
To be covered by a flood, or to overwhelm a sound.

definition: A priest in ancient Celtic religion.
note: Via French and Latin Druidae, from Gaulish. The name may mean 'oak-knower', as they were linked with oak trees.
hints: Associated with Stonehenge in popular belief.
A priest of the ancient Celts.

definition: Having had too much alcohol.
note: From Old English druncen, the past participle of drincan. It is both an adjective and a noun.
hints: Wobbly after too many pints.
The opposite of sober.

definition: A machine that removes moisture.
note: From Middle English driere, 'one who dries'. A laundry machine and a hair device both go by it.
hints: Hot machine for wet laundry.
A hairdresser's hot-air device.

definition: In a flat, humorous way with no show of feeling.
note: From dry plus -ly. Dry humour is said to be delivered with a straight face.
hints: The way a deadpan joke is told.
Said with a straight face and no smile.

definition: The territory ruled by a duke or duchess.
note: From Old French duche, from Latin dux, 'leader'. Cornwall and Lancaster are English ones.
hints: The land a duke governs.
Prince Charles held the one in Cornwall.

definition: In a lifeless or slow way.
note: Built from dull plus -ly. Dull originally meant 'slow-witted' before it described blades and colours.
hints: How a blunt knife cuts, or a sleepy voice speaks.
Without sparkle or interest.

definition: A model of a person; or a baby's pacifier.
note: From dumb plus -y. The sense of a fake model, like a shop-window figure, is from a mute, silent stand-in.
hints: A ventriloquist's partner.
A fake used in crash testing a car.

definition: Short and stout.
note: First recorded in 1750, of uncertain origin. It may be related to dumpling.
hints: A squat, round figure.
Describes a plump little teapot.

definition: A person who is slow to learn.
note: Named for John Duns Scotus, a medieval Scottish thinker. His followers were mocked after his ideas fell out of favour.
hints: Wore a pointed cap in the corner of a classroom.
A slow learner.

definition: Dim, dark or shadowy in colour.
note: From dusk plus -y. It describes the half-light of evening or a deep, muted shade.
hints: The colour of the sky just after sunset.
A soft, dark shade, like a plum.

definition: Covered in fine dry particles.
note: From Old English dustig, from dust plus -y. It describes shelves and old books.
hints: An attic that hasn't been cleaned for years.
A bookshelf nobody touches.

definition: A soft quilt for a bed.
note: From French duvet, 'down', from Old French dumet, meaning the soft feathers of young birds. It was originally filled with down.
hints: British word for a bed cover filled with feathers.
Goes inside a cover and keeps you warm in bed.

definition: A very small being in fairy tales; or something much smaller than usual.
note: From Old English dweorg, a Germanic word for the small beings of folklore. It also names small stars and plants.
hints: Snow White lives with seven of them.
A small kind of planet, such as Pluto.

definition: To live in a place.
note: From Old English dwellan, which meant 'to lead astray' or 'delay'. The sense of staying in a place came from lingering.
hints: A poetic way to say 'to live'.
To keep thinking about something, as in 'don't ___ on it'.

definition: Approaching death or the end.
note: From die plus -ing. Die comes from Old Norse deyja.
hints: What a fire is as the embers fade.
Last words are often called a person's this.

definition: Keen and impatient to do something.
note: From Old French aigre, 'sharp', from Latin acer. Eager once meant sharp or sour, and keenness came from that sharpness.
hints: A child waiting at a school gate on the last day.
Describes the beaver who is always busy, in a saying.

definition: A large bird of prey.
note: From Old French aigle, from Latin aquila. It has long been a symbol of strength and empire.
hints: Appears on the American national seal.
A large raptor with a sharp beak.

definition: Before the usual or expected time.
note: From Old English aerlic, from aer, 'before'. It is related to the word ere.
hints: The bird who gets the worm.
The opposite of late.

definition: A stand that holds a painting.
note: From Dutch ezel, 'donkey', from Latin asellus, 'young ass'. It was named because it carries a load like a donkey.
hints: An artist's three-legged stand.
What a canvas rests on while painting.

definition: Having been consumed as food.
note: The past participle of eat, from Old English eten. The -en ending is a trace of older verb forms.
hints: Said of a meal once it is gone.
Follows 'has' or 'have' after dinner.

definition: A person or animal that eats.
note: From Old English etere, built on the verb eat. It is a common ending in words like 'meat-eater'.
hints: A fussy one is picky.
Also a creature defined by its diet.

definition: A hard, dark black wood.
note: From Greek ebenos, ultimately from an Egyptian word for the wood. It has been traded since ancient times.
hints: Piano keys were once made from it.
A very dark colour, like polished wood.

definition: To teach or uplift someone morally or mentally.
note: From Old French edifier and Latin aedificare, 'to build'. To edify someone is to build up their mind or character.
hints: A good lecture should do this.
To improve by instruction.

definition: A white wading bird with long legs.
note: From Anglo-Norman egret, related to the word for heron. The word also names a plume of feathers.
hints: A graceful white bird that stands in water.
A type of heron.

definition: The number after seven.
note: From Old English eahta, from an ancient root shared by many Indo-European languages. It is a very old number word.
hints: A spider has this many legs.
An octopus's arms.

definition: To force out.
note: From Latin eicere, 'to throw out'. It is used for pilots, discs and troublemakers.
hints: What a pilot does from a damaged plane.
What a bouncer does to a rowdy guest.

definition: To fill with great joy.
note: From Latin elatus, 'lifted up'. Feeling elated is feeling uplifted.
hints: A win might do this to a team.
To lift someone's spirits high.

definition: The joint in the middle of your arm.
note: From Old English elnboga, 'ell-bow', where ell means the forearm length and bow means a bend. It is literally the bend of the arm.
hints: You can bend it to flex your arm.
What you use to nudge someone gently.

definition: An older person; or the older of two.
note: From Old English eldra, 'older', from a Germanic root. In many communities an elder is a respected senior person.
hints: An older sibling is this.
A respected senior member of a community.

definition: To choose by voting.
note: From Latin electus, 'chosen', from eligere, 'to pick out'. It is a cousin of the word select.
hints: What citizens do on voting day.
To pick for office.

definition: A sad poem for someone who has died.
note: From Greek elegeia, a poem in a certain metre, which in time came to mean mournful verse. Thomas Gray wrote a famous one in a country churchyard.
hints: A poem for the dead.
A mournful poem recited at a funeral.

definition: Small, delicate and a bit magical.
note: From Old English elfen, 'elf', from elf plus a feminine ending. It describes features like those of an elf.
hints: Describes small pointed ears and a pixie haircut.
Dainty, like a fairy.

definition: To leave out a sound or part of a word.
note: From Latin elidere, 'to strike out'. Speakers elide sounds when saying 'cuppa' for 'cup of'.
hints: What we do to a letter when saying 'fish 'n' chips'.
To omit or skip over.

definition: To run away secretly to get married.
note: From Anglo-Norman aloper, 'to run away', from a Germanic word related to leap. It once simply meant to escape.
hints: Lovers do it without telling their parents.
A secret dash to a wedding chapel.

definition: To escape or avoid someone cleverly.
note: From Latin eludere, 'to evade', from ex- and ludere, 'to play, trick'. It is related to ludicrous and illusion.
hints: A fox does this to the hounds.
How the answer sometimes behaves when you can't remember it.

definition: A message sent by computer.
note: From electronic plus mail. The word electric goes back to Greek elektron, 'amber', since amber was rubbed to produce static.
hints: Sent from one inbox to another.
What you check when you open your computer in the morning.

definition: To fix firmly within something.
note: From en- plus bed. It means to set something in a surrounding mass.
hints: A journalist travels with troops as one.
To set a stone firmly in cement.

definition: The host of an event who introduces the acts.
note: A pronunciation spelling of the letters MC, short for 'master of ceremonies'. It later also came to mean a rapper.
hints: The person with the microphone at an event.
Introduces the acts at a show.

definition: Having nothing inside.
note: From Old English aemtig, 'vacant, free, idle', from a word meaning leisure or free time. A person without work had empty hands.
hints: A glass after the last drop.
The opposite of full.

definition: To make into law, or to act out.
note: From Middle English enacten, from en- and act. It's said of laws and of plays.
hints: A government might do this to a bill.
To perform a scene on stage.

definition: To give money or a gift to support something.
note: From Middle English endowen, 'to provide with assets'. A generous donor might do it for a college.
hints: A rich donor might do this for a university.
To provide with a talent, as 'nature has ___ed her'.

definition: A person or group that is hostile to you.
note: From Old French enemi, from Latin inimicus, 'not a friend'. It is made up of in-, 'not', and amicus, 'friend'.
hints: The opposite of a friend.
A foe in battle.

definition: To take pleasure in something.
note: From Old French enjoier, 'to give joy, rejoice', from en- and joy. Enjoying something is bringing joy into it.
hints: What you wish a diner before they eat.
To take delight in a film.

definition: A feeling of weary boredom.
note: Borrowed from French, from Latin in odio, 'in hatred', the same root that gave us annoy. It means a restless dissatisfaction.
hints: A French word for listless boredom.
A sense of dull, tired boredom.

definition: To follow as a result.
note: From Old French ensuivre, from Latin insequi, 'to follow close upon'. The word is often used in news reports of a chaotic scene.
hints: What happens after a fight breaks out and chaos follows.
To come afterwards.

definition: To go into a place.
note: From Old French entrer, from Latin intrare, 'to go in'. It also means to type or register something.
hints: A key on your keyboard.
Come in through the door.

definition: The act of going in; or a way in.
note: From Old French entree, from Latin intrare. It names a doorway, an item in a list or a contest submission.
hints: A door or gate is one.
A submission to a competition.

definition: A messenger or representative, often of a government.
note: From French envoye, 'sent', from envoyer, 'to send'. The title is for a diplomat ranking just below an ambassador.
hints: Sent abroad with a message from the government.
A diplomat below an ambassador in rank.

definition: A strong glue that hardens when two parts are mixed.
note: From Greek oxys, 'sharp' and a chemical prefix. It is a hard resin used in adhesives and coatings.
hints: Comes in two tubes that you mix together.
A powerful glue for repairing ceramics.

definition: The same in size, value or rights.
note: From Latin aequalis, from aequus, 'level, even'. Equal means level, like a fair scale.
hints: What the sign made of two lines stands for.
Having the same rights as everyone else.

definition: To supply with what is needed.
note: From French equiper, 'to fit out', first said of ships. It may come from a Norse word for a ship.
hints: To fit out a ship or a team.
To give someone the tools for a job.

definition: To rub out or remove.
note: From Latin eradere, 'to scrape out'. It was first used for scraping words off wax tablets.
hints: What a rubber at the end of a pencil does.
To wipe a file or a whiteboard clean.

definition: Upright and standing straight.
note: From Latin erectus, 'upright', from erigere, 'to raise'. It can also mean to build, as in 'erect a tent'.
hints: To put up a tent.
Standing with straight posture.

definition: To wear away slowly.
note: From French eroder and Latin erodere, 'to gnaw away'. Wind and water do it to rock.
hints: What waves do to a cliff over time.
To gradually weaken, as trust might.

definition: A mistake.
note: From Old French error, from Latin error, 'a wandering about', from errare, 'to wander'. A mistake was seen as wandering off the right path.
hints: A typo is one.
A message that pops up when a program fails.

definition: To burst out suddenly.
note: From Latin eruptus, 'broken out', from erumpere, 'to burst out'. It is related to the word rupture.
hints: A volcano does it with lava.
Anger might do it at a dinner table.

definition: A short piece of writing on a topic.
note: From Middle French essai, 'a trial or attempt', a meaning the writer Montaigne gave it in the 1500s. An essay was originally an attempt to work out your thoughts.
hints: Students write one for homework.
A short piece of nonfiction prose.

definition: A kind of chemical compound often with a fruity smell.
note: The name was coined in German, likely as a contraction of a word for vinegar ether. Many fruit flavours are esters.
hints: Chemistry class compound behind fruity smells.
Formed from an acid and an alcohol.

definition: A clear volatile liquid once used as an anaesthetic; or the upper sky.
note: From Greek aither, 'upper air, bright sky'. Ancient thinkers pictured it as the pure air of the heavens.
hints: Old surgeons used it to put patients to sleep.
Something broadcast 'over the ___' goes through the air.

definition: A moral principle that guides behaviour.
note: From Late Latin ethicus, from Greek ethikos, 'moral'. Its plural gives the field of moral philosophy.
hints: A strong work one is a personal value.
A moral rule about right and wrong.

definition: The spirit or values of a community or culture.
note: From Greek ethos, 'character, custom, habit'. Aristotle used it for a speaker's character as a way of persuading.
hints: A company's guiding values.
The characteristic spirit of a culture.

definition: A short piece of music for practising a skill.
note: Borrowed from French etude, 'study', in the 1830s. Chopin and Liszt wrote famous ones.
hints: Pianists practise one to improve technique.
French for 'study'.

definition: Something that happens, especially a planned occasion.
note: From Latin eventus, 'an occurrence', from evenire, 'to happen, come out'. It is related to the word venture.
hints: A concert or a wedding.
Anything that takes place at a particular time.

definition: Each one of a group, without leaving any out.
note: From Old English aefre aelc, meaning 'ever each'. It is a blend of the words that gave us ever and each.
hints: All of them, one at a time.
A word that often comes before 'single'.

definition: To force someone to leave their home.
note: From Latin evictus, 'conquered completely', the same word as evince. In law it meant to recover property by judgment.
hints: What a landlord may do if the rent isn't paid.
To throw tenants out for not paying.

definition: To bring a memory or feeling to mind.
note: From French evoquer and Latin evocare, 'to call out'. It is related to voice.
hints: A smell that takes you back to childhood.
To call up a feeling, as music can.

definition: Precisely correct.
note: From Latin exactus, 'perfected, measured', from exigere, 'to demand, measure'. It is used of measurements and times.
hints: The ___ amount of change needed.
Not approximate.

definition: To praise highly or raise in rank.
note: From Old French exalter and Latin exaltare, 'to raise up'. It is an elevated word for lifting up.
hints: What worshippers do to their god.
To lift someone to a higher position.

definition: To be outstanding at something.
note: From Latin excellere, 'to rise, surpass', built from ex-, 'out' and a root meaning to be high. Spreadsheets borrowed the name.
hints: To be better than the rest.
What a top student does in class.

definition: Forced absence from your home country.
note: From Old French exil and Latin exilium, from exul, 'banished person'. Napoleon was sent to Elba and later St Helena.
hints: What happens to a banished ruler.
Napoleon spent his last years in it.

definition: To be real, to have being.
note: From French exister and Latin existere, 'to stand forth', from ex- and sistere, 'to set, place'. To exist is to stand out into being.
hints: Dragons are said not to.
To be alive or real.

definition: To force out.
note: From Latin expellere, 'to drive out', from ex- and pellere, 'to drive'. Schools and bodies do it.
hints: A school can do it to a student who misbehaves.
To drive away or throw out, as a diplomat.

definition: To praise enthusiastically.
note: From Latin extollere, 'to lift up, raise high'. It is a more formal way of praising.
hints: To sing someone's virtues.
To praise someone highly.

definition: To rejoice greatly, especially in triumph.
note: From Middle French exulter and Latin exsultare, 'to leap up', from salire, 'to jump'. It's a joy that makes you leap.
hints: What a winning team does on the pitch.
To rejoice in victory.

definition: A short story with animals that teaches a lesson.
note: From Old French fable and Latin fabula, 'story', from fari, 'to speak'. Aesop is the best-known author of them.
hints: The tortoise and the hare is one.
A story with a moral at the end.

definition: One of the flat faces of a cut gem; or an aspect.
note: From French facette, 'little face', a diminutive of face. A cut gem sparkles through many small faces.
hints: A diamond cutter polishes each one.
One side of a complex issue.

definition: Weak or barely noticeable; or to pass out briefly.
note: From Old French faint, 'feigned, sluggish', from feindre, 'to feign'. A faint sound is feeble, and a swoon is a failure of strength.
hints: A sound you can barely hear.
To pass out for a moment from heat.

definition: A tiny magical creature with wings.
note: From Old French faerie, 'enchantment', from fae, 'fairy', from Latin fata, 'the fates'. It first named the land of fays, then its inhabitants.
hints: Tinker Bell is one.
Visits under your pillow to collect a tooth.

definition: Strong trust or belief.
note: From Old French feid and Latin fides, 'trust, belief'. It is related to the word fidelity.
hints: 'Leap of ___' means trusting without proof.
Religion or deep trust in a person.

definition: Not true or not real.
note: From Old English fals and Latin falsus, 'deceived, mistaken'. It names things untrue or fake.
hints: The opposite of true.
What a lie is.

definition: Elaborate or high-class; or to like.
note: A contraction of fantasy, from Greek phantasia. It first meant the imagination, then a liking, then something elaborate.
hints: A formal restaurant might be this.
Decorated or showy.

definition: A comedy full of ridiculous situations.
note: From French farce, 'stuffing', a cooking term. Comic interludes were 'stuffed' into serious religious plays.
hints: A silly play with slamming doors and mistaken identities.
A ridiculous situation.

definition: Causing death.
note: From Middle French fatal, from Latin fatalis, 'of fate'. Something fated could not be escaped.
hints: A ___ error is one that ends everything.
A disease that kills.

definition: Blame; or a defect.
note: From Old French faute, from Vulgar Latin fallita, 'shortcoming', related to fail. A fault is a failing.
hints: 'It's not my ___' is a common excuse.
A crack in the earth where earthquakes happen.

definition: The animals of a region or period.
note: From New Latin, from Fauna, a Roman goddess and sister of Faunus, god of forests. Linnaeus adopted it as a counterpart to flora.
hints: Flora's partner when describing an ecosystem.
All the animals of a place.

definition: A kind act for someone.
note: From Old French favor and Latin favor, from favere, 'to be kind'. 'Ask a ___' means to request a kindness.
hints: Doing someone a good turn.
Something you ask a friend to do for you.

definition: A large, special meal.
note: From Old French feste and Latin festa, 'holiday'. It is a cousin of fiesta and festival.
hints: A banquet to celebrate.
Thanksgiving dinner.

definition: An informal word for a man or a guy.
note: A casual spelling of fellow, which comes from an Old Norse word for a business partner. It sounds like relaxed speech.
hints: A chatty name for a man.
A pal might be called a good one.

definition: The thigh bone.
note: Borrowed directly from Latin femur, 'thigh'. It is the longest and strongest bone in the body.
hints: Between hip and knee.
The longest bone in your body.

definition: A barrier around land.
note: Short for defence, from Old French defens. It also names sword fighting and a person who sells stolen goods.
hints: Made of wooden posts around a garden.
Sword fighting takes this name.

definition: A boat that carries people across water.
note: From Old English ferian, 'to carry'. The verb came first, before the boat service.
hints: Crosses a river with cars and passengers.
The way to get to an island without a bridge.

definition: Relating to an unborn baby in the womb.
note: From fetus plus -al. Fetus is a Latin word meaning 'offspring'. A fetal position is curled up tightly, with knees tucked in.
hints: A curled-up sleeping posture.
Kind of position a worried person may curl into.

definition: To go and bring back.
note: From Middle English fecchen, 'to get and bring back'. A dog does it with a stick.
hints: What you tell a dog to do with a ball.
To go and bring back something.

definition: Smelling very bad.
note: From Latin fetidus, from fetere, 'to stink'. It is a literary word for a foul odour.
hints: A swamp can have this smell.
Rotten, like old rubbish.

definition: An unborn baby in the later stages of pregnancy.
note: A learned borrowing from Latin fetus, 'offspring'. It is a doublet of fawn.
hints: An unborn child.
What a doctor sees on a pregnancy scan.

definition: A body temperature higher than normal.
note: From Old English fefer and Latin febris, 'fever'. It is a common sign of illness.
hints: A sign you may have a cold.
A thermometer shows it.

definition: A smaller number of.
note: From few plus -er. The old rule says fewer goes with things you can count.
hints: Used with countable things like apples.
A grammar pedant corrects 'less'.

definition: A thin thread of material; or roughage in food.
note: From French fibre, from Latin fibra. It also describes nutrients that help digestion.
hints: Whole grains are rich in it.
A thin strand, as in cloth or nerves.

definition: A plant in the fig family, often grown indoors.
note: Borrowed from Latin ficus, 'fig'. Houseplants like the rubber tree are of this genus.
hints: A potted rubber plant.
In the same genus as the fig.

definition: An open area of land, often with crops or sports.
note: From Old English feld, 'open country'. It is a very old Germanic word.
hints: Cows graze in it.
Where a football game is played.

definition: An evil spirit; or a wicked person.
note: From Old English feond, 'enemy'. It is related to the word foe's older forms.
hints: A demon in a horror story.
A wicked person; also an obsessive addict, as in 'sweet-toothed ___'.

definition: Burning, or full of passion.
note: From Middle English fyry, from fyr, 'fire', plus -y. It describes flames or tempers.
hints: Describes a hot-headed temper.
Red like flames.

definition: Number five in a sequence.
note: From Old English fifta, which came from fif, 'five'. The 'th' ending turns a number into an order.
hints: The one after the fourth.
A music interval, or a bottle size in the US.

definition: The number after forty-nine.
note: From Old English fiftig, from fif plus -tig, meaning 'tens'. Half of one hundred.
hints: Half of a hundred.
A big birthday for many.

definition: To struggle against someone with force.
note: From Old English feohtan, 'to fight, combat', a very old Germanic word. It covers punches, wars and campaigns alike.
hints: Boxers do it in a ring.
A pillow one is a playful kind.

definition: A person who files papers or submits documents.
note: From file plus -er. The word file comes from Latin filum, 'thread', because papers were once threaded on a string.
hints: Someone who sorts papers into cabinets.
Submits a tax return on time.

definition: A boneless cut of meat or fish.
note: From French filet, 'thread' or 'small band'. It is a spelling of fillet that keeps its French look.
hints: A tender cut on a fancy menu.
Mignon is the cut that often follows it on menus.

definition: A young female horse.
note: From Old Norse fylja, related to foal. It names a horse that has not yet reached full age.
hints: A young mare, not yet grown.
The female of a foal.

definition: Thin and see-through, like a film.
note: From film plus -y. Film comes from Old English filmen, meaning 'membrane' or 'thin skin'.
hints: How a gauzy curtain looks.
A thin layer, like a veil.

definition: Disgusting dirt.
note: From Old English fylth, from foul plus -th. It is the noun for the quality of being foul.
hints: What a garbage heap is covered in.
Dirt of the most revolting kind.

definition: Coming at the end.
note: From Old French final and Latin finalis, 'of the end', from finis, 'end'. It is the last of a series.
hints: The last match of a tournament.
The exam at the end of a term.

definition: A small seed-eating songbird.
note: From Old English finc, a Germanic word thought to imitate the bird's call. Darwin studied those on the Galapagos.
hints: Darwin made them famous in the Galapagos.
A small, colourful songbird.

definition: Of better quality, or thinner and more delicate.
note: The comparative of fine, which came from Old French fin, 'perfect' or 'pure'. The things in life are sometimes called the 'finer things'.
hints: Comparing two cuts of cloth.
The 'things in life' idiom often uses it.

definition: Coming before all others.
note: From Old English fyrst, a superlative form meaning 'foremost'. It is related to the word for 'fore'.
hints: The one at the front of the line.
Gold medal position.

definition: Smelling of fish; or suspicious.
note: From fish plus -y. The sense of suspicious comes from the smell of something gone off.
hints: A poor alibi may seem this.
Describes a story that doesn't add up.

definition: Someone who arranges things or repairs problems, sometimes shadily.
note: From fix plus -er. In film and journalism, a fixer arranges local contacts for visiting crews. It also names a photographic chemical.
hints: A person who arranges things quietly.
Also a darkroom chemical that sets a photo.

definition: Full of bubbles.
note: From fizz plus -y. The word imitates the sound of bubbles escaping.
hints: A cola is described this way.
Sparkling water is this.

definition: A long, narrow sea inlet between steep cliffs.
note: From Norwegian fjord, from Old Norse fjordr, related to ford. Norway is famous for them.
hints: Norway's coast is full of them.
A deep water channel cut by a glacier.

definition: A press agent; also a barrage of criticism.
note: Used in the US for a publicist, a sense whose origin is uncertain. Do not confuse it with 'flak', the anti-aircraft fire.
hints: Defends a celebrity to reporters.
Spokesperson for hire.

definition: To wave one's arms wildly.
note: From Middle English flayle, a tool for threshing grain, from Old English fligel. A flailing arm swings like that tool.
hints: What you do with your arms when you slip.
A farm tool once used to beat the grain.

definition: A natural talent or stylish ability.
note: From Old French flair, 'scent', from flairier, 'to smell'. A flair was first a nose for something.
hints: Style or a knack for doing things well.
A chef with a natural gift for presentation.

definition: Breaking off in thin pieces; or unreliable.
note: From flake plus -y. The sense of unreliable is informal and describes someone who cancels plans.
hints: A pastry like a croissant is this.
A friend who cancels at the last minute.

definition: The visible, glowing part of a fire.
note: From Old French flamme, from Latin flamma. It also names an old sweetheart.
hints: Flickers from a candle.
What a match lights.

definition: The side of an animal or army.
note: From Old French flanc, probably of Frankish origin. A flank steak is cut from the side of the animal.
hints: An army tries to attack the enemy's.
The side of a horse's body.

definition: A sudden brief burst of light.
note: Partly from Middle English flasshen, 'to sprinkle, splash', likely imitative. It also means a very short time.
hints: A camera makes one in the dark.
Lightning does it in a storm.

definition: A narrow-necked bottle.
note: From Old English flasce and Medieval Latin flasco, 'bottle'. It names a lab vessel and a pocket bottle.
hints: A scientist heats one over a flame.
A small metal bottle for a hot drink.

definition: A tiny spot or mark.
note: From Old Norse flekkr, 'spot'. It is often used for specks of paint or colour.
hints: A tiny speck of paint on a shirt.
A small spot of colour.

definition: A group of ships or vehicles; or swift.
note: From Old English fleot, 'ship', related to float. The adjective sense, 'swift', has a separate Norse origin.
hints: A navy's ships all together.
A taxi company's cars.

definition: The soft part of a body.
note: From Old English flaesc, a Germanic word. It is the soft tissue covering the bones.
hints: The part of a fruit you eat.
What lies between skin and bone.

definition: A quick light movement or touch.
note: From Middle English flykke, 'a light blow'. It is imitative, like a snap of the fingers.
hints: What you do to a switch.
A film is also called one.

definition: To throw something carelessly; or a brief affair.
note: From Middle English fling, from a Norse source. Another sense is a brief romance.
hints: To toss a hat in the air.
A short and carefree romance.

definition: A hard grey stone that makes sparks when struck.
note: From Old English flint, a Germanic word. Early fire-lighters and guns used it.
hints: Early people struck it with steel to make a spark.
A stone used with a firestarter.

definition: To rest on top of liquid without sinking.
note: From Old English flotian, 'to float'. It is related to fleet.
hints: What a cork does in water.
A parade vehicle is called this.

definition: A group of birds or sheep.
note: From Old English flocc, 'group of people or animals'. It was once used for people as well.
hints: Sheep gather in one.
Birds fly in one.

definition: An overflow of water onto land.
note: From Old English flod, related to flow. It also means any overwhelming amount.
hints: Noah's story features a great one.
What heavy rain may cause by a river.

definition: The surface you walk on indoors.
note: From Old English flor, 'floor, pavement, deck'. It also names the level of a building.
hints: Opposite of ceiling.
A level in a tall building.

definition: The plants of a region.
note: From Latin Flora, a Roman goddess of flowers. It is the plant counterpart of fauna.
hints: Fauna's plant-loving partner.
All the plants of a place.

definition: A thread used to clean between teeth.
note: Of unclear origin, perhaps from French floche, 'tuft of wool'. It also names soft silk fibre.
hints: Dentists tell you to use it daily.
Candy spun from sugar is named for it.

definition: Ground grain, used for baking.
note: The same word as flower, because flour was 'the flower', or finest part, of the meal. The spellings only separated in the 1800s.
hints: What bread is baked from.
Wheat is ground into it.

definition: To openly disregard a rule.
note: Perhaps from Middle English flouten, 'to play the flute', hence to mock. It is often mixed up with flaunt.
hints: A driver may do this to a speed limit.
To show contempt for a law.

definition: Having travelled through the air; the past participle of fly.
note: From Old English flogen, past participle of fleogan, 'to fly'. A bird that has left the nest is said to have this.
hints: What a bird has done once it has left.
Follows 'has' or 'have' for a trip by air.

definition: Soft light material like down.
note: From earlier floow, 'down, nap, lint', from West Flemish. It also means a minor mistake or trivial content.
hints: What a pillow is stuffed with.
A cat's loose hair on a sofa.

definition: A substance that flows.
note: From Latin fluidus, from fluere, 'to flow'. It covers liquids and gases.
hints: Water or air is this.
Neither a solid nor held in a fixed shape.

definition: A narrow channel carrying water.
note: From Old French flum and Latin flumen, 'river', from fluere, 'to flow'. Water parks borrowed it for rides.
hints: A log ride at a theme park goes down one.
A man-made channel for carrying water.

definition: To fail an exam or class.
note: Of uncertain origin, perhaps related to funk or flinch. It is American student slang from the 1800s.
hints: What a student does with a bad grade.
The opposite of pass.

definition: To turn red; or to clean with rushing water.
note: Of uncertain origin; one sense is to startle birds from cover. Flush also means level, or having plenty of money.
hints: What you do to a toilet.
Your face does this when you blush.

definition: A woodwind played by blowing across a hole.
note: From Old French flaute, of uncertain origin. Champagne is served in a tall glass of the same name.
hints: The Pied Piper played one.
A slim wind instrument.

definition: Something or someone that flies; also a paper handbill.
note: Built from fly plus -er. The paper sense, a leaflet handed out in the street, is a separate later use.
hints: A thin paper handed out on the street.
A frequent one collects airline miles.

definition: Full of foam or froth.
note: From Old English famig, 'frothy', built from foam plus -y. Beer, surf and a shaken soda can all be this.
hints: Describes the head on a beer.
Surf or soap suds might look this way.

definition: Relating to a point of attention.
note: From focus plus -al, borrowed from New Latin. It's used for the main point.
hints: A ___ point is the centre of attention.
Describing the main point of a camera lens.

definition: The point of attention or clarity.
note: From Latin focus, 'hearth, fireplace', related to fuel. Kepler used it for the point where light converges.
hints: What you adjust on a camera.
To concentrate on one thing.

definition: Covered in thick mist; or vague.
note: From fog plus -y, originally meaning 'covered in long grass or marshy'. Foggy now describes mist or confused thoughts.
hints: A morning when you can barely see ahead.
How your memory feels when you're tired.

definition: To pass off something unwanted on someone.
note: Probably from old Dutch vuisten, 'to take in the hand', from vuist, 'fist'.
hints: A seller might do this with a worthless item.
To force an unwanted thing on someone sneakily.

definition: A foolish act or idea.
note: From Old French folie, 'madness', from fol, 'mad'. It also names a decorative building with no use.
hints: A rash plan that was bound to fail.
A tower built just for show on an estate.

definition: A short, bold venture into new territory.
note: From Middle English forrayen, 'to pillage', from a word for a raider. It began as a military raid.
hints: A raid into enemy land.
A first try at a new field, like a chef's into baking.

definition: Strength or power.
note: From Old French force and Late Latin fortia, from Latin fortis, 'strong'. It also names a push or pull in physics.
hints: What Jedi use in Star Wars.
A push or pull that moves an object.

definition: To do without something.
note: From Middle English forgon, 'to pass up', from Old English forgan. The for- is the same as in forbid.
hints: To skip dessert, for example.
To give up a pleasure.

definition: Something someone does especially well.
note: From French fort, 'strong', influenced by Italian forte, from Latin fortis. In music, it means to play loudly.
hints: Cooking is her ___, you might say.
A musical direction meaning loud.

definition: Onward or outward.
note: From Old English forth, 'forward'. It appears in 'back and ___' and in old phrases like 'go ___ and multiply'.
hints: What goes with 'back and' in a phrase.
The word in 'set ___' on a journey.

definition: The number after thirty-nine.
note: From Old English feowertig, 'four tens'. It is built from four and the old word -tig meaning tens.
hints: Twice twenty.
Ali Baba had that many thieves.

definition: A place or meeting for public discussion.
note: From Latin forum, 'marketplace, public place'. The Roman Forum was the heart of the city. It is also an online discussion board.
hints: A place for open discussion online.
The central square of ancient Rome.

definition: Past tense of find; also, to establish an institution.
note: The past tense comes from Old English fand. The verb meaning 'to establish' comes from Latin fundare, 'to lay a base', and is a different word.
hints: What you did once you discovered the lost keys.
A word that also means to start a company.

definition: An entrance hall in a building.
note: Borrowed from French foyer, 'hearth', from Latin focus. In French it first meant the fireplace room where actors warmed up.
hints: The room just inside the front door.
Where a theatre audience gathers at interval.

definition: Weak and easily hurt.
note: From Old French fraile, from Latin fragilis, 'breakable'. It is a cousin of fragile.
hints: An elderly person who needs assistance.
Easily broken or damaged.

definition: A structure that holds something in place.
note: From Old English framian, 'to be helpful, profit'. The Middle English sense was to construct or put together.
hints: What a picture hangs in.
A bed's supporting structure.

definition: Deliberate trickery for gain.
note: From Old French fraude and Latin fraus, 'deceit, injury'. It has been recorded since 1345.
hints: Selling a fake painting as real is this.
A crime of lying to get money.

definition: Something very unusual.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may come from a Germanic word meaning quick or bold. It first meant a sudden whim.
hints: A ___ storm hits without warning.
An unusual accident.

definition: More free; with fewer limits.
note: The comparative of free, from Old English freo. The same word also names someone who sets another free.
hints: Comparing two kinds of liberty.
A word one might use for a bird out of its cage.

definition: New or not stale.
note: From Old English fersc, 'fresh, pure, sweet'. It once described water as well as food.
hints: Bread straight from the oven.
The opposite of stale.

definition: A member of certain religious orders who live among the people.
note: From Old French frere, from Latin frater, 'brother'. Friars owned nothing and begged, unlike monks who stayed in one monastery.
hints: Like a monk, but more often out among the public.
Tuck is the famous one in Sherwood Forest.

definition: Cooked in hot oil or fat.
note: The past tense of fry, from Old French frire, from Latin frigere, 'to roast or fry'. In slang it also means worn out.
hints: How chicken or eggs may be served.
Cooked in a pan with oil.

definition: A decorative gathered edge of fabric.
note: Of uncertain origin. 'No-___s' means a plain service without extras.
hints: A pleated edge on a dress.
An unnecessary extra.

definition: To search someone by patting down.
note: From Middle French frisque, 'lively, merry'. A frisky animal skips about, and then to pat someone's clothes was added.
hints: What a security guard may do to you.
To skip about playfully, as a puppy does.

definition: A state of being broken, used in 'on the fritz'.
note: The phrase is first recorded in 1902. Its origin is unknown, though the German name Fritz has been suggested.
hints: What a machine does when it is going wrong.
Found in an idiom about broken machines.

definition: The leaf of a fern or palm.
note: Borrowed from Latin frons, 'leafy branch'. It is usually seen with ferns and palms.
hints: What a palm tree waves.
A large feathery leaf.

definition: The forward-facing part.
note: From Old French front and Latin frons, 'forehead'. The face of something was its forehead.
hints: The opposite of back.
Where a battle line is drawn.

definition: A mass of small bubbles.
note: From Old Norse frodha, 'froth, foam'. It is also used for trivial matters.
hints: The top of a cappuccino.
Sea foam on a wave.

definition: To wrinkle your brow in displeasure.
note: From Middle English frounen, 'to frown', with an old sense of a threatening look. The opposite of a smile.
hints: The opposite of a smile.
What your face does when you're annoyed.

definition: The sweet seed-bearing part of a plant.
note: From Latin fructus, 'enjoyment, produce'. It also means a result, as in the fruits of labour.
hints: An apple or a pear.
