What a tree produces.

definition: A soft, sweet candy; or to avoid being exact.
note: Probably a variant of fadge, 'to fit together'. The verb means to bend facts and the candy sense came from mixing.
hints: Chocolate treat sold in slabs.
To fake or bend the truth.

definition: A piece of music in which voices chase each other.
note: From Italian fuga, 'flight', from Latin fugere, 'to flee'. The voices seem to flee and pursue one another.
hints: Bach wrote famous ones.
A state of amnesia where someone wanders off.

definition: Completely; to the greatest extent.
note: From Old English fullice, built from full plus -ly. It is used to stress that nothing is missing.
hints: Not partly, but the whole way.
Often goes before 'booked' or 'aware'.

definition: Mushrooms, moulds and yeasts, as a group; the plural of fungus.
note: Borrowed from Latin, where fungi is the plural of fungus. Fungi form their own kingdom, separate from plants and animals.
hints: Mushrooms and moulds belong to this group.
The plural of a word for a mushroom.

definition: Stylishly offbeat; or smelly.
note: From funk plus -y. Funk once meant a strong smell, then a style of music with a heavy groove.
hints: Describes music with a heavy bass groove.
Eccentric and cool.

definition: Amusing; or strange.
note: From fun plus -y. It describes jokes, but also something odd, as in 'a funny smell'.
hints: What a good joke is.
Odd, as in 'that's ___ - the door was open'.

definition: A wave of public outrage or excitement.
note: From Latin furor, 'rage, madness', from furere, 'to rage'. It is related to the word fury.
hints: The public outcry over a scandal.
A burst of uproar.

definition: Covered with soft hair.
note: From fur plus -y. It describes animals and toys.
hints: A teddy bear is.
Soft and covered in fur.

definition: Hard to please or too concerned with small details.
note: From fuss plus -y. It describes babies who cry and people who care too much about details.
hints: A child who won't eat vegetables.
Too particular about tiny details.

definition: Covered with soft short fibres; or unclear.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may be from fuzz plus -y, or the other way around. It also describes a blurry picture.
hints: A peach's skin is this way.
A blurry photo is this.

definition: An embarrassing mistake in public.
note: Borrowed from French gaffe, 'blunder', and a doublet of gaff. Politicians dread making one.
hints: Calling someone by the wrong name, perhaps.
A social blunder.

definition: In a cheerful, lively way.
note: Built from gay plus -ly. Gay came from Old French gai, and long meant 'merry' and 'bright'.
hints: How a bright flag might wave.
In a lively and bright mood.

definition: A person who plays games, especially video games.
note: From game plus -er. The word now mostly means a video game enthusiast.
hints: Someone with a headset and a console.
A person with high scores.

definition: The third letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: Borrowed from Greek gamma. In science it names rays of high energy.
hints: Comes after alpha and beta.
A type of ray emitted by radioactive material.

definition: The complete range of something.
note: From gamma ut, a medieval note name that meant the lowest note of the scale. It grew to mean the whole range.
hints: 'To run the ___' is to experience everything from one end to the other.
The full range of notes in a scale.

definition: Full of gas.
note: From gas plus -y. It describes a fizzy drink or a bloated stomach.
hints: A can of soda that's been shaken.
Bloated after beans.

definition: Flashy and tasteless.
note: From Middle English gaudi, from a word for an ornament or trinket.
hints: A very bright, over-decorated outfit.
Too flashy for good taste.

definition: An instrument for measuring.
note: From Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French gauger, 'to measure'. To gauge is also to estimate someone's mood.
hints: A fuel one shows how much is left.
To estimate how people feel.

definition: Thin and haggard.
note: From Middle English gaunt, 'lean, slender', of uncertain origin. It's used for people who look drawn and hungry.
hints: A face worn from illness.
Looking bony and tired.

definition: A thin, see-through fabric.
note: From French gaze, from Arabic qazz, 'silk'. It is used in bandages and curtains.
hints: A bandage wrapped over a cut.
A very light, open-weave cotton.

definition: A small mallet used by a judge or chair.
note: From the Old English gafol, 'tribute, rent', for one sense; the mallet's own origin is uncertain. Auctioneers use one too.
hints: A judge bangs one to call order.
An auctioneer uses it to close a sale.

definition: Awkward and clumsy in movement.
note: From gawk plus -y. A gawky teenager hasn't yet grown into their limbs.
hints: A teenager who has grown too quickly.
All elbows and knees.

definition: A person who looks steadily at something.
note: Built from gaze plus -er. Stargazers are the best known kind.
hints: Might be found staring at the sky.
The 'star' kind looks upward at night.

definition: A small, mostly nocturnal lizard with sticky toe pads.
note: English probably took it from Dutch gekko in the 1700s. Many geckos can climb smooth walls and ceilings.
hints: A small lizard found in warm places.
Known for walking up walls and glass.

definition: Showing an enthusiastic, slightly awkward devotion to technical or niche interests.
note: Built from geek plus the -y ending. It was once an insult but is now often worn proudly.
hints: Describes someone absorbed in gadgets or fandoms.
Said of a person who loves sci-fi and coding.

definition: A magical spirit who grants wishes.
note: From French génie, which was matched to the Arabic jinn. English picked it up through translations of the Arabian Nights.
hints: Lives in a lamp in fairy tales.
Often grants three wishes.

definition: A category of art, music or writing with shared style.
note: Borrowed unchanged from French, from the same Latin root as gender and genus.
hints: Western, horror and romance are examples.
A label that sorts books and films.

definition: A spirit said to feed on the dead.
note: Borrowed from French, which got it from Arabic ghul via Persian. It was first a desert demon in Arabic stories.
hints: Haunts graveyards in horror stories.
A creature that robs graves.

definition: A being of enormous size, especially in myth.
note: Through Old French from Latin gigas, which came from Greek gigas, the name of the mythical race that fought the gods.
hints: Jack climbed a beanstalk to meet one.
Anything much bigger than its kind.

definition: Dizzy, or lightheaded with excitement.
note: Middle English gidi once meant mad or possessed by a spirit, long before it became merely dizzy.
hints: How a fast spin on a roundabout can leave you.
Feeling silly with delight.

definition: Seen as typical of girls; also fussily pretty.
note: Built from girl plus -y. Girl itself arrived in Middle English meaning a young person of either sex.
hints: A word for things like pink and glitter.
A description of a sort of style.

definition: The distance around something, such as a tree or a waist.
note: From Old Norse gjord, a band. The original sense was the strap that holds a saddle on a horse.
hints: The measurement around a thick trunk.
The strap that keeps a saddle in place.

definition: Handed over; also taken for granted.
note: The past participle of give, from Old English gifen. As a noun it means something taken as true without proof.
hints: What a present is once handed over.
A word for an assumption you do not question.

definition: A person who gives.
note: From Middle English, built from give plus -er. It is the opposite of a taker.
hints: Someone who donates.
Contrasts with 'taker' in a saying.

definition: An organ that makes and releases substances such as hormones or sweat.
note: From French glande, tracing to Latin glandula, a small acorn. The Latin word was used for throat glands.
hints: The thyroid is one in your neck.
It secretes something the body needs.

definition: A fierce stare, or harsh bright light.
note: From Middle English glaren, probably tied to shining. It was used for brightness before it described angry looks.
hints: What an annoyed person gives you.
Sunlight on a windscreen can cause it.

definition: A shiny coating, as on pottery or a doughnut.
note: From Middle English glasen, from the word glass. Glazed pottery gets a thin glassy surface.
hints: Painted onto clay before it is fired.
What makes a ham or pastry shine.

definition: A soft, brief flash of light.
note: From Middle English glem, a shaft of light or radiance. It can also mean a faint sign, as in a gleam of hope.
hints: What polished silver does in the sun.
A faint light, or a spark in the eye.

definition: To gather bit by bit, as information or leftover grain.
note: Middle English glenen meant to gather the grain left behind by reapers. The sense later widened to picking up facts.
hints: Poor villagers once did this in harvested fields.
Picking up clues from scattered sources.

definition: To move smoothly and effortlessly.
note: From Old English glidan. It describes birds and aircraft moving without power.
hints: What an eagle does on rising air.
Skaters do it across ice.

definition: A tiny flash of reflected light.
note: Borrowed from Scots glint, likely from Old Norse. It also names a quick sparkle of emotion in the eyes.
hints: The flash from a blade or coin.
A sparkle in someone's eye.

definition: To enjoy your own success or someone else's failure openly.
note: Middle English likely took it from Old Norse glotta, to grin scornfully. It still carries a smug grin.
hints: Winners should not do this.
Rubbing a rival's loss in his face.

definition: A sphere, especially a model of the Earth.
note: Via French from Latin globus, a ball. It is also used for the planet itself.
hints: A spinning map on a stand.
Another word for the whole world.

definition: Darkness, or a mood of heavy sadness.
note: From Old English glom, meaning twilight. The dark of dusk became a dark mood.
hints: What a rainy grey day can bring.
Opposite of cheer.

definition: Great honour and fame won by achievement.
note: Via Old French from Latin gloria, meaning fame or renown.
hints: What soldiers and athletes chase.
Often follows 'hallelujah' or 'days of'.

definition: A shine on a surface, or a brief explanation of a word.
note: The shine sense probably came from a Nordic language. The explanation sense is separate, from Greek glossa, tongue.
hints: Used loosely for a shine on a surface.
A shine on lips, paint or nails.

definition: A covering for the hand with separate fingers.
note: From Old English glof. It is an old word, kept almost unchanged for over a thousand years.
hints: Worn to keep hands warm.
Boxers and surgeons both wear them.

definition: A carved symbol or character.
note: Borrowed from French, from Greek gluphe, a carving. Mayan hieroglyphs are a famous example.
hints: Carved on ancient temple walls.
One symbol in a writing system.

definition: To grind the teeth together in anger or pain.
note: Origin uncertain, perhaps imitating the sound. The silent g is kept from older spellings.
hints: Teeth do it in a rage.
Paired with 'wailing' in a biblical phrase.

definition: A small bearded creature of folklore, often a garden figure.
note: From New Latin gnomus, a term used by the physician Paracelsus for earth spirits.
hints: Wears a pointed red hat.
Found standing in lawns.

definition: Devoted to God; pious.
note: From Old English, formed from god plus the -ly ending. It has long described a righteous way of life.
hints: Often said of a very devout person.
The opposite of wicked.

definition: Moving or leaving; also the condition of the ground or progress.
note: From Old English gan, 'to go', with -ing. 'Heavy going' once described muddy ground and came to mean slow progress.
hints: Setting out on a trip.
Ground may be described as 'rough' or 'heavy' for this.

definition: A figure of clay brought to life by magic in Jewish legend.
note: Borrowed from Hebrew golem. The most famous tale concerns a rabbi in Prague.
hints: Made of mud and animated with words.
A lumbering servant that cannot speak.

definition: A mild old-fashioned cry of surprise.
note: A euphemism for God from the 1700s, softened to avoid swearing.
hints: An exclamation your grandfather might use.
Often said as 'Well, ...!'

definition: Someone or something doomed or beyond saving.
note: From gone plus -er, recorded from around 1850.
hints: Said of a plant that will not recover.
You are this if the cliff crumbles.

definition: A treat; or an exclamation of delight.
note: Built from good plus -y, a casual ending. As a noun it means a sweet or small treat; as a cry it is an exclamation of delight.
hints: Something good to eat, in a bag at a party.
A cry a child may make at a treat.

definition: Soft, sticky and messy.
note: Formed from goo plus the -y ending. It can also mean sappy and sentimental.
hints: Describes warm melted cheese or caramel.
A brownie fresh from the oven might be this.

definition: Silly in a harmless, playful way.
note: Built from goof plus -y. It is also the name of a cartoon dog.
hints: Describes a funny grin or a silly walk.
Not serious at all.

definition: A large waterbird with a long neck, related to ducks and swans.
note: From Old English gos, with relatives across the Germanic languages and deeper still. The plural geese is a leftover vowel change.
hints: Flies south in a V formation.
Honks loudly and lays golden eggs in a fable.

definition: A deep narrow valley, or to stuff yourself with food.
note: From Old French, meaning throat. A gorge is a throat cut in the land, and gorging is feeding the throat.
hints: A river may cut one through rock.
What you do at an all-you-can-eat buffet.

definition: To dig or scoop out roughly, or to overcharge.
note: From Old French for a curved chisel. Overcharging sense came later in American use.
hints: A deep scratch in a wooden table.
What a price-hiking seller might do.

definition: A hard-shelled fruit of a vine, such as a pumpkin relative.
note: Via Anglo-Norman from Latin cucurbita. Dried ones were used as bottles and bowls.
hints: Decorative in autumn displays.
Hollowed and dried for use as a container.

definition: A level of quality, or a mark given for schoolwork.
note: From Latin gradus, a step. A grade is a step on a ladder of quality.
hints: What you get on a test.
Fifth in a school year.

definition: To join a shoot onto another plant, or to engage in corrupt gain.
note: Originally from Greek graphein via the Old French word for a stylus, because a cutting looks like a pen. The corruption sense is later.
hints: Gardeners do it to fruit trees.
Skin is moved in this way in surgery.

definition: The legendary cup sought by King Arthur's knights.
note: From Old French graal, meaning cup. It now means any object of a long quest.
hints: Subject of a medieval quest.
Holy, in the legend.

definition: Impressive in size or style.
note: Via Old French from Latin grandis, meaning large.
hints: A piano may be this kind.
Slang for a thousand dollars.

definition: To give or allow, or money given for a purpose.
note: From Old French granter, to promise or agree. It also names funds awarded to researchers.
hints: A wish may be this by a genie.
A scholarship is one kind.

definition: A small juicy fruit that grows in bunches on a vine.
note: Via Old French grappe, a cluster, which was originally a hook for picking fruit.
hints: Crushed to make wine.
Dried, it becomes a raisin.

definition: A diagram showing how quantities relate.
note: A clipping of 'graphic formula', from the 1870s.
hints: Lines and bars on a chart.
Plots one value against another.

definition: To take hold of firmly, or to understand.
note: From Middle English graspen, to grope or feel around. Understanding an idea is likened to getting a hand around it.
hints: What fingers do to a rope.
To finally get what a hard lesson means.

definition: To shred against a rough surface, or to irritate.
note: The noun for an iron frame comes from Latin for a hurdle or lattice. The verb for scraping is a separate word.
hints: Cheese is shredded this way.
A noise that does it to your nerves.

definition: A hole in the ground for a burial, or very serious.
note: From Old English graf, meaning a trench or cave. The serious adjective is a different word, from Latin gravis, heavy.
hints: A churchyard is full of them.
A word to describe a doctor's solemn warning.

definition: A sauce made from the juices of cooked meat.
note: Middle English gravey, perhaps from a word for the sediment of melted fat. Its exact origin is uncertain.
hints: Poured over roast dinners.
Turkey's partner at a holiday table.

definition: To feed on grass, or to scrape the skin lightly.
note: The feeding verb comes from the Old English word for grass. The scratching sense is later and may be a separate use.
hints: What cows do in a field.
A scrape on the knee after a fall.

definition: Very large, or very good.
note: From Old English great, which meant big, thick or coarse. It only later became a word of praise.
hints: Britain is called this in its formal name.
A word of enthusiastic approval.

definition: An excessive desire for more than you need.
note: Back-formed from greedy around 1600.
hints: One of the seven deadly sins.
Wanting more money than you could ever spend.

definition: The colour of grass and leaves.
note: From Old English grene, related to grow and grass. All three come from the same Germanic root.
hints: Sits between yellow and blue.
Signals go on a traffic light.

definition: To welcome someone with words or a gesture.
note: From Old English gretan, to approach or address. It once carried the sense of coming up to someone.
hints: What you do when a guest arrives.
A handshake or a hello does this.

definition: Deep sorrow, especially after a loss.
note: From Old French grief, heavy, from Latin gravis. Grave is the same root.
hints: What follows a bereavement.
Heavy sorrow, or trouble given to someone.

definition: To cook over direct heat on a metal grid.
note: From French gril, ultimately from a Latin word for a small lattice. It can also mean to question someone intensely.
hints: Used for burgers outdoors.
What police may do in an interrogation.

definition: Dirt that is ground in and hard to remove.
note: Middle English grim meant soot on the face. It is also a London music genre.
hints: What builds up on an unwashed window.
A mechanic's hands might be coated in it.

definition: Covered with ground-in dirt.
note: From grime plus -y. Grime comes from Middle Dutch grime, 'soot' or 'dirt'.
hints: How hands look after mechanic's work.
The word for a city window thick with soot.

definition: To crush into small pieces, or a tiring routine.
note: From Old English grindan. The sense of dull daily labour is likened to turning a mill.
hints: What a coffee mill does to beans.
The daily slog of work.

definition: To complain, especially about small things.
note: From Old English gripan, to seize. It has the same root as grip.
hints: What a grumbler does about the food.
A minor complaint.

definition: A low sound made in pain, boredom or disapproval.
note: From Old English granian, to lament or murmur.
hints: How the audience reacts to a bad pun.
Floorboards may make this noise too.

definition: The crease where the thigh meets the lower body.
note: The exact origin is uncertain. Architects also use it for the edge where two vaults intersect.
hints: A muscle strain might occur here.
Part of the body near the hip.

definition: Someone about to marry, or to tend an animal's coat.
note: Short for bridegroom. The verb came from stable servants, who brushed horses.
hints: Stands at the altar beside the bride.
What you do to a horse with a brush.

definition: Disgusting, or total before deductions.
note: From Old French gros, big or thick, from Latin grossus. Gross pay is the large full amount.
hints: What a mouldy sandwich is.
Pay before tax comes off.

definition: A number of people or things gathered together.
note: Through French from Italian gruppo, probably a Germanic word. It first meant a cluster in painting.
hints: A band or a team is one.
Friends who meet regularly.

definition: Thin mortar used to fill gaps between tiles.
note: From Old English grut, coarse meal or dregs. The building material kept the sense of a coarse paste.
hints: Fills the lines between bathroom tiles.
It can go mouldy if damp.

definition: A low, rumbling sound of anger, made in the throat.
note: From Middle English groulen, first used of the bowels rumbling.
hints: A dog makes it to warn you off.
A bear's warning noise.

definition: Fully developed; the past participle of grow.
note: From Old English growan. It is also used for adults, as in 'grown-up'.
hints: Describes what an adult is.
What a seed is after it has sprouted.

definition: A thin porridge of oats or other grain.
note: From Old French gruel, coarse meal. It was food of the poor and the sick.
hints: What Oliver Twist was served.
A meagre watery meal.

definition: Rough and abrupt in manner or voice.
note: From Dutch grof, coarse or rude, in the 1500s.
hints: A grumpy old man's tone.
Describes the billy goats in a fairy tale.

definition: A short, low sound, or a basic infantry soldier.
note: From Old English grunnettan, imitating the pig's noise.
hints: A pig makes it in a pen.
What a teenager answers in place of words.

definition: To protect, or someone who does so.
note: Through Old French from a Germanic root related to ward and warden.
hints: Stands by the palace gate.
Prisons employ them.

definition: A tropical fruit with pink or white flesh and many seeds.
note: From Spanish guayaba, which came from a Taino word. It was recorded in English in the 1500s.
hints: Grows in warm climates.
Often made into paste or juice.

definition: To estimate without full knowledge.
note: Middle English gessen, probably from a Scandinavian word. It once meant to aim or take aim.
hints: What you do when you don't know.
A try at a riddle.

definition: Someone invited to a home, event or hotel.
note: From Old Norse gestr. It shares a root with Latin hostis, which gave host and hostile.
hints: Arrives when you throw a party.
A visitor who stays the night.

definition: An association of craftsmen or merchants in the Middle Ages.
note: From Middle English gilde, from Old Norse gildi, meaning payment. Members paid dues to join.
hints: A medieval group of weavers or masons.
Often found in fantasy role-playing games.

definition: Cunning used to deceive.
note: From Old French guile, deception, via a Frankish word for a trick. It is related to wile.
hints: What a fox is said to have.
A trickster wins by it, not force.

definition: The state of having done wrong, or the feeling that comes with it.
note: From Old English gylt, a crime or fault.
hints: The feeling after a broken promise.
What a jury must decide.

definition: A narrow, steep-sided ravine, often cut by a stream.
note: A word chiefly from American English. Gold-rush stories place prospectors in them.
hints: Prospectors panned in one.
A deep ditch in the mountains.

definition: A narrow channel cut in the ground by flowing water.
note: Origin uncertain, possibly connected with an old word for the throat.
hints: Rain carves one down a hillside.
A narrow ditch beside a road.

definition: A thick Louisiana stew thickened with okra.
note: From Louisiana French gombo, which traces to a Bantu word for okra.
hints: A speciality of New Orleans.
Served over rice with sausage or shrimp.

definition: Sticky or chewy; also a chewy sweet.
note: From gum plus -y. Gum comes from Greek kommi, a tree's sticky sap.
hints: Like a chewy, sticky candy.
Resembling a bear-shaped candy.

definition: A small, colourful freshwater aquarium fish.
note: Named by mistake after Robert Guppy, who sent specimens from Trinidad to London.
hints: A beginner's pet fish.
Gives birth to live young.

definition: Hearty enthusiasm in doing something.
note: From Italian gusto, taste, ultimately from Latin gustus.
hints: Eating a meal with it means relishing every bite.
Sung with it means belting it out.

definition: Blowing in sudden strong bursts.
note: Built from gust plus -y. Gust probably came from Old Norse gustr, 'a blast of wind'.
hints: How wind sounds during a storm.
The weather when umbrellas turn inside out.

definition: A routine you do regularly, often without thinking.
note: From Latin habitus, condition or dress, from habere, to have. A monk's habit is the clothing worn as a routine.
hints: Nail biting can be a bad one.
Something repeated until automatic.

definition: Covered with hair; also risky.
note: From Old English-derived hair plus -y. The informal sense of dangerous is later.
hints: Describes a gorilla's arms.
A tense or scary moment, informally.

definition: To divide into two equal parts.
note: From Old English words for half. The silent l is kept from the older spelling.
hints: What you do with a cake for two people.
Cut an apple down the middle.

definition: Useful, or conveniently near.
note: From Middle English handi, formed on hand. It once meant skilful.
hints: A tool within reach is this.
Said of a person good at fixing things.

definition: Feeling pleasure or contentment.
note: From Middle English hap, meaning luck or chance. To be happy was first to be lucky.
hints: The opposite of sad.
What a smiling face expresses.

definition: Tough and able to endure difficult conditions.
note: From Old French hardi, bold, probably connected to the word for becoming hard.
hints: Describes plants that survive winter frost.
A word for a sturdy mountain pony.

definition: The women's private quarters in a traditional Muslim household.
note: Borrowed from Turkish, from Arabic haram, meaning 'forbidden' or 'protected'. The word carried the idea of a place set apart.
hints: A section of a house set apart.
A word from the Ottoman court.

definition: A mythical bird-woman, or a nagging woman.
note: From Latin harpyia, from Greek harpuiai, meaning snatchers. The creatures grabbed food and people in myth.
hints: A winged monster in Greek stories.
An insulting term for a shrill, grasping person.

definition: Rough, severe or unpleasantly strong.
note: From Middle English harsk, linked to Old Norse harskr, which meant rancid. It later widened to cover anything rough or cruel.
hints: Describes a bitter winter or a stern punishment.
A word for grating light or a cruel remark.

definition: Speed in doing something, often too much of it.
note: Middle English hast, from Old French. A proverb warns that it makes waste.
hints: What a hurried packer shows.
Often followed by 'makes waste'.

definition: To emerge from an egg, or a small door in a floor or deck.
note: The door sense comes from Old English hec, a gate. The egg sense is a separate word of uncertain origin.
hints: What a chick does from its shell.
An opening in a ship's deck.

definition: Someone who dislikes or criticises others out of spite.
note: Built from hate plus -er, and old in English. The slangy modern sense is of a person who sneers at others' success.
hints: The sort who scorns someone's success.
Slang for a negative critic.

definition: To visit a place repeatedly, as a ghost does.
note: From Old French hanter, to frequent. It originally meant just to reside or often visit.
hints: What a ghost does to an old house.
A memory can do it to you.

definition: A safe place, or a sheltered harbour.
note: From Old English haefen, meaning harbour. A port and a refuge were the same idea.
hints: A sheltered bay for ships.
Somewhere you feel safe and protected.

definition: Widespread destruction and chaos.
note: From Old French in the phrase 'cry havoc', a battle signal for soldiers to seize plunder.
hints: A storm can wreak it.
What a toddler loose in a kitchen causes.

definition: A tree that bears edible nuts, or a light brown-green colour.
note: From Old English haesl, with ancient Germanic roots. The eye colour is named after the nut.
hints: Its nuts are used in spread.
A shade of eye between brown and green.

definition: Intoxicating, or exciting to the senses.
note: From Middle English hedi, formed from head plus -y. It first meant headstrong.
hints: Describes strong wine or a thrilling success.
Perfume that goes straight to your head.

definition: Past tense of hear.
note: From Old English heard, the past form of hieran, 'to hear'. It is spelled like 'herd', and the two sound the same.
hints: What your ears did with a sound.
A word that sounds like a flock of cattle.

definition: The muscle that pumps blood, or the seat of feeling.
note: From Old English heorte, with roots shared across Germanic languages and Latin cor.
hints: It beats in your chest.
The shape on a Valentine's card.

definition: To lift or throw with great effort.
note: From Old English hebban, to lift. It also means to retch.
hints: What sailors do hauling a rope.
A struggle to move a heavy trunk.

definition: Weighing a great deal.
note: From Old English hefig, from the root of heave. The heavy thing is what one has to heave.
hints: Opposite of light.
A loaded suitcase might be this.

definition: Large, weighty and powerful.
note: Built from heft, weight, plus -y in the 1800s. The resemblance to German heftig is a coincidence.
hints: Describes a large, weighty parcel.
A burly man with a mighty swing.

definition: A spiral curve like a corkscrew or a coiled spring.
note: Latin helix, from Greek helix, something twisted.
hints: DNA has a double one.
Shape of a spiral staircase.

definition: A common greeting.
note: First recorded in 1826, from earlier holla and hollo. It became the standard telephone greeting in the late 1800s.
hints: A friendly word when meeting.
What you say when you answer the phone.

definition: From this place or time; for this reason.
note: From Middle English hennes, from Old English heonan, away.
hints: Used in phrases like 'a week from now'.
A formal way of saying therefore.

definition: A tall wading bird with a long neck and sharp bill.
note: From Old French, from a Frankish word of Germanic origin.
hints: Stands motionless in shallow water.
Hunts fish with a quick stab.

definition: Having many hills.
note: From Middle English hilly, built from hill plus -y.
hints: A word for rolling countryside.
Not flat; the opposite of a plain.

definition: A joint on which a door or lid swings.
note: From Middle English henge, related to hang. A hinge is something a door hangs on.
hints: What a door swings on.
Squeaks if it needs oil.

definition: A large African river animal; short for hippopotamus.
note: A clipping of hippopotamus, a Greek word meaning 'river horse'.
hints: A massive animal that spends its days in rivers.
Short for a 'river horse'.

definition: A small problem, or a knot or quick fastening.
note: Probably from Middle English hicchen, to move with a jerk. Its origin is obscure.
hints: A snag in the plans.
To thumb a ride, informally.

definition: An activity done for pleasure in spare time.
note: From Middle English hobyn, a small horse. A hobbyhorse was a toy, so the word gradually came to mean a pastime.
hints: Stamp collecting is one.
Something you do for fun after work.

definition: To raise something, especially with ropes or a pulley.
note: An alteration of hoise, from Middle Dutch hisen. It is first a nautical word.
hints: A flag may be pulled up this way.
A crane does it with a heavy load.

definition: An evergreen shrub with spiky leaves and red berries.
note: From Old English holegn. It is associated with Christmas decoration.
hints: A festive door wreath.
Prickly leaves and red berries.

definition: A home run in baseball.
note: Short for 'home run' with an -er ending. It is also the name of an old Hebrew unit of volume.
hints: A big hit that clears the fence.
A baseball hit that sends the runner round all four bases.

definition: A sweet golden fluid made by bees.
note: From Old English hunig, an ancient Germanic word. As an endearment it has been used for centuries.
hints: Spread on toast.
Made in a hive.

definition: Great respect, or a code of moral integrity.
note: From Old French honor, from Latin honor.
hints: A knight's code of conduct.
To pay it is to show respect.

definition: A huge crowd, often moving noisily.
note: From Polish horda and Russian orda, a nomadic tribe's camp. It entered English in the 1500s.
hints: A swarm of tourists.
Zombies come in these.

definition: A large hoofed animal used for riding and pulling loads.
note: From Old English hors, an old Germanic word.
hints: Has a mane and gallops.
Ridden in a race.

definition: A building offering rooms to paying guests.
note: From French hotel, which once meant a town mansion. The word shares a root with hospital and host.
hints: You check into it on holiday.
A porter carries your bags in it.

definition: In an intense or passionate way.
note: From Old English hatlice, built from hot plus -ly. A hotly debated issue stirs up strong feeling.
hints: How an argument may be waged.
Often follows 'disputed' or 'contested'.

definition: A hunting dog, or to pursue persistently.
note: From Old English hund, which was once the general word for dog.
hints: A basset or beagle is one.
Reporters do this to a celebrity.

definition: A building where people live.
note: From Old English hus, a very old Germanic word.
hints: Where a family lives.
It has rooms, a roof and a door.

definition: A small, miserable dwelling.
note: From Middle English hovel, a shed or shelter.
hints: A rundown shack.
The opposite of a mansion.

definition: To hang in the air in one place.
note: From Middle English hoveren, to float or linger.
hints: What a helicopter or hummingbird does.
A wasp lingering above a picnic.

definition: An informal cowboy-style greeting.
note: Shortened from how do you do.
hints: What a Texan might say as hello.
A friendly western hello.

definition: A person, or relating to people.
note: From Latin humanus, probably related to homo, man, with a link to humus, earth.
hints: Not an animal or a robot.
Our species.

definition: Damp with water vapour in the air.
note: From Latin humidus, from umere, to be moist.
hints: A tropical summer day feels it.
Weather that makes your clothes cling.

definition: The quality of being funny.
note: An American spelling of humour, from Latin humor, 'fluid'. Medieval medicine held that four body fluids shaped a person's temperament.
hints: What a joke is meant to have.
Said to be what laughter responds to.

definition: A grunt that shows doubt or annoyance.
note: An exclamation first recorded in the sixteenth century, an imitation of the sound itself.
hints: A noise of disapproval.
A snort from a grumpy person.

definition: Dark organic matter in soil made from rotted plants.
note: Borrowed straight from Latin humus, meaning earth or soil.
hints: Gardeners love it for rich soil.
Decayed leaves become this.

definition: A feeling about something without proof, or to curve the shoulders.
note: Originally a lump or hump, and the verb meant to push. The feeling sense came later.
hints: A gut feeling.
How you sit over a desk with poor posture.

definition: Attractive and muscular; also chunky.
note: Built from hunk plus -y. Hunk meant a big lump before it became slang for a strong, handsome man.
hints: Describes a muscle-bound film star.
Said of a good-looking and strong man.

definition: To move or act quickly.
note: From Middle English horien, to rush, perhaps imitating a buzzing sound.
hints: What you do when you are late.
Opposite of dawdle.

definition: Hoarse and rough, or a strong sled dog.
note: From husk plus -y. A voice was called husky because it sounds as dry as a husk.
hints: A throaty voice.
A dog that pulls sleds in the Arctic.

definition: A small cage for a pet rabbit, or a cabinet.
note: From Middle English hucche, a storage chest.
hints: A rabbit's home in a garden.
A dresser with shelves on top.

definition: Relating to water; also a name for electricity in Canada.
note: From Greek hydor, 'water'. In Canada it names electricity because early power came from hydroelectric dams.
hints: A prefix about water that also stands alone.
A word for the power bill in Canada.

definition: A doglike African carnivore known for its laughing cry.
note: From Greek huaina, via Latin. The name may come from a word for pig.
hints: Scavenges on the savanna.
Known for a cackling call.

definition: Overexcited or overactive.
note: Clipped from hyperactive, with hyper- from Greek huper, 'over' or 'beyond'.
hints: How a child may be after too much sugar.
A word that means 'over'.

definition: In a cold, unfriendly way.
note: Built from icy plus -ly. Icy comes from Old English isig.
hints: How a frosty stare may be given.
Said with no warmth at all.

definition: A perfect standard, or being perfect for a purpose.
note: From Late Latin idealis, meaning existing in idea. An ideal was first something that exists only as a thought.
hints: Perfect weather for a picnic.
What you aim for but rarely reach.

definition: A phrase whose meaning isn't clear from its words alone.
note: From Greek idioma, a peculiarity. 'Kick the bucket' is one.
hints: 'It's raining cats and dogs' is an example.
A figure of speech particular to a language.

definition: A person who does nothing useful with their time.
note: Built from idle plus -er. Idle once meant 'empty' or 'vain'.
hints: Someone lounging about with nothing to do.
A loafer who avoids all work.

definition: A peaceful, charming scene or period, often rural.
note: From Greek eidyllion, a little picture, used for short pastoral poems.
hints: A quiet country summer.
A perfect, pastoral setting.

definition: A dome-shaped shelter built from blocks of snow.
note: From Inuktitut iglu, which means a house of any kind, not just one of snow.
hints: Built in the Arctic.
Home of ice blocks.

definition: A picture, or a likeness of someone or something.
note: From Old French image, from Latin imago, a copy or likeness.
hints: A photo or painting.
What a mirror shows.

definition: To fill or saturate with a quality or feeling.
note: From Latin imbuere, to wet or moisten. It first meant to soak, as with dye.
hints: A teacher may do it with curiosity.
To fill with a feeling or idea.

definition: To drive or urge someone to act.
note: Borrowed from Latin impellere, to push against.
hints: A strong sense of duty may do it.
To push forward, as if forced.

definition: To suggest something without stating it outright.
note: From Old French emplier, from Latin implicare, to fold in. The meaning is folded inside what's said.
hints: Hinting rather than saying.
What a raised eyebrow may do.

definition: Silly and empty of meaning.
note: From Latin inanis, empty or void.
hints: Pointless chatter.
A mindless remark.

definition: The folder where incoming messages arrive.
note: Formed from in plus box. It began as a tray for incoming paper.
hints: Where new email lands.
Often needs clearing to reach zero.

definition: To bring something unwelcome upon yourself.
note: From Latin incurrere, to run into.
hints: What you do when you rack up debt.
A late fee is one you may do.

definition: An alphabetical list at the back of a book, or a pointing finger.
note: From Latin index, one who points out. The index finger is the one used to point.
hints: Find a topic quickly in a book.
The finger next to the thumb.

definition: Clumsy or unskilled.
note: Via French from Latin ineptus, not fitting. It shares a root with apt.
hints: Said of a bungling beginner.
Opposite of skilled.

definition: Without power to move or react.
note: From Latin iners, inactive or unskilled.
hints: Neon and argon are examples of such gases.
A lifeless, still lump.

definition: To conclude from evidence.
note: From Latin inferre, to bring in.
hints: What a detective does with clues.
To work out a conclusion.

definition: A block of cast metal, such as gold or iron.
note: Middle English ingot meant a mould for casting metal. Its origin is uncertain.
hints: Poured into a mould.
A bar of gold in a vault.

definition: To set a decorative piece into a surface.
note: Formed from in plus lay.
hints: A wooden box with a mother-of-pearl design.
A dentist may fit one into a tooth.

definition: A narrow arm of water leading into land.
note: From Middle English inlete, from the verb to let in.
hints: A small bay or cove.
Where the sea reaches inland.

definition: Located farther inside.
note: From Old English innera, comparative of inne, within.
hints: Opposite of outer.
A circle of your closest friends.

definition: What is put into a system, or advice offered to it.
note: Formed from in plus put.
hints: What you type on a keyboard.
Your opinion offered to a group.

definition: To bury a dead body.
note: Borrowed from Old French enterrer, from Latin in terra, 'in the earth'. Its relative 'interment' is a funeral word.
hints: What a graveyard crew does.
A solemn word for burial.

definition: A short form of introduction.
note: Clipped from introduction, which comes from Latin introducere, 'to lead in'.
hints: The opening part of a song or show.
The start of a book or a performance.

definition: Relating to ions, or to a style of Greek column.
note: From ion, a Greek word for 'going', plus -ic. The other Ionic is an order of Greek architecture marked by scroll-shaped capitals.
hints: A chemistry word about charged particles.
A style of column with scrolls.

definition: A contrast between what is said and what is meant, or between expectation and outcome.
note: From Greek eironeia, feigned ignorance. Socrates used the technique in questioning others.
hints: Rain at a weather forecaster's picnic.
When something turns out the opposite of what is expected.

definition: A very small island.
note: From Middle French islette, a little isle.
hints: Too small for more than a few trees.
A speck of land in the sea.

definition: A topic of concern, or to send out.
note: From Old French issue, which comes from Latin exire, to go out.
hints: A magazine appears in one each month.
A problem to be resolved.

definition: Feeling a need to scratch.
note: From Old English giccig, from itch plus -y.
hints: What a mosquito bite makes you.
Wool jumpers can make skin this way.

definition: The hard white material of elephant tusks, or a creamy colour.
note: Through Anglo-Norman from Latin eboreus, from ebur. The colour is named after the material.
hints: Piano keys were once made of it.
A pale shade between white and cream.

definition: A short trip taken for pleasure.
note: Origin uncertain. It first meant a tiring journey and later a pleasant one.
hints: A quick day out.
A brief pleasure trip.

definition: Flashy and lively; or in the style of jazz.
note: Built from jazz plus -y. The origin of jazz itself is uncertain.
hints: Describes a bright and showy outfit.
Music with a swinging, improvised feel.

definition: A wobbling dessert, or a fruit spread.
note: From French gelee, from Latin gelare, to freeze.
hints: It wobbles on a plate.
Spread on toast with peanut butter.

definition: Moving in sudden starts and stops, or dried strips of meat.
note: From jerk plus -y. The meat sense comes from a different word, charqui, from Quechua.
hints: A bumpy ride feels this way.
A dried beef snack.

definition: A structure built out into water to protect a harbour or moor boats.
note: From Old French jetee, something thrown out.
hints: Boats tie up at one.
A small pier.

definition: A precious stone, or a valued ornament.
note: From Anglo-Norman juel. Its ultimate origin is uncertain.
hints: A gem in a crown.
A ruby in a ring.

definition: A very short moment.
note: Origin unknown. It was said to be thieves' slang for lightning.
hints: Said in 'I'll be back in a ...'.
A very brief time.

definition: A horizontal beam that supports a floor or ceiling.
note: From Old French giste, from gesir, to lie down. A joist lies across the structure.
hints: Floorboards rest on them.
A timber hidden under a floor.

definition: A person who jokes, or a card in a pack.
note: From joke plus -er. The playing card is possibly named from German Jucker, tied to euchre.
hints: A card with a jester on it.
A prankster.

definition: Cheerful and merry.
note: From Old French joli, merry. The word was used for happy people long before it meant extremely.
hints: Santa is described this way.
Full of good spirits.

definition: A combat between two mounted knights with lances.
note: From Old French jouster, from a Latin word meaning near. It means to come together.
hints: A medieval tournament event.
Two horsemen charge each other.

definition: A person who decides legal cases, or to form an opinion.
note: From Old French juge, from Latin iudex.
hints: Wears a robe in court.
What you do when you assess someone.

definition: The liquid squeezed from fruit or vegetables.
note: From Old French jus, from Latin ius, which meant broth or sauce.
hints: Squeezed from oranges.
A breakfast drink in a glass.

definition: Full of juice, or full of tempting gossip.
note: Middle English jousy meant drunken, literally full of liquor. The sense of something rich and exciting grew from there.
hints: Ripe peaches are this.
Gossip that is exciting.

definition: Unusually large.
note: Named after Jumbo, a huge African elephant bought by P. T. Barnum in 1882.
hints: A giant-sized pack.
A big jet plane.

definition: Nervous and easily startled.
note: Built from jump plus -y. It describes someone who jumps at small sounds.
hints: How a person feels after too much coffee.
What a startled cat might be.

definition: A group of military officers ruling a country after seizing power.
note: Borrowed from Spanish junta, a thing joined, from Latin iungere, to join.
hints: Takes over after a coup.
Military leaders running a state.

definition: A member of a jury.
note: From Anglo-Norman jurour, from Old French jurer, to swear. Jurors take an oath.
hints: One of twelve in a trial.
Listens to evidence in court.

definition: The tenth letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Greek kappa, which came from a Semitic word that meant 'palm' or 'hand'. It is the root of the letter K.
hints: A Greek letter whose Latin cousin is K.
Comes after iota and before lambda.

definition: The idea that your actions bring matching consequences.
note: From Sanskrit karman, meaning act or deed. It is a concept in Hindu and Buddhist thought.
hints: What goes around comes around.
Good deeds are said to earn it.

definition: A small covered boat paddled with a double-bladed paddle.
note: From Inuktitut qayaq, a hunter's boat.
hints: Paddled by one person.
Used in the Arctic and in whitewater.

definition: Pieces of grilled or roasted meat, often on a skewer.
note: From Arabic kabab, by way of Turkish and other languages.
hints: Served in pitta with salad.
Meat roasted on a stick.

definition: A dull yellowish-brown colour, or cloth in that colour.
note: From Hindustani khaki, 'dusty', from Persian khak, 'dust' or 'earth'. British troops in India adopted it for uniforms.
hints: A common colour for army trousers.
A word that literally means dusty.

definition: A small booth selling newspapers, snacks or tickets.
note: From Persian kushk, a pavilion, via Turkish and French.
hints: A tiny stall on a street corner.
A self-service ticket machine.

definition: A pet name for a cat; also a shared pot of money.
note: As a cat name it is from kitten plus -y. The money sense is an older, separate word of uncertain origin.
hints: A cat, in baby talk.
Where friends put money for a shared purpose.

definition: A natural talent for doing something easily.
note: From Middle English knak, a sharp sound. How it came to mean skill is unclear.
hints: You either have it or you don't.
A clever trick of doing a job.

definition: To go down on your knees.
note: From Old English cneowlian, formed from knee.
hints: What you do to propose or pray.
A knight did this before a king.

definition: To strike a door to be let in.
note: From Old English cnocian, likely imitating the sound.
hints: A polite way to announce yourself at a door.
Rap on wood.

definition: A small round hill.
note: From Old English cnoll, a summit.
hints: A grassy rise in a meadow.
Smaller than a hill.

definition: Recognised or familiar; the past participle of know.
note: From Old English cnawen. Something known is something that is not a mystery.
hints: The reverse of a word like 'unfamiliar'.
How a famous person is described to the public.

definition: A grey tree-climbing Australian marsupial that eats eucalyptus.
note: From the Dharug word gula. It is not a bear, despite its look.
hints: Sleeps most of the day.
Cuddly marsupial from Australia.

definition: Tiny shrimp-like sea creatures eaten by whales.
note: From Norwegian kril, meaning small fish fry.
hints: Baleen whales feed on them.
A swarm in cold southern oceans.

definition: A tag showing what something is or costs.
note: From Old French label, a strip, from a Frankish word for a rag.
hints: Stuck on a jar or sewn inside a shirt.
What a price sticker is.

definition: Work; or the process of giving birth.
note: An American spelling of labour, from Latin labor, meaning 'toil'. Both work and childbirth were called by this word.
hints: The workers of the world.
A day in September is named for it in the United States.

definition: Weighed down with a load.
note: The old past participle of lade, 'to load', from Old English hladan. It is also found in 'fully laden'.
hints: How a donkey with baggage looks.
Burdened with a heavy load.

definition: A deep long-handled spoon for serving soup.
note: From Old English hlaedel, from a root meaning to load.
hints: Used to serve soup from a pot.
A big spoon for punch.

definition: A long spear used by a mounted knight.
note: From Old French lance, from Latin lancea.
hints: A jousting weapon.
To cut open a boil.

definition: Tall, thin and a bit awkward.
note: From lank plus -y.
hints: Said of a gangly teenager.
Long-limbed.

definition: The folded flap on the front of a jacket.
note: Formed from lap plus a small ending, meaning a little fold.
hints: A pin may be worn on it.
Part of a suit jacket collar.

definition: A brief slip or a gradual passing of time.
note: From Latin lapsus, from labi, to slip.
hints: A moment of poor judgement.
What a membership does if not renewed.

definition: Of great size.
note: From Old French large, from Latin largus, abundant.
hints: Opposite of small.
A big size on a clothing tag.

definition: The early, wormlike stage of an insect.
note: From Latin larva, meaning ghost or mask. The larva was seen as a mask hiding the adult.
hints: What a caterpillar is.
Hatches from an egg before pupating.

definition: A rope with a loop used to catch cattle.
note: From Spanish lazo, from Latin laqueus, a snare. It is a doublet of lace.
hints: A cowboy swings it overhead.
A looped rope for catching a calf.

definition: A simple catch that holds a door or gate shut.
note: From Middle English lacchen, to seize or catch.
hints: Lift it to open a gate.
Fastens a garden gate.

definition: At a time after now.
note: From Old English lator, the comparative of late. It is the adverb you use to put something off.
hints: What you say when you cannot do something now.
The opposite of 'sooner'.

definition: A machine that spins wood or metal so it can be shaped.
note: Origin uncertain.
hints: Makes table legs round.
Spins material against a cutting tool.

definition: Coffee made with steamed milk.
note: Short for Italian caffe latte, meaning milk coffee.
hints: Ordered at a cafe.
Espresso topped with foam.

definition: To make sounds that show amusement.
note: From Old English hlehhan, thought to imitate the sound.
hints: The reaction to a joke.
The sound that follows a good joke.

definition: A single thickness of something spread over a surface.
note: From lay plus -er.
hints: A cake has several.
Onions have many.

definition: To drain away by liquid passing through.
note: From Old English words for a muddy stream.
hints: Rain does this to nutrients in soil.
To soak out slowly, as chemicals into water.

definition: Covered with or full of leaves.
note: From leaf plus -y. Leaf comes from Old English leaf, a word shared across the Germanic languages.
hints: Describes a green salad or a shady suburb.
A word for trees in summer.

definition: Letting liquid or gas escape through a gap.
note: From leak plus -y. Leak is a word for something that lets water or gas escape, and it can also describe someone who spills secrets.
hints: A boat with a hole might be this.
How a faulty pipe is described.

definition: To gain knowledge or a skill.
note: From Old English leornian. Strangely, learn once could also mean to teach.
hints: What you do at school.
Pick up a new skill.

definition: A contract to rent property for a set time.
note: From Anglo-Norman lesser, to let go.
hints: Signed with a landlord.
Often runs for a year.

definition: A strap used to hold a dog.
note: From Old French lesse, from a verb meaning to let go.
hints: Walkies need one.
Keeps a pet from running off.

definition: Smallest in amount or degree.
note: From Old English laest, the superlative of less. 'At least' is a way of naming the smallest acceptable amount.
hints: The opposite of 'most'.
Opposite of the biggest amount.

definition: To go away from, or to let remain.
note: From Old English laefan, to let stay.
hints: What you do when you depart.
To go away or let something stay.

definition: A narrow shelf jutting out from a wall or cliff.
note: From Middle English legge, from an Old English word for a bar.
hints: A narrow rock shelf.
Where a bird nests on a cliff.

definition: A blood-sucking worm, or a person who lives off others.
note: From Old English laece, a blood-sucking worm. The old word for doctor is a separate one.
hints: Used by doctors long ago to draw blood.
A freeloader.

definition: Wary and suspicious.
note: First recorded in the 1700s, from an old sense of leer, a sideways glance.
hints: A sideways look of doubt.
Distrustful of a stranger's offer.

definition: A left-handed person.
note: From left plus -y. Left descends from Old English lyft, an old word meaning 'weak' or 'worthless'.
hints: A pitcher who throws with the other hand.
Also a nickname for someone on the political left.

definition: Allowed by law.
note: From Latin legalis, from lex, law. Loyal is a doublet of the same word.
hints: What a lawyer is concerned with.
Permitted under the rules of the land.

definition: A sour yellow citrus fruit.
note: Through Old French from Arabic laymun, a word for citrus.
hints: Squeezed on fish or into tea.
Also a defective car, informally.

definition: A long-tailed primate native to Madagascar.
note: From Latin lemures, Roman spirits of the dead. Linnaeus chose the name for animals that come out at night.
hints: Ring-tailed ones live in Madagascar.
A primate with a banded tail.

definition: Flat and even, or a floor of a building.
note: From Old French livel, from Latin libella, a small balance or plumb tool. Its root is libra, scales.
hints: A spirit one shows if a shelf is straight.
A stage in a video game.

definition: A bar that turns on a fixed point to lift or move something.
note: From Old French leveor, a lifter, from Latin levare, to raise.
hints: Archimedes said he could move the world with one.
Pull it to start the machine.

definition: A false written statement that damages someone's reputation.
note: From Latin libellus, a little book. It first meant any small written document.
hints: Sued in court by a defamed celebrity.
Slander's written counterpart.

definition: A feudal lord to whom loyalty is owed.
note: From Old French liege, probably from a Germanic word meaning free.
hints: A vassal's sworn lord.
Knights swore fealty to their ...

definition: Brightness that makes things visible, or not heavy.
note: From Old English leoht, from a root also behind lucid.
hints: Switched on in a dark room.
Opposite of heavy or dark.

definition: To compare one thing to another.
note: From Middle English liknen, built on like. It is nearly always followed by 'to'.
hints: Done when you say something is just like another.
A word that often sits before 'to' in a sentence.

definition: A shrub with fragrant purple blossoms, or a pale purple colour.
note: Ultimately from Persian nilak, bluish, via Arabic and Spanish. The shade is named after the flower.
hints: Blooms in spring with a sweet smell.
A pale shade of purple.

definition: An uncertain in-between state.
note: From Latin limbus, an edge. In medieval belief it was the borderland of hell for souls who could not enter heaven.
hints: Waiting with no decision made.
Also a dance with a low bar.

definition: A boundary that cannot be passed.
note: Through Old French from Latin limes, a boundary path between fields.
hints: What a speed sign shows.
The point beyond which you cannot go.

definition: Cloth woven from flax.
note: From Old English linen, meaning made of flax. The word lin was the plant itself.
hints: Tablecloths and bedsheets.
Woven from the flax plant.

definition: A large passenger ship, or a layer that fits inside something.
note: Built from line plus -er. The ship sense is short for 'ocean liner', a ship that ran regularly on a fixed line of route.
hints: A big cruise vessel.
A bin may have a bag inside as this.

definition: The specialised language of a particular group.
note: Probably from Latin lingua, tongue, via Portuguese or a similar source.
hints: Jargon of sailors or gamers.
Slang used by a particular profession.

definition: A fat or oil-like substance in living cells.
note: From Greek lipos, fat.
hints: Cholesterol is one.
A scientific word for fats.

definition: Slim, flexible and graceful.
note: From Old English lithe, which meant gentle or mild. The sense of supple came later.
hints: Describes a dancer or a cat.
Moves with easy grace.

definition: The large organ that filters blood and makes bile.
note: From Old English lifer, a very old Germanic word.
hints: Eaten with onions.
Alcohol harms it.

definition: Furiously angry, or a bruised bluish colour.
note: From Latin lividus, 'bluish, leaden', the colour of a bruise. 'Livid with rage' described a face gone dark, and the anger outlived the colour.
hints: Furious enough to turn colour.
A very angry parent.

definition: A woolly South American animal related to the camel.
note: From Spanish llama, from Quechua.
hints: Spits when annoyed.
Carries loads in the Andes.

definition: Having soil rich in clay, sand and decayed matter.
note: From loam plus -y. Loam is an old Germanic word for earth or clay.
hints: The best kind of garden soil.
A word from the garden shed.

definition: Unwilling; reluctant.
note: From Old English lath, which meant hateful or evil.
hints: Describes your feeling about going to a boring meeting.
Reluctant to do something.

definition: Belonging to a nearby place.
note: From Late Latin localis, from locus, a place.
hints: A shop in your neighbourhood.
Not from far away.

definition: A particular place or point where something occurs.
note: Borrowed from Latin locus, place.
hints: The scene of a crime.
A central point of activity.

definition: A small house or cabin, or to stay somewhere briefly.
note: From Old French loge, a hut or arbour, from a Germanic root.
hints: A hunting cabin in the woods.
To submit a complaint officially.

definition: Very high, or noble and proud.
note: From Middle English loft, sky or upper room, plus -y.
hints: A mountain peak or an ambition.
Aims that are grand and ambitious.

definition: Reasoning that follows strict rules.
note: Through Old French from Greek logike, from logos, word or reason.
hints: A step-by-step argument.
What Mr Spock prizes.

definition: The details or act of signing into a computer system.
note: A noun made from the verb phrase 'log in'. The log is a ship's record book, and recording who entered gave 'log in' its sense.
hints: A username and a password.
What a website asks for before letting you in.

definition: Silly or a bit crazy.
note: From loop plus -y.
hints: A word for a scatterbrained idea.
A little off your rocker.

definition: Not tight or firmly fixed.
note: From Old Norse lauss, meaning free or empty.
hints: A wobbly tooth is this.
Not fastened.

definition: A large motor vehicle for carrying goods.
note: Origin uncertain, perhaps from a dialect verb meaning to drag.
hints: What Americans call a truck.
A large goods vehicle on a motorway.

definition: A person or team that does not win.
note: From Middle English, built from lose plus -er. As an insult it may come from the older word losel, meaning 'worthless fellow'.
hints: The team that comes second.
The unlucky side of a contest.

definition: A tiny wingless insect that lives on skin or hair.
note: From Old English lus, an old Germanic word. The plural is lice.
hints: Found in hair.
A contemptible person, informally.

definition: Very bad or poor in quality.
note: From louse plus -y. Being infested with lice was a miserable state.
hints: A rotten day.
Terrible service in a restaurant.

definition: A person who loves another or loves a thing.
note: From Middle English lovere, built from love plus -er. It can also mean a fan, as in a 'music lover'.
hints: Someone devoted to a hobby, or a sweetheart.
A person who adores books is one of these.

definition: Further down; or to bring something down.
note: From low plus -er, the comparative form. As a verb it means to move something down gently.
hints: Opposite of 'upper'.
What you do to a flag at sunset.

definition: Humble, or of low rank.
note: Built from low plus -ly. Though it looks like an adverb, it is an adjective meaning of modest standing.
hints: A word for the least important people in a hierarchy.
Describes a peasant, a servant or a worm.

definition: Faithful to a person or cause.
note: From Old French loial, from Latin legalis. Legal is its doublet.
hints: Describes a dog or a friend.
Sticks by you through thick and thin.

definition: Clearly expressed or thinking clearly.
note: From Latin lucidus, bright, from lucere, to shine.
hints: An explanation that is easy to follow.
A dream where you know you are dreaming.

definition: A unit measuring the amount of light from a source.
note: From Latin lumen, light. It was adopted as a unit in 1894 by André Blondel.
hints: Printed on a lightbulb box.
A measure of brightness.

definition: Full of lumps; not smooth.
note: From lump plus -y. Lump itself is a Germanic word for a shapeless piece.
hints: How badly mixed gravy might be.
A bad mattress or custard can be this.

definition: A meal eaten in the middle of the day.
note: First recorded in 1580 as a word for a lump or hunk of food.
hints: Midday meal.
What a sandwich is often for.

definition: A sudden forward thrust, as in fencing.
note: From French allonge, from a Latin root meaning long.
hints: A fencer does it with a sword.
An exercise stepping forward on one leg.

definition: A long-term illness in which the body's immune system attacks itself.
note: Latin for 'wolf'. The disease took the name in the Middle Ages, often explained by its facial sores resembling wolf bites.
hints: A medical term from the Latin for a wild animal.
A condition in which the immune system turns on the body.

definition: To stagger or move suddenly and unsteadily.
note: Originally a nautical word for a ship's sudden roll, of unknown origin.
hints: A boat in rough waves.
Staggering after too many drinks.

definition: Shocking and sensational, or glaringly vivid.
note: From Latin luridus, pale yellow or wan.
hints: A tabloid's gruesome details.
Harsh and garish colours.

definition: Telling untruths; or resting flat.
note: From lie plus -ing. The two meanings come from two different verbs that happen to look alike.
hints: Opposite of telling the truth.
What you do when you rest flat on a bed.

definition: Relating to poetry that expresses a speaker's own feelings, or the words of a song.
note: Via French and Latin from Greek lurikos, 'of the lyre'. Lyric poetry was first the kind sung to a lyre.
hints: Songwriters write these words.
Poetry of personal feeling, or what the singer sings.

definition: A large, brightly coloured parrot from tropical America.
note: From Portuguese macau, of unknown origin.
hints: A loud, colourful tropical bird.
A big parrot with a long tail and a hooked beak.

definition: Aggressively or showily masculine.
note: Borrowed from Spanish macho, 'male', from Latin masculus, which also gave English 'male'.
hints: Describes a man keen to prove his toughness.
Spanish for male, now a word for swagger.

definition: Large in scale; also a stored set of commands.
note: From Greek makros, 'long' or 'large'. In computing a macro is a short command that stands in for many.
hints: A prefix that points to the big picture.
Opposite of micro.

definition: A polite way to address a woman.
note: From Old French ma dame, 'my lady'. The same word also names a woman who runs a household or a brothel.
hints: How a shop assistant might address a customer.
Polite counterpart to 'sir'.

definition: In a wild, frantic, or extreme way.
note: From Middle English madly, built from mad plus -ly. It can also mean extremely, as in 'madly in love'.
hints: How a rushing person moves.
A word before 'in love'.

definition: The use of rituals or supposed supernatural forces to make things happen, or a trick that seems to.
note: Traced back through Greek to Old Persian, where the root referred to the priests known as magi.
hints: Wizards and stage performers both claim it.
Abracadabra is a word for summoning it.

definition: Hot molten rock beneath the earth's surface.
note: From Greek magma, 'a kneaded mass', from massein, 'to knead'. It is called lava once it erupts.
hints: What fills a volcano before an eruption.
Rock so hot that it flows.

definition: Corn; the cereal plant Zea mays, or its grain.
note: Borrowed from Spanish maiz, from Taino, the language of the Caribbean people who grew it.
hints: Another name for corn, used in Britain.
A golden crop that the Americas gave the world.

definition: Greater in size, importance or rank.
note: From Latin maior, 'greater'. Its opposite, minor, comes from Latin minor.
hints: The opposite of minor.
A military rank above captain, or a main subject at university.

definition: A person or thing that makes something.
note: From Middle English, built from make plus -er. In religion it can name God as the creator.
hints: Someone who builds things.
A craftsman or the company that builds a product.

definition: A lively Latin dance and its music.
note: The dance came from Cuba in the 1940s, from Cuban Spanish mambo. The word itself comes from Haitian Creole, a priestess's title.
hints: A Latin dance with a quick beat.
Number five in a Lou Bega hit.

definition: A Japanese comic or graphic novel.
note: Borrowed from Japanese, written with characters meaning roughly 'whimsical' and 'picture'.
hints: Read right to left, often in black and white.
Japanese comics with large-eyed characters.

definition: A skin disease of animals caused by mites, leaving them itchy and patchy.
note: From Old French manjue, 'itch', from mangier, 'to eat'.
hints: A scruffy stray dog might suffer from it.
Mites cause this itchy hair-loss condition.

definition: A sweet, juicy tropical fruit with a large stone.
note: Reached English from Portuguese, ultimately from Tamil and Malayalam words for the fruit.
hints: A tropical fruit with orange flesh.
A summer smoothie flavour that is also a chutney.

definition: Scruffy and worn, as if suffering from mange.
note: Formed from 'mange' plus -y, and extended from diseased animals to anything shabby.
hints: Describes a patchy, flea-ridden stray.
Shabby and bald in places.

definition: An extreme, obsessive enthusiasm, or a state of manic excitement.
note: From Greek mania, 'madness', from the verb mainesthai, 'to rage'.
hints: A craze that sweeps a crowd.
Madness, in Greek; now also a craze.

definition: Wildly energetic or frantic.
note: From Greek mania, 'madness', via the clinical term for the elevated state.
hints: Describes a frenzied burst of activity.
Often paired with 'depressive' in a diagnosis.

definition: Showing qualities thought typical of a man.
note: From Old English manlic, built from man plus -ly. It once simply meant 'befitting a person' and was used for noble conduct.
hints: Describes a deep voice or a firm handshake.
A word for traditionally male traits.

definition: A large country house with its land, or the estate itself.
note: From Old French manoir, 'dwelling', from Latin manere, 'to stay'.
hints: A lord's country estate in medieval England.
A grand house in the countryside.

definition: A tree with lobed leaves, known for its syrup and autumn colour.
note: From Middle English mapel, the name of the tree.
hints: Canada's flag features its leaf.
Tree that is tapped for sweet syrup.

definition: To walk in a steady, regular rhythm, as soldiers do.
note: From Old French marchier, 'to stride, to trample'.
hints: What soldiers do in step.
Also the month after February.

definition: To take someone as a husband or wife.
note: From Latin maritare, 'to wed', from maritus, 'husband'.
hints: What happens at a wedding.
To tie the knot.

definition: Low, wet ground with grasses and reeds.
note: From Old English mersc, a word for low wet ground.
hints: Wet land where reeds and herons live.
A boggy lowland, less deep than a swamp.

definition: A person who builds with stone or brick.
note: From Old French maçon, from Late Latin, 'bricklayer'. The Freemasons take their name from medieval stoneworkers.
hints: Cuts and lays stone for walls.
A jar sharing this name is used for preserves.

definition: Friendly and chummy; also a pirate's way of addressing a shipmate.
note: Built from mate plus -y. Mate is an old word for a companion who eats at the same table.
hints: A pirate might use it for a friend.
Describes a very pally mood.

definition: A pale, purplish colour.
note: French for 'mallow', the plant with purple flowers. It was also the name of the first synthetic dye, which was this colour.
hints: A pale shade between lilac and violet.
Named for a flowering plant, via French.

definition: A short saying that states a rule or truth.
note: From Latin maxima, via French, used for a basic principle or axiom.
hints: A pithy line of advice.
'Look before you leap' is one.

definition: Perhaps; possibly.
note: Made from the phrase 'it may be', squashed into one word. Compare the old word mayhap.
hints: A non-committal answer.
Neither yes nor no.

definition: The elected head of a town or city.
note: From Old French maire, from Latin maior, 'greater'.
hints: Leads a city council.
Wears a chain of office on formal occasions.

definition: Soft, dry and powdery like ground grain; also, pale.
note: From meal plus -y. Meal is ground grain, from Old English melu. A mealy-mouthed person speaks without frankness.
hints: Describes a mushy, dry apple.
A word that can come before 'mouthed'.

definition: Full of meat; or full of substance.
note: From meat plus -y. Meat once meant food in general, in Old English mete.
hints: A big burger might be said to be this.
A role with much to chew on.

definition: The news and entertainment industries, or means of communication.
note: Latin for 'middle', plural of medium. It became the term for the channels that stand between sender and audience.
hints: Newspapers, television and the internet.
The 'social' kind is all over your phone.

definition: A doctor or someone with medical training, such as one serving with soldiers.
note: From Latin medicus, 'physician'.
hints: Someone shouts for one on a battlefield.
Short for a person who treats the wounded.

definition: A confused, close-quarters fight.
note: Borrowed from French melee, from Old French meslee, 'to mix'.
hints: A scrappy brawl in which nobody is in charge.
A tangled fight with everyone mixed up.

definition: A large, sweet fruit with juicy flesh and a thick rind.
note: From Old French melon, from Late Latin and ultimately Greek melopepon, a word that combined 'apple' and 'gourd'.
hints: Cantaloupe and honeydew are types.
A big juicy summer fruit eaten in slices.

definition: Kindness shown by sparing someone who deserves punishment.
note: From Old French merci, from Latin merces, 'wages, price'.
hints: What a judge might show.
Begged for by a defeated enemy.

definition: To combine into one.
note: Borrowed from Latin mergere, 'to dip, plunge, immerse'.
hints: What two lanes of traffic do.
Two companies become one.

definition: The quality of being worthy of praise or reward.
note: From Old French merite, from Latin meritum, 'something earned'.
hints: Judged on this rather than favours.
A school badge might reward it.

definition: Cheerful and full of fun.
note: From Old English myrge, meaning 'pleasing, agreeable'.
hints: A word for festive cheer.
Christmas greetings include it.

definition: A hard, shiny, conductive material such as iron or copper.
note: From Greek metallon, a word for a mine or quarry, which came to mean what was mined.
hints: Iron and gold are examples.
Conducts heat and electricity well.

definition: A device that measures, such as the amount of gas or electricity used.
note: From Middle English metere, 'one who measures', related to 'mete out'.
hints: The taxi one runs up the fare.
Read monthly by the utility company.

definition: An underground railway system in a city.
note: French, clipped from metropolitain, ultimately from Greek words for 'mother' and 'city'. It was first used for the Paris railway.
hints: The Paris one has art nouveau entrances.
Another name for the subway or tube.

definition: Very small.
note: From Greek mikros, 'small'. It is also short for microwave or microprocessor.
hints: A prefix for tiny things.
Opposite of macro.

definition: A tiny biting or swarming fly.
note: From Old English mycg, a word for a midge, gnat or mosquito.
hints: Clouds of them plague Scottish summers.
A small fly that swarms near water.

definition: The middle of something; among.
note: From Middle English middes, reshaped from older phrases like 'in middes'. It appears in the phrase 'in the midst of'.
hints: A word for the centre of the action.
Found in 'in the ... of'.

definition: Power or strength; also a word for what is possible.
note: From Old English miht, 'power'. The helping verb is related, since being able is a form of having power.
hints: Strength, as in 'with all your ___ and main'.
A word for great force.

definition: Like milk; pale and cloudy.
note: From Old English meolcig, built from milk plus -y. The Milky Way is named for its pale band of stars.
hints: A galaxy is named after it.
A pale cloudy colour.

definition: To copy someone's voice or behaviour, or an animal that copies another's appearance.
note: From Latin mimicus and Greek mimikos, 'belonging to mimes'.
hints: A parrot is good at this.
Copy someone's voice, often to tease.

definition: To chop very fine; also to walk with small steps.
note: From Old French mincier, from Latin minutia, 'smallness'. 'Mince words' means to soften what you say.
hints: What a cook does with an onion or beef.
Said of walking with tiny steps.

definition: A person who digs for coal or metals underground.
note: From mine plus -er. Mine comes from Old French, a word for a tunnel or a vein of ore.
hints: Wears a helmet with a lamp.
Digs for coal or gold.

definition: Smaller or less important, or a person under legal adulthood.
note: From Latin minor, 'lesser', which gives the opposite of 'major'.
hints: The opposite of major.
Someone not yet old enough to vote.

definition: Tasting or smelling of mint.
note: From mint plus -y. Mint comes from Old English minte, from Latin menta.
hints: How fresh toothpaste tastes.
A chewing gum flavour.

definition: Less, or the sign for subtraction.
note: From Latin minus, the neuter of minor, 'less'.
hints: Takes away rather than adds.
The short horizontal sign in arithmetic.

definition: A young girl; also a scolding way to address a girl.
note: From miss plus -y. Miss itself is short for mistress.
hints: How a parent might address a cheeky girl.
A stern name used in a scolding.

definition: A coffee flavoured with chocolate.
note: Named for Mocha, a Red Sea port in Yemen that was a major coffee marketplace under Ottoman rule.
hints: A coffee shop order with chocolate.
Named after a port city in Yemen.

definition: Relating to a mode, or a helper verb such as can or must.
note: From Medieval Latin modalis, from Latin modus, 'measure' or 'manner'. A modal verb shows possibility or necessity.
hints: A grammar word for a kind of helper verb.
Can, must and might are examples.

definition: A person who displays clothes, or a small copy or representation of something.
note: From Latin modus, 'measure', through a diminutive form.
hints: Walks a catwalk wearing the designer's clothes.
A scaled-down version of a building or plane.

definition: A device that connects a computer to the internet.
note: A blend of 'modulator-demodulator'. It once turned digital signals into sound that could pass down phone lines.
hints: A box with blinking lights near the router.
Old ones screeched when they connected.

definition: A rich and powerful person in some industry.
note: Figurative use of Moghul, which meant Mongol and referred to the Mughal Empire of India.
hints: A media tycoon.
A Hollywood boss, or a bump on a ski slope.

definition: Slightly wet; damp.
note: From Old French moiste. Cake, soil and eyes can all be this.
hints: A good sponge cake is this.
Between dry and wet.

definition: Covered in mould.
note: Built from mold plus -y. Mold, the fungus, comes from Middle English mowlde.
hints: How old bread ends up.
What forgotten leftovers become.

definition: What people use to buy and sell things.
note: From Old French moneie, from Latin Moneta, a title of the goddess Juno, in whose temple Roman coins were made.
hints: Coins and notes.
A word whose Roman root names a temple of Juno.

definition: One of the twelve parts of a year.
note: From Old English monath, related to 'moon', since months followed the moon's phases.
hints: January is one.
About thirty days.

definition: The largest deer, with broad flat antlers, found in North America.
note: From an Eastern Algonquian word such as Narragansett moos, adopted into English.
hints: Large antlered animal of Canadian forests.
Named by Algonquian speakers.

definition: Concerned with right and wrong, or the lesson of a story.
note: From Latin moralis, from mos, 'custom, manner'.
hints: Fables end with one.
Concerned with ethics.

definition: To change shape smoothly; also a unit of linguistic form.
note: As a verb it is short for metamorphosis, from Greek morphe, 'form'. A film effect of the same name blends one image into another.
hints: A film effect that blends two faces.
A word for transforming.

definition: Covered with moss.
note: From moss plus -y. Moss comes from Old English mos, 'bog'.
hints: How an old stone wall may look.
A fallen log in a damp wood.

definition: A roadside hotel for motorists.
note: A blend of 'motor' and 'hotel'.
hints: Often found beside a highway.
Where the motorist sleeps over.

definition: A recurring theme or pattern in a work of art.
note: From French motif, in the sense of 'main idea', and a doublet of 'motive'.
hints: A repeated pattern on wallpaper.
A theme that keeps returning in a story or song.

definition: A machine that turns energy into movement.
note: From Latin motor, 'mover', from movere, 'to move'.
hints: Powers a car or a fan.
The thing under the bonnet that makes it go.

definition: A short phrase that states a guiding principle.
