note: Borrowed from Italian motto, 'a word, a saying', from Latin muttum, 'a mutter, a grunt'.
hints: Often written under a coat of arms.
A school's Latin slogan.

definition: To shed feathers, fur or skin so that new ones can grow.
note: From Latin mutare, 'to change', via Old English and Middle English.
hints: What a bird does each year.
Snakes and birds do it.

definition: A raised heap of earth or other material.
note: From a Middle English word meaning a fence or protection, from Old English mund, 'hand, protection'.
hints: A small hill piled up by hand.
A baseball pitcher stands on one.

definition: To climb or get onto something; also a hill.
note: From Old English munt and from Latin mons, 'hill'. A rider mounts a horse, and a picture is mounted on a card.
hints: What a rider does to a horse.
A word before a famous peak's name.

definition: A small rodent, or a handheld computer pointing device.
note: From Old English mus, the same word as in German Maus.
hints: Cats chase it.
You click it beside your keyboard.

definition: The opening in the face used for eating and speaking, or where a river meets the sea.
note: From Old English muth, from a Germanic root.
hints: Where food goes in.
A river has one where it meets the sea.

definition: Someone who moves things, or who is in motion.
note: From move plus -er. Movers carry furniture from one home to another.
hints: A job that involves a truck and heavy boxes.
The people who carry your sofa.

definition: A film shown in cinemas or at home.
note: From 'moving picture' plus -ie, attested by 1912 in American English.
hints: Watched with popcorn.
A short form of 'moving picture'.

definition: A machine or person that cuts grass.
note: From mow plus -er. Mow comes from Old English mawan, 'to cut grass'.
hints: What you push across the lawn.
It gets loud on Saturday mornings.

definition: Dirty with muck or mud.
note: From muck plus -y. Muck is from Old Norse myki, 'dung'.
hints: How boots look after a farm walk.
A British word for filthy.

definition: The slippery fluid made by the lining of the nose and throat.
note: Learned borrowing from Latin mucus.
hints: Produced when you have a cold.
A slimy bodily secretion.

definition: Covered with or full of mud.
note: From mud plus -y, found in Middle English. It can also describe cloudy water or a dull colour.
hints: How boots look after a wet walk.
A pond stirred up can look this way.

definition: A layer of material spread over soil to protect and feed plants.
note: Probably from Middle English melsche, 'soft', from an Old English word for 'mellow' or 'honeyed'.
hints: Gardeners spread it around plants.
Bark chips on a flowerbed.

definition: A preserved dead body wrapped in bandages, or a mother.
note: From Arabic mumiya, 'embalmed body', itself from a Persian word.
hints: Ancient Egyptians preserved them.
Horror films show one lurching in bandages.

definition: To chew noisily and with enjoyment.
note: Probably imitative of the sound of chewing, from Middle English monchen.
hints: What you do to crisps.
Chew loudly on a snack.

definition: A large painting made directly on a wall.
note: From French mural, from Latin murus, 'wall'.
hints: Painted on the side of a building.
Wall art on a grand scale.

definition: Dark, cloudy and hard to see through.
note: From Middle English mirky, built from 'murk' plus -y.
hints: Describes a swamp's water.
Cloudy water you cannot see to the bottom of.

definition: Soft and pulpy.
note: From mush plus -y. Mush may be a variant of mash.
hints: Overcooked peas end up this way.
Overripe fruit can feel like it.

definition: Organised sound made for pleasure, using melody and rhythm.
note: From Latin musica and Greek mousike, 'art of the Muses'.
hints: Played by an orchestra.
Named for the nine Greek goddesses of the arts.

definition: Having the strong, heavy smell of musk.
note: From musk plus -y. Musk reached English through Late Latin and Greek from Sanskrit, and names a strong-smelling substance from the male musk deer.
hints: A perfume or an animal might smell this way.
Describes a heavy, earthy scent.

definition: Smelling stale and damp.
note: From Late Middle English musty, of uncertain origin. It describes the smell of closed rooms and old books.
hints: How an unopened attic smells.
The smell of a damp, shut-in basement.

definition: A fragrant, bitter resin from certain trees, used in incense and perfume.
note: From Greek murra, from a Semitic source; compare Arabic murr, 'bitter'.
hints: One of the gifts of the Magi.
Brought to the infant Jesus along with gold and frankincense.

definition: Lacking experience and too ready to trust.
note: Borrowed from French naive, the feminine of naif, from Latin nativus, 'native, natural'.
hints: Believing everything you are told.
Innocent, and easy to fool.

definition: A person employed to care for children at home.
note: From nan plus -y, where nan is a child's word for grandmother or nursemaid. The goat of the same name is a separate usage.
hints: Looks after the kids while parents work.
Mary Poppins was one.

definition: Relating to the nose.
note: From Medieval Latin nasalis, from Latin nasus, 'nose'. A nasal voice sounds as if it comes through the nose.
hints: A kind of voice or a kind of spray.
Describes a voice that hums through the nose.

definition: Very unpleasant, or spiteful.
note: From Middle English nasty, 'unclean, filthy', of obscure origin.
hints: A word for a cruel remark.
Not nice at all.

definition: Relating to birth.
note: From Latin natus, 'born'. It is a close relative of words like native and nation.
hints: A word you may see before 'care' in a hospital.
Your chart in astrology is based on when you were born.

definition: Relating to a navy or to ships.
note: From Latin navalis, from navis, 'ship'. It is not related to the word for the belly button, though the two sound alike.
hints: A battle at sea or an officer's rank.
Describes a force that sails warships.

definition: The small scar on the belly where the umbilical cord was attached.
note: From Old English nafola, from a Germanic root.
hints: Also called the belly button.
An orange can be named for this.

definition: Lacking what is necessary; or too reliant on reassurance.
note: From Old English nedig, built from need plus -y. It can mean poor or, in slang, someone who wants constant attention.
hints: Describes a person asking for help often.
A friend who always wants reassurance.

definition: The long high call of a horse.
note: From Old English hnaegan, from a Germanic root meaning 'to neigh'.
hints: The sound a horse makes.
A stable sound.

definition: Like a nerd; keen on studies or technical hobbies.
note: From nerd plus -y. Nerd is a mid-twentieth-century slang word of unknown origin.
hints: Wearing glasses and loving maths, perhaps.
Obsessed with gadgets or comics.

definition: At no time; not ever.
note: From Old English naefre, built from ne, 'not', plus aefre, 'ever'. The first part is the same negative seen in 'no' and 'none'.
hints: The opposite of always.
A word for not on any occasion.

definition: Very recently.
note: From Old English niwlice, built from new plus -ly. It often goes with a participle, as in 'newly wed'.
hints: Used to describe recent arrivals.
Describes the paint or the married.

definition: A shallow recess in a wall, or a small specialised area of a market.
note: Borrowed from French niche, from Old French nicher, 'to make a nest'.
hints: A spot in the wall for a statue.
A small market that suits a few buyers well.

definition: The daughter of your brother or sister.
note: From Old French nece, from Late Latin neptia.
hints: Your sibling's daughter.
Her counterpart is a nephew.

definition: A covert warrior of feudal Japan, or anyone stealthy and skilled.
note: Borrowed from Japanese, with an underlying sense of 'hidden person'.
hints: Wears black and moves silently.
A throwing star is its signature weapon.

definition: Number nine in order.
note: From Old English nigotha, from nigon, 'nine'. The n was put back in later to match the number.
hints: The one after the eighth.
Beethoven's final symphony is this one.

definition: Of high birth, or having fine moral qualities.
note: From Old French noble, from Latin nobilis, 'known, famous, of high birth'.
hints: A knight or duke has this rank.
Showing generosity and honour.

definition: In a way that shows high character.
note: From Middle English, built from noble plus -ly. It is often used for brave or generous deeds.
hints: Describes a kind act or a brave sacrifice.
Acting with honour and generosity.

definition: A loud or unpleasant sound.
note: From Old French noise, 'dispute, wrangle, strife, noise', of uncertain origin.
hints: What neighbours make at night.
Sound you would rather not hear.

definition: Making a lot of loud sound.
note: Built from noise plus -y. Noise comes from Old French, though its earlier source is uncertain.
hints: A classroom or street full of racket.
Opposite of quiet.

definition: A person who moves from place to place with no fixed home.
note: From Greek nomas, 'roaming', used of wandering shepherds in search of pasture.
hints: A herder who follows his animals.
Lives out of a tent, travelling.

definition: A loop of rope that tightens when pulled.
note: From Middle English nose, 'noose, loop', of unclear origin.
hints: A rope with a sliding knot.
A hangman's loop.

definition: A small V-shaped cut, or a step upward in level.
note: Recorded since 1577, likely a rebracketing of 'an otch', from Old French ochier, 'to cut a notch'.
hints: Cut into a stick to count days.
A belt is tightened one of these at a time.

definition: A long work of fiction, or something new and original.
note: From Old French novel, 'new', from Latin novellus, a diminutive of novus.
hints: A book of invented story.
An idea that has never been tried.

definition: A gentle push, often with the elbow.
note: Dating from around the seventeenth century, perhaps from a Scandinavian word meaning 'to push' or 'to rub'. It is also used for a small push towards a choice.
hints: What an elbow gives to get your attention.
A light poke that suggests an action.

definition: A person trained to look after the sick.
note: From Old French norrice, from Latin nutrix, 'a woman who nourishes'. It once named a woman who suckled a child.
hints: Works with a doctor on a ward.
Wears scrubs in a hospital.

definition: Tasting of nuts; also, informally, crazy.
note: From nut plus -y. Nut comes from Old English hnutu. The crazy sense is a 1900s slang use.
hints: The taste of a brown, toasted flavour.
Also slang for someone a bit mad.

definition: A strong, stretchy synthetic fibre.
note: Coined by DuPont in 1938, formed from a random syllable plus a common fibre ending.
hints: Used for stockings and ropes.
The first fully synthetic fibre.

definition: A female nature spirit in Greek myth, or a young insect.
note: From Greek numphe, which meant 'bride' or 'young woman'. The insect sense is for a young form that has not yet grown wings.
hints: A spirit of rivers and woods.
A young dragonfly before it takes wing.

definition: Made of oak.
note: From Old English acen, 'of oak', built from oak plus -en. It is a poetic word for sturdy wooden things.
hints: Describes a bucket or a door.
A type of strong timber, in poems.

definition: Extremely overweight in a way that affects health.
note: From Latin obesus, 'having eaten away', from ob- plus edere, 'to eat'.
hints: Clinical term for being very overweight.
A health risk measured by BMI.

definition: To happen, or to come to mind.
note: From Latin occurrere, 'to run to meet'.
hints: What an accident does.
When an idea does this, it comes to mind.

definition: A vast body of salt water covering much of the Earth.
note: From Greek Okeanos, the great river believed to circle the world, via Latin and Old French.
hints: The Atlantic and the Pacific are examples.
Bigger than any sea.

definition: A group of eight, especially eight musicians.
note: From oct-, 'eight', plus the ending -et.
hints: A chamber piece for eight players.
A group of eight.

definition: More strange or unusual.
note: The comparative of odd, which came from Old Norse oddi, 'point of land', and later 'third or uneven number'.
hints: Comparing two peculiar things.
Stranger than strange, when set beside another.

definition: In a strange or unexpected way.
note: From odd plus -ly. Odd goes back to Old Norse oddi, a triangle's point, which led to the sense of 'uneven'.
hints: How a strange noise can seem.
Used before 'enough' to introduce a surprise.

definition: The organs of an animal, such as liver and kidney, used as food.
note: From Middle English offal, built from 'off' and 'fall': what falls off in butchering.
hints: Liver and kidneys are examples.
Butcher's leftovers that some cooks prize.

definition: To hold out something for someone to accept.
note: From Old English offrian, 'to make a sacrifice'.
hints: What a shop does with a discount.
Put forward for acceptance.

definition: Many times; frequently.
note: From Middle English ofte, with an -n added by analogy with 'seldom'.
hints: Its opposite is seldom.
Happens again and again.

definition: Of old; from a past time.
note: From Middle English olden, probably an old plural form of old. It remains mostly in the phrase 'olden days'.
hints: Used for times long gone by.
Often paired with 'days'.

definition: Having lived or existed longer.
note: The comparative of old, from Old English ald. Elder is a related older form.
hints: Comparing two ages.
A sibling born first is this.

definition: A small oval fruit eaten or pressed for oil, or a dull green colour.
note: From Old French olive, from Latin oliva.
hints: A martini garnish.
Pressed to make a Mediterranean cooking oil.

definition: A shading of colour from light to dark; also an old card game.
note: From French, meaning 'shaded'. The card game came from Spanish hombre, 'man'.
hints: A gradient on hair, nails or fabric.
A colour that fades gradually.

definition: The last letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Greek o mega, 'great o', to tell it apart from the short omicron.
hints: Opposite of alpha.
The final letter, meaning the end.

definition: A round vegetable with layers that makes people cry when cut.
note: From Old French oignon, from Latin unio.
hints: Cutting one brings tears.
A layered bulb with a sharp smell.

definition: The beginning of something, usually something unwelcome.
note: Formed from 'on' plus 'set'.
hints: The start of a fever or a storm.
The first moment a symptom appears.

definition: A drama in which the words are sung to an orchestra's accompaniment.
note: Borrowed from Italian opera, 'work'. It is a doublet of 'opus'.
hints: Sung in grand theatres, often in Italian.
A fat lady is said to end it by singing.

definition: To give or state an opinion.
note: From Latin opinari, 'to think or suppose'. Today it is often used with a slightly formal or mocking tone.
hints: What a pundit does on television.
To give your two cents, in a stuffy way.

definition: A narcotic drug made from the juice of the poppy.
note: From Greek opion, from opos, 'juice'.
hints: Made from a flower's sap.
Source of morphine and heroin.

definition: Relating to the eye or sight.
note: From Greek optikos, 'of sight'. It appears in 'optic nerve', which carries signals from the eye to the brain.
hints: A nerve that joins the eye to the brain.
A word in a kind of fibre that carries light.

definition: A command; or an arrangement in sequence.
note: From Old French ordre, from Latin ordo, 'row' or 'rank'. The word later stretched to cover commands and religious brotherhoods.
hints: What a waiter writes down.
Alphabetical is a type of it.

definition: A part of the body with a particular job, or a large keyboard instrument with pipes.
note: From Greek organon, 'tool, instrument', via Latin and Old French.
hints: The heart or liver is one.
A church instrument with pipes and pedals.

definition: Different from the one already mentioned.
note: From Old English other, from a root that meant 'second'. It is related to the Germanic word for 'either'.
hints: A word for not this one.
The remaining one of two.

definition: A playful, water-loving mammal with webbed feet and a long body.
note: From Old English otor, from a Germanic root that is related to the word 'water'.
hints: It slides down muddy riverbanks.
Sea ones hold hands while they sleep.

definition: Indicates duty or what is right to do.
note: From Old English ahte, the past of agan, 'to own'. What you ought to do was once what you owed.
hints: A helping verb of obligation.
Used before 'to' with duties.

definition: A unit of weight equal to one sixteenth of a pound.
note: From Latin uncia, a Roman unit that was a twelfth part of something.
hints: A small unit used in cooking and mail.
Sixteen make a pound.

definition: To do better than someone else.
note: Built from out- plus do, from Old English. To outdo is to go beyond another's effort.
hints: What rivals try to do to each other.
To surpass a competitor.

definition: On the outside; farther from the centre.
note: From Old English utera, a comparative of ut, 'out'. It is the opposite of inner.
hints: Space is this kind, beyond Earth.
Opposite of inner.

definition: To go beyond or surpass; also, money spent.
note: From Old English utgan, built from out and go. As a noun it means money going out, the opposite of income.
hints: Money that leaves your account.
A financial word that is the reverse of 'income'.

definition: The organ in which eggs are made, or the part of a flower that holds the ovules.
note: From New Latin ovarium, from Latin ovum, 'egg'.
hints: Where eggs are produced.
The base of a flower's pistil.

definition: Shaped like an egg.
note: From Latin ovatus, from ovum, 'egg'. Botanists use it for leaves wider at the base.
hints: A leaf shape in botany.
Like an egg outline.

definition: Done openly, not hidden.
note: From Old French overt, 'open'.
hints: Done in plain sight.
Hidden actions are its opposite.

definition: Relating to sheep.
note: From Late Latin ovinus, from ovis, 'sheep'. It is the sheepish counterpart to bovine for cattle.
hints: A formal word about a woolly animal.
Cousin of the adjective that describes cows.

definition: Shaped like an egg.
note: From Latin ovum, 'egg', plus -oid, 'resembling'. It is a geometry word for an egg-like shape.
hints: Like an egg or a rugby ball, roughly.
A rounded shape, longer than a circle.

definition: A person who owns something.
note: From Old English agnere, from the verb agan. 'Own' is actually a back-formation from it in the sense of owner.
hints: The person with the deed or the receipt.
A dog's human.

definition: A compound of oxygen and another element.
note: From Greek oxus, 'sharp, acid', the same root that gave 'oxygen'.
hints: Rust is one.
A chemical made by burning something with air.

definition: A form of oxygen with three atoms, found in a protective layer high above the Earth.
note: Coined in 1840 by Christian Friedrich Schonbein, from Greek ozon, 'smelling', because of its sharp smell.
hints: A layer high up shields us from ultraviolet rays.
Its hole over the poles worried the world.

definition: A flooded field in which rice grows.
note: Borrowed from Malay padi, 'rice plant'.
hints: Rice grows in one.
A wet field in Asia.

definition: A follower of an old or non-mainstream religion.
note: From Latin paganus, 'rural' or 'civilian', from pagus, 'village'. The Church used it for those who did not join Christianity.
hints: A word from early church history.
Once meant someone from the countryside.

definition: Coloured liquid that dries to coat a surface.
note: From Latin pingere, 'to paint', via Old French.
hints: Applied with a brush or roller.
An artist mixes it on a palette.

definition: A condition of paralysis, often with shaking.
note: From Old French and Latin paralysis, from Greek, meaning 'loosening'. Bell's palsy is a modern named example.
hints: An old name for paralysis.
Bell's is a famous kind.

definition: A flat section of a surface, or a group of people chosen to discuss something.
note: From Middle English panel, which could mean a piece of cloth or a list of jurors, from Old French.
hints: A door can have one set in it.
A group of experts on a show.

definition: Relating to the pope.
note: From Medieval Latin papalis, from papa, 'father'.
hints: Describes a pope's decree.
A bull issued from Rome.

definition: A tool for peeling or trimming.
note: Built from pare, 'to trim off the outer layer', plus -er. A paring knife is its close cousin.
hints: A tool for peeling fruit.
Used to trim the skin off an apple.

definition: A hooded jacket for cold or wet weather.
note: Reached English by 1780 through Russian and Aleut, ultimately from a Tundra Nenets word.
hints: A hooded coat for the Arctic.
A hooded coat with a fur-trimmed edge for the Arctic.

definition: To ward off an attack or a question.
note: From Italian parare, 'to ward off' via French.
hints: A fencer's defensive move.
Deflect a question without really answering it.

definition: To break a sentence into its grammatical parts, or to analyse code.
note: Probably from Middle English pars, 'parts of speech', from Latin pars, 'part'.
hints: Done to a sentence in a grammar lesson.
A computer does it to a line of code.

definition: A social gathering, or a group or person involved in something.
note: From Old French partie, 'part, side, share'.
hints: Held with music and cake.
A political group, or a person in a lawsuit.

definition: A food made from wheat dough, shaped and boiled.
note: Borrowed from Italian pasta, 'paste, dough', from Greek.
hints: Spaghetti is one kind.
Eaten with sauce, from Italy.

definition: A soft, sticky mixture, or to stick something with glue.
note: From Old French paste, 'dough', from Greek.
hints: A soft, sticky mixture.
Copy, then do this on a computer.

definition: Pale and unhealthy-looking; or a baked meat pie.
note: The adjective is from paste plus -y. The pie is a separate word, from Old French paste, 'pastry'.
hints: A sickly complexion.
A Cornish miner's lunch.

definition: A piece used to cover a hole, or a small area.
note: From Middle English patche, of uncertain origin.
hints: Sewn on a worn elbow.
A pirate might wear one over an eye.

definition: A paved outdoor area beside a house.
note: From Spanish patio, 'courtyard', of uncertain origin.
hints: Where a barbecue might be set up.
A paved spot outside the back door.

definition: A small flat cake of minced food, such as meat.
note: Earlier meant 'small pie', from French pate.
hints: The meaty part of a burger.
A flat round of ground beef.

definition: A short stop or rest.
note: From Latin pausa, from Greek pausis, 'stopping'.
hints: A button on a video player.
A brief silence.

definition: The person receiving a payment.
note: From pay plus -ee, the ending for a person who receives. A cheque is written to this person.
hints: Whose name goes on a cheque.
The one who gets the money.

definition: A person who pays.
note: From pay plus -er. In law, the payer of a bill is the person responsible for settling it.
hints: Who hands over the money.
Opposite of the one who is paid.

definition: Freedom from war, or a state of calm.
note: From Old French pais, from Latin pax.
hints: What a treaty aims for.
The dove is its symbol.

definition: A soft, juicy, downy-skinned fruit with a large stone.
note: From Latin persicum, 'Persian apple', via Old French peche.
hints: A fuzzy summer fruit.
Its Latin name points to Persia.

definition: A smooth, round gem formed inside an oyster.
note: From Old French perle, of uncertain origin.
hints: Found inside an oyster.
A string of these is a classic necklace.

definition: A sweet, buttery nut from an American tree.
note: From French pacane, from an Algonquian word.
hints: The nut in a Southern pie.
Related to the walnut.

definition: A foot-operated lever, as on a bicycle or piano.
note: From Latin pes, 'foot', via French pedale.
hints: Pushed round by a cyclist.
A piano has two or three at the bottom.

definition: Relating to punishment, especially by law.
note: From Latin poenalis, from poena, 'punishment'.
hints: Relating to punishment under the law.
A criminal code or a prison colony may carry this word.

definition: A short pasta shaped like quills.
note: Borrowed from Italian, where it is the plural of penna, 'feather' or 'quill'. The tube ends are cut diagonally like a pen nib.
hints: A type of pasta served with sauce.
A tubular Italian pasta.

definition: A place to sit; also a freshwater fish.
note: From Old French perche, 'pole', from Latin pertica. The fish is named from a Greek word, perke.
hints: Where a bird sits on a branch.
A spiny freshwater fish.

definition: Serious and immediate danger.
note: From Old French peril, from Latin periculum, 'trial' or 'danger'. It gives us the adjective perilous.
hints: What a hero in a film is in.
A grave kind of danger.

definition: Cheerful and lively.
note: From perk plus -y. Perk is a verb meaning to brighten up.
hints: How a morning person may seem.
Describes a bright, bouncy mood.

definition: Annoying; causing trouble.
note: Possibly a US alteration of pest or pesty, with an uncertain history.
hints: What a swarm of flies can be.
A mild word for irritating.

definition: A green sauce made from basil, nuts, cheese and oil.
note: From Italian pesto, 'pounded', because the ingredients are crushed together. It comes from Genoa.
hints: A sauce for pasta.
Basil-based and green.

definition: One of the coloured parts of a flower.
note: From Greek petalon, 'leaf'. Roses and daisies are ringed with them.
hints: Plucked in 'he loves me, he loves me not'.
The soft coloured part of a bloom.

definition: Small and unimportant; or mean over trivial things.
note: From Old French petit, 'small'. 'Petty cash' means a small fund for minor spending.
hints: Describes a spat over something trivial.
Cash is the small kind in an office drawer.

definition: One stage in a series of changes.
note: From Greek phasis, 'appearance'. The Moon goes through four of these each month.
hints: A stage the moon goes through.
A teenager's passing stage.

definition: A device for talking to people far away.
note: Short for telephone, from Greek tele, 'far', and phone, 'sound'. It is now often a pocket computer.
hints: Rings or buzzes in your pocket.
A device you tap, swipe and call from.

definition: Fake or insincere.
note: Of unknown origin, though it may come from an old slang word for a swindlers' brass ring. It is used for anything pretending to be real.
hints: A word for a fraud.
Describes a smile that is not genuine.

definition: A large keyboard instrument played with hammers striking strings.
note: Short for pianoforte, Italian for 'soft-loud', because it could play both quietly and loudly. Earlier keyboards could not vary volume with touch.
hints: Has black and white keys.
A concert grand is a big one.

definition: Fussy about what you will accept.
note: From pick plus -y. A picky eater chooses carefully among what is offered.
hints: A child refusing vegetables may be this.
One who is hard to please at dinner.

definition: A part broken or cut from something larger.
note: From Old French piece, from Late Latin pecia, of uncertain origin. It also names a single item in a set, such as a chess man.
hints: A slice of cake or a chess man.
One part of a jigsaw.

definition: Deep devotion to religion or duty.
note: From Latin pietas, meaning dutiful respect. It shares a root with pity.
hints: A word for being religious.
Sister word of 'pity'.

definition: A little pig, or a pet name for one.
note: From pig plus -y. It is used in 'piggy bank', a savings pot shaped like the animal.
hints: What a child may call a young swine.
A bank with a coin slot in its back.

definition: A person who flies an aircraft or steers a ship.
note: From Middle French pilot, from Italian pilota. It first meant a ship's guide into harbour before being used for aircraft.
hints: Sits in the cockpit.
A first episode of a series is called this.

definition: The smallest finger on the hand.
note: From a Dutch word for 'little', pink or pinkje, and the -y ending. The shade pink is a different word.
hints: The finger you swear a promise with.
The little one on your hand.

definition: A horse or bean with a patchy, spotted coat.
note: From Spanish pinto, 'painted' or 'mottled'. It names piebald horses and a speckled bean.
hints: A spotted horse in a western.
A kind of bean in chilli.

definition: A person who plays a pipe or bagpipes.
note: From pipe plus -er. The Pied one in the old tale lured rats and children.
hints: A famous one led rats out of a town.
Plays the bagpipes at a Scottish parade.

definition: Irritation caused by hurt pride; or to stir interest.
note: From French piquer, 'to prick'. Curiosity can be this, in the phrase 'to ___ someone's interest'.
hints: A feeling after a slight to your pride.
A fit of this makes someone storm off.

definition: A black sticky substance; also to throw, or the tone of a sound.
note: The tar sense is from Old English pic, from Latin pix. The throwing sense is a separate word of uncertain origin.
hints: What a baseball player throws.
How high or low a note sounds.

definition: Short and full of meaning.
note: From pith plus -y. Pith is the spongy centre of a plant stem, and by extension the core of an idea.
hints: Describes a short, sharp remark.
A quip is this.

definition: The smallest dot of a digital image.
note: A blend of 'pix', for pictures, and 'element'. A screen is built from millions of them.
hints: A tiny square on a screen.
A camera rating is counted in millions of them.

definition: A small mischievous fairy.
note: The word is first recorded in the seventeenth century in the folklore of south-west England. Its origin is uncertain.
hints: A mythical creature with pointed ears.
Associated with Cornish folklore.

definition: A round flat bread baked with tomato and cheese.
note: Borrowed from Neapolitan, first recorded in Naples in 1590. It reached English in 1931.
hints: Often delivered in a box.
Naples is its famous home.

definition: A particular spot or position.
note: From Old English place and Old French place, both from Latin platea, 'broad street'. It can name a position, a home, or a rank.
hints: Where something is located.
What you take at the table.

definition: Cloth with a pattern of crossing stripes.
note: From Scots plaid, of uncertain origin, and ultimately from Scottish Gaelic plaide, 'blanket'. In North America it names any tartan-like pattern.
hints: A pattern on a lumberjack shirt.
Tartan is a close cousin.

definition: Simple and without decoration; also a flat stretch of land.
note: From Old French plain, from Latin planus, 'flat'. Both senses come from the idea of something smooth and even.
hints: Opposite of fancy.
A great, flat grassland.

definition: A braid of hair or straw.
note: From Old French pleit, from Latin plectere, 'to weave'. A pleat is a related form.
hints: A braid in a girl's hair.
Three strands woven together.

definition: A long, flat piece of timber.
note: From Old Northern French planque, from Latin planca. It also names a sport exercise and a part of a political platform.
hints: A pirate victim walked off one.
A flat board used to build a deck.

definition: A public square in a town.
note: From Spanish plaza, from Latin platea, 'broad street'. It is a word for an open gathering space.
hints: Where people meet in a city centre.
A Spanish word for a town square.

definition: To beg earnestly; or to enter a response in court.
note: From Old French plaidier, 'to bring a legal case'. A defendant pleads guilty or not guilty.
hints: What a child does for a treat.
A defendant makes one in court.

definition: A fold pressed into cloth.
note: From Middle English, a variant of plait. A kilt is full of them.
hints: A crease sewn into a skirt.
Folds in a kilt.

definition: A person who plies; also a tool, in the plural.
note: From ply plus -er. You are far more likely to see it as 'pliers', a gripping tool.
hints: Singular of a gripping tool's name.
You rarely see this form without an s.

definition: To pull sharply; also courage.
note: From Old English pluccian, 'to pull'. The sense of courage is figurative, as in 'having the pluck to try'.
hints: What you do to a guitar string.
Courage, as in having plenty of it.

definition: Exactly vertical; also a lead weight on a line.
note: From Old French plombe, from Latin plumbum, 'lead'. A plumber originally worked with lead pipes.
hints: A builder checks a wall is this.
Weight hanging from a string.

definition: A large feather, or a rising column of smoke.
note: From Latin pluma, 'feather'. Smoke or water rising in a feathery shape is named after it.
hints: A feather on a hat.
What smoke rising from a chimney can form.

definition: Pleasantly rounded or chubby.
note: From Middle Dutch plomp. It was once also used to mean 'blunt', as in 'a plump refusal'.
hints: A cheek or a fruit might be this.
Round and well-fed.

definition: To drop or place with a dull sound.
note: Imitative of the sound. The noun is recorded earlier than the verb.
hints: A sound like a pebble landing in water.
How a heavy coin lands in a jar.

definition: Luxurious and soft; or a soft fabric.
note: From French peluche, 'fluff'. Toy bears made of it are called by the same word.
hints: A soft toy bear's fabric.
A velvet-like fabric, or very luxurious.

definition: An old word for poetry.
note: From Old French poesie, from Greek poiesis, 'a making'. It has a bookish, old-fashioned feel.
hints: A dusty word for verse.
What a bard composes.

definition: A sharp end; also a purpose or a score.
note: From Old French point, from Latin punctum, 'a prick'. It covers a tip, a dot, a score and the main idea.
hints: The sharp end of a pencil.
The idea behind an argument.

definition: Calm balance and self-assurance.
note: From Old French pois, 'weight'. Balanced weight became balanced bearing.
hints: A graceful and steady manner.
What a ballerina has on one foot.

definition: A card game of betting and bluffing; also an iron rod.
note: The card game is American, of uncertain origin. The tool for stirring a fire is a separate word, from poke.
hints: A game where you hold your cards close.
What you stir the fireplace with.

definition: Relating to the Earth's poles.
note: From Latin polus, from Greek polos, 'pivot'. Bears and ice caps are described with it.
hints: A bear that lives in the Arctic.
A cold region at the top of the globe.

definition: A lively dance from Bohemia.
note: From Czech, probably from pulka, 'half', for the half-step. It spread across Europe in the nineteenth century.
hints: Spotted pattern as well as a dance.
Dots, in the name of a pattern.

definition: A small growth; or a tubelike sea creature.
note: From Greek polypous, 'many-footed'. Coral is made of colonies of these.
hints: A tiny animal that builds a reef.
A word for a growth with many feet, in Greek.

definition: A pet dog.
note: Its origin is uncertain. It has been used as a friendly term for a dog since the early twentieth century.
hints: A friendly name for a dog.
What you walk each evening.

definition: A bright red flower; also its colour.
note: From Old English popig, from Latin papaver. Red ones are worn on Remembrance Day.
hints: A red flower worn in November.
Its seeds go on a bagel.

definition: A covered entrance or veranda at the front of a house.
note: From Old French porche, from Latin porticus, 'portico'. It is where you may sit on a swing.
hints: Where a rocking chair sits.
The covered part by a front door.

definition: A hard puzzle; or someone who pretends.
note: From pose plus -er. It also means a person who acts in a false way to impress.
hints: A brain-teaser.
Someone who acts like what they are not.

definition: To put forward as a basis for argument.
note: From Latin positus, 'placed'. Philosophers posit theories before testing them.
hints: To suggest an idea for debate.
What a scientist does with a hypothesis.

definition: A group summoned to chase a criminal.
note: Short for Latin posse comitatus, 'the power of the county'. It is now a casual word for a group of friends.
hints: In old westerns, a sheriff gathers one.
A band of friends, in slang.

definition: A small bag; or a kangaroo's pocket.
note: From Old French pouche, from a Frankish word. Marsupials carry their young in one.
hints: Where a kangaroo carries its baby.
A small bag on a belt.

definition: A unit of weight or of British money; also to hit repeatedly.
note: From Old English pund, from Latin pondo, 'weight'. The hitting sense is a separate word.
hints: Sterling money unit.
What a hammer does to a nail.

definition: Tending to pout.
note: Built from pout plus -y. Pout is a verb for pushing out the lips in sulkiness.
hints: How a sulking child's lips look.
Sticking out the lower lip.

definition: The ability to do something, or control over others.
note: From Old French povoir, from Latin potis, 'able'. It covers strength, authority, and electricity.
hints: What a strong engine produces.
What a ruler holds over a country.

definition: A mischievous trick played for fun.
note: Of uncertain origin; it may be linked to an old verb meaning to show off or dress up. 1 April is the day it is most expected.
hints: A whoopee cushion on a chair.
A harmless trick on April Fools' Day.

definition: A large edible shellfish like a shrimp.
note: First recorded in the early fifteenth century in several spellings. It has no clear relatives in other languages.
hints: Often served in a cocktail.
A seafood close to a shrimp.

definition: To tidy feathers, or to admire yourself.
note: From Middle English, from an old word for a pin. Birds preen to keep their feathers neat, and people preen to look good.
hints: A bird does it to its feathers.
What a vain person does before a mirror.

definition: To push firmly; also newspapers or a printing machine.
note: From Old French presser, from Latin pressare, 'to press'. The newspapers sense comes from the printing press.
hints: What you do to a doorbell.
A collective word for journalists.

definition: The cost of something.
note: From Old French pris, from Latin pretium, 'worth'. Price and prize were once the same word.
hints: What a tag shows.
What a shopper checks before buying.

definition: A feeling of satisfaction in your own worth; also a group of lions.
note: From Old English pryde, from an older word for 'proud'. A group of lions is called a pride, a poetic use.
hints: A feeling after a big win.
A group of lions.

definition: Best in quality; or first in importance.
note: From Latin primus, 'first'. A prime number has only itself and one as factors.
hints: A number such as seven, in maths.
The highest quality, as of beef.

definition: First-rate; excellent.
note: Borrowed from Italian primo, 'first'. It is a doublet of prime.
hints: Slang for top quality.
An Italian word for 'first'.

definition: To mark letters onto paper; or a mark left behind.
note: From Middle English prenten, shortened from emprinten, 'to imprint'. It names text, pictures and a fingerprint.
hints: What a machine does with ink.
A mark left by a thumb.

definition: Coming before in time; also a monastery official.
note: From Latin prior, 'earlier'. In law it describes a previous conviction.
hints: Earlier in time, as in a previous commitment.
A head of a small monastery.

definition: A glass shape that splits light into colours.
note: From Greek prisma, 'something sawn off'. Newton used glass ones to show light breaking into a spectrum.
hints: Used to make a rainbow of light.
A shape with triangular ends.

definition: Sharing in secret knowledge; also an outhouse.
note: From Old French prive, 'private'. 'Privy to' means let in on a secret.
hints: Told in confidence, you are said to be this to it.
A word for an old outdoor toilet.

definition: To explore or investigate; or a tool or craft for exploring.
note: From Latin probare, 'to test'. It names a doctor's instrument and a spacecraft.
hints: What space agencies send to far planets.
A journalist might do it into a scandal.

definition: Lying face down; or likely to suffer something.
note: From Latin pronus, 'bent forward'. People are prone to colds, or lie prone on the ground.
hints: Lying face down on the floor.
Likely to suffer something, as in 'accident-___'.

definition: A pointed tip of a fork.
note: From Middle English pronge. A trident has three.
hints: One tip on a fork.
A tooth of a pitchfork.

definition: Evidence that shows something is true.
note: From Old French prove, from Latin probare, 'to test'. It is also the strength of alcohol.
hints: What a lawyer must show a court.
What a maths exercise ends with.

definition: Feeling deep satisfaction in yourself or others.
note: From Old English prud, 'proud' or 'haughty'. The word moved from vanity towards healthy satisfaction.
hints: How a parent feels at a graduation.
Said of someone pleased with an achievement.

definition: To show that something is true.
note: From Old English profian and Old French prover, from Latin probare, 'to test'. It once meant to try or test something.
hints: What evidence does to a claim.
Show that a claim is correct.

definition: To move quietly in search of prey.
note: From Middle English prollen, of unknown origin. Cats and burglars prowl.
hints: What a tiger does at night.
A burglar might do it around a house.

definition: A person or thing authorised to stand in for another.
note: From Middle English, a contraction of procuracie, from Latin procuratio, 'management'. In computing it relays web traffic.
hints: One who votes in your place.
A server that relays web traffic.

definition: A dried plum; also to cut back a plant.
note: The fruit is from Old French prune, from Latin prunum. The cutting verb is separate, from Old French proignier.
hints: A wrinkled dried fruit.
What a gardener does to a rose bush.

definition: A sacred song or poem of praise.
note: From Old English psealm, from Greek psalmos, 'song sung to a harp'. The Bible contains 150 of them.
hints: A song in the Bible.
Sung by choirs in church.

definition: Short and plump.
note: From pudge, a word of uncertain origin, plus -y. It is often used affectionately for children's fingers.
hints: A chubby baby's hands.
Round and soft.

definition: Swollen or full, as if inflated.
note: From puff plus -y. It describes eyes after crying or a jacket full of down.
hints: What eyes look like after crying.
A jacket filled with down.

definition: Soft and fleshy; or in a cheap sensational style.
note: From pulp plus -y. Pulp is the soft inside of fruit, and cheap magazines were once printed on pulp paper.
hints: Orange juice with bits.
Like the cheap fiction of old magazines.

definition: A blow with the fist; also a fruity drink.
note: The blow is from Old French ponchonner, 'to punch'. The drink is a separate word, likely from Hindi.
hints: A boxer throws one.
A bowl at a party with fruit juice.

definition: Relating to the stage between larva and adult insect.
note: From pupa plus -al. Pupa is Latin for 'girl' or 'doll'.
hints: A stage in a butterfly's life.
The chrysalis phase.

definition: A student; also the dark centre of the eye.
note: From Latin pupillus, 'orphan' or 'ward'. The eye sense is from Latin pupilla, 'little doll', after the tiny reflection seen in it.
hints: A student in a class.
The black centre in the middle of the iris.

definition: A young dog.
note: From earlier puppie, once a woman's pet dog, of uncertain origin. It was probably from French poupee, 'doll'.
hints: A young dog that chews your shoes.
Eight weeks old and full of play.

definition: Food blended to a smooth paste.
note: Borrowed from French puree. Baby food is often this.
hints: A smooth blend of cooked vegetables.
What a blender makes of soup.

definition: To rid of something unwanted.
note: From Old French purgier, from Latin purgare, 'to make pure'. It is used for cleansing and for removing members of a group.
hints: To clear out what is unwanted.
A political clearing out of rivals.

definition: A small bag for money; or to tighten the lips.
note: From Old English purs, from Latin bursa, 'bag'. Lips are said to be pursed when pressed tight.
hints: A handbag or coin holder.
What lips do when puckered.

definition: Aggressively assertive.
note: From push plus -y. A pushy salesperson does not take no for an answer.
hints: A salesman who will not accept refusal.
A person who shoves forward to get ahead.

definition: A soft paste that sets hard, used to fix window glass.
note: From French potee, 'potful', originally a polishing powder. It stays soft until it dries.
hints: What holds a pane in its frame.
Clay-like stuff for sealing cracks.

definition: The cry of a duck; or a fake doctor.
note: Imitative of the duck's call. The fraud sense is short for quacksalver, someone who boasts of remedies.
hints: What a duck says.
A fraudulent healer.

definition: To shrink back in fear; also a small game bird.
note: The verb is from Middle Dutch queilen. The bird is a separate word, from Old French quaille.
hints: What a coward might do before a bully.
A small game bird with speckled feathers.

definition: A tiny particle that makes up protons.
note: Coined in 1963 by physicist Murray Gell-Mann, apparently an arbitrary word. It is also a fresh cheese in German.
hints: A tiny part of a proton.
Up and down are two flavours.

definition: A quarter of a gallon.
note: From Old French quarte, from Latin quartus, 'fourth'. It equals two pints.
hints: Two pints of milk.
A fourth of a gallon.

definition: To put an end to; to annul.
note: From Old French quasser, from Latin quassare, 'to shake'. Courts quash verdicts and rebels are quashed.
hints: What a judge does to a conviction.
To crush a rebellion.

definition: Seemingly; almost but not quite.
note: Latin for 'as if'. It is used as a prefix, as in 'quasi-official'.
hints: A Latin word meaning 'as if'.
Used as a prefix, as in '-official'.

definition: A female monarch, or the wife of a king.
note: From Old English cwen, 'woman' or 'wife'. It is also a chess piece and a card.
hints: Wears a crown.
The strongest piece on a chessboard.

definition: To calm or put down.
note: From Old English cwellan, 'to kill'. It now means to suppress, as of riots or fears.
hints: What police do to a riot.
To calm fears.

definition: A question.
note: From Latin quaere, 'ask'. It is a word for a database request.
hints: Typed into a search box.
A question put to a database.

definition: A long search for something.
note: From Old French queste, from Latin quaerere, 'to seek'. Knights went on one for the Holy Grail.
hints: What knights set out on.
A game mission with a reward.

definition: A line of people waiting.
note: From Old French cue, 'tail', from Latin cauda. British people are famed for joining one.
hints: What people form at a bus stop.
A British word for a line.

definition: Fast; taking little time.
note: From Old English cwic, which meant 'alive'. The old sense survives in 'the quick and the dead' and in 'quicksand'.
hints: Opposite of slow.
Once meant 'alive' in Old English.

definition: Making little or no noise.
note: From Old French quiet, from Latin quietus, 'at rest'. It is related to the word quit.
hints: What a library asks for.
What a room is when everyone is silent.

definition: A large feather, or a pen made from one.
note: First recorded in the early fifteenth century for a reed fragment and a feather shaft. Porcupines also have these sharp spines.
hints: A pen dipped in ink, long ago.
A spine on a porcupine.

definition: A padded bed covering stitched in layers.
note: From Old French cuilte, from Latin culcita, 'mattress'. Patchwork ones are sewn from scraps.
hints: A patchwork bed covering.
Grandma may have sewn one.

definition: A peculiar habit or twist of character.
note: First recorded in the 1540s, of uncertain origin. It is possibly from an old Norse word for a bend or angle.
hints: A small oddity of someone's character.
A habit that makes a person unique.

definition: Fairly, or completely.
note: From Middle English quite, from Old French quite, 'free' or 'clear', from Latin quietus. It once meant 'completely'.
hints: A word that can mean fairly or entirely.
As in 'it's ___ cold'.

definition: An old word meaning 'said'.
note: From Old English cwæth, the past tense of cwethan, 'to say'. The raven in Poe's poem is famously 'quoth' nevermore.
hints: An old past tense of say.
Poe's raven did it.

definition: A Jewish teacher and religious leader.
note: From Hebrew, meaning 'my master', and later passed into Greek and Latin. It was a title of respect for scholars.
hints: Leads a synagogue.
A title meaning 'my master' in Hebrew.

definition: Infected with rabies; or fanatical.
note: From Latin rabidus, 'raging', from rabies. It is often used of fierce supporters.
hints: How a mad dog might be described.
Fanatical, as in a very eager fan.

definition: Someone or something that takes part in races.
note: Built from race plus -er. Race itself came from Old Norse ras, 'a running'.
hints: Drives a fast car on a track.
What a runner is in a sprint.

definition: A system that finds objects by bouncing radio waves off them.
note: An acronym for 'radio detection and ranging'. It was developed in the 1930s and 1940s.
hints: Used by air traffic controllers.
Something that is 'under' it goes unnoticed.

definition: A device or system that broadcasts sound by waves.
note: Short for radiotelegraphy, with radio- from Latin radius, 'ray'. It carries music and talk.
hints: Plays music in the car.
A device with a tuning dial.

definition: Having a lot of rain.
note: From Old English reginig, built from rain plus -y. People save money 'for a ___ day', meaning for hard times.
hints: A day to take an umbrella.
The sort of weather that fills puddles.

definition: To lift up or increase.
note: From Old Norse reisa, 'to raise'. It is the causative of rise.
hints: What you do with your hand to ask a question.
To bring up a child or lift a flag.

definition: An Indian prince or king.
note: From Hindi raja, from Sanskrit rajan, 'king'. It is a relative of the Latin rex.
hints: A ruler in India.
A prince of old India.

definition: Wheat noodles served in broth.
note: Borrowed from Japanese, which took it from Chinese la mian, 'pulled noodles'. Instant packets are a cheap staple.
hints: A noodle soup from Japan.
Instant packets feed students.

definition: A large farm for cattle or horses.
note: From American Spanish rancho, 'small farm'. It was recorded in English in 1808.
hints: Cowboys work on one.
Also a creamy salad dressing.

definition: A line of mountains; or the extent of something.
note: From Old French rengier, 'to arrange in a row', from renc, 'rank'. It also names a stove and a shooting area.
hints: A line of mountains.
A big cooker in a kitchen.

definition: Very fast.
note: From Latin rapidus, 'swift', from rapere, 'to seize'. Rivers have these, in the plural.
hints: White water in a river.
Very quick in motion.

definition: Rough and scratchy in sound.
note: From rasp plus -y. A rasp is a coarse file, and by extension a harsh sound.
hints: A voice after shouting all day.
Hoarse and scratchy.

definition: Shabby or run down; or in a bad mood.
note: From rat plus -y. It can mean worn-out and rodent-like.
hints: A worn-out old sweater.
British slang for irritable.

definition: A large black bird with a deep croak.
note: From Old English hraefn. Edgar Allan Poe's famous poem is about one.
hints: A big black bird in a Poe poem.
A bird kept at the Tower of London.

definition: A soft fabric made from cellulose fibre.
note: The name was chosen in 1924 in the United States, probably from French for 'ray of light', because of its shine.
hints: A silky cloth made from wood pulp.
A fabric first made as artificial silk.

definition: A sharp blade used for shaving.
note: From Old French rasour, from raser, 'to scrape'. It is also the name of a thin shell.
hints: What a barber uses.
Used on a beard.

definition: To stretch out to touch something; or to arrive at.
note: From Old English raecan, 'to stretch out'. It covers extending a hand and getting to a place.
hints: What you do for a top shelf.
What an arm does to grab something.

definition: To respond to something.
note: From re- plus act. In chemistry, substances do it when mixed.
hints: What you do when startled.
Chemicals do it when mixed.

definition: Prepared and set to go.
note: From Old English raede, 'prepared'. It is the starting word in 'set, go'.
hints: Said before the starting gun.
The first word in a countdown.

definition: A kingdom or domain.
note: From Old French reaume, of unclear origin, possibly from Latin regalis, 'royal'. It is used for fantasy lands too.
hints: A kingdom in a fairy tale.
A word for a field of activity.

definition: To supply with weapons again.
note: From re- plus arm. A rebuilding army or nation does it.
hints: What a disarmed country might do.
To load up weapons again.

definition: Steel rods used to strengthen concrete.
note: A blend of 'reinforcing' and 'bar'. It gives concrete the tensile strength it lacks.
hints: Hidden inside concrete.
Steel bars inside a wall.

definition: A person who resists authority.
note: From Old French rebelle, from Latin rebellis, 'waging war again'. Teenagers are often called one.
hints: One who defies those in charge.
The sort who defies a government.

definition: A puzzle that uses pictures to stand for words.
note: From French, from Latin rebus, 'by things'. A picture of an eye plus a can might spell something.
hints: A picture puzzle.
A wordless word game.

definition: A short summary of what happened.
note: Short for recapitulation. It is often shown at the start of a TV episode.
hints: A summary at the start of a TV show.
What an announcer gives of the story so far.

definition: To happen again.
note: From Latin recurrere, 'to run back'. A recurring dream is one you have often.
hints: A dream that repeats.
Said of events that come around again.

definition: To cut again.
note: From re- plus cut. A film can be this when editors reshape it.
hints: What an editor may do to a film.
Trimming something a second time.

definition: Thin and high in sound; or full of reeds.
note: From reed plus -y. Reed instruments can have this tone.
hints: A high, thin tone.
A marsh grown over with tall grass.

definition: To mention, or send to another source.
note: From Old French referer, from Latin referre, 'to carry back'. It is a doublet of relate.
hints: What a doctor does for a specialist.
To point to a source.

definition: To repair or fit out again.
note: From re- plus fit. Ships are said to get one in dock.
hints: What a ship gets in a dock.
A makeover of a vessel.

definition: Fit for a king or queen.
note: From Old French regal, from Latin regalis, from rex, 'king'. A stately posture is called it.
hints: Like a royal.
Stately, like a monarch.

definition: Treatment to recover from addiction or injury.
note: A clipping of rehabilitation. It is used for treatment centres.
hints: A place to recover from addiction.
Treatment after an injury.

definition: To become calm and less tense.
note: From Latin relaxare, 'to loosen', from laxus, 'loose'. It is a command many give to the anxious.
hints: What a spa promises.
What you do on a sofa.

definition: A race in which team members pass a baton; or to pass on.
note: From Old French relaier, 'to exchange tired animals for fresh'. It first named fresh hounds or horses along a route.
hints: A track race passing a baton.
To pass a message along.

definition: An old object that survives from the past.
note: From Old French relique, from Latin reliquiae, 'remains'. It also names a saint's remains kept in a church.
hints: An ancient artefact.
Part of a saint kept in a church.

definition: Relating to the kidneys.
note: From Latin ren, 'kidney'. Doctors use it in terms like 'renal failure'.
hints: A medical adjective for an organ.
Doctors use it for kidney matters.

definition: To make new again, or extend.
note: From re- plus new. You do it to a library book or a passport.
hints: What you do to a subscription.
What you do to a library loan.

definition: To pay back what you owe.
note: From Old French repaier, from re- plus paier, 'to pay'. It covers debts and kindnesses.
hints: What you do with a loan.
Return a favour.

definition: To drive back or push away.
note: From Latin repellere, 'to drive back'. Insect sprays do it to mosquitoes, and magnets of the same pole do it to each other.
hints: What a spray does to mosquitoes.
Like poles do it to each other.

definition: A repeat of a television show.
note: From re- plus run. Summer schedules are often full of them.
hints: A repeat broadcast.
TV in summer is full of them.

definition: To set back to the starting state.
note: From re- plus set. A button on a device often does this.
hints: What a button on a router does.
To restore a clock to zero.

definition: A sticky substance from trees, or a synthetic one like it.
note: From Greek retine, through Latin and Old French. Amber is fossilised tree resin.
hints: What amber was before it hardened.
Sticky sap used to make glue and varnish.

definition: To strain as if about to vomit.
note: From Old English hraecan, 'to clear the throat, cough up'. It describes the heaving without the result.
hints: What a bad smell may make you do.
A dry heave.

definition: Styled after the past.
note: Borrowed from French retro, from Latin retro, 'backwards'. It names fashions that deliberately look old.
hints: A throwback style from decades ago.
Old-school fashion that is back in style.

definition: To try again.
note: From re- plus try. Software offers a button for it after a failure.
hints: What a failed upload invites.
What a court may do in a second trial.

definition: To use something again.
note: From re- plus use. It sits alongside reduce and recycle.
hints: Part of a green slogan, with reduce and recycle.
Using a bag a second time.

definition: To take great delight; or a noisy celebration.
note: From Old French reveler, 'to be disorderly', from Latin rebellare, 'to rebel'. It is a doublet of rebel.
hints: What partygoers do at a feast.
To take joy in something.

definition: A stage show of sketches, songs and dances.
note: Borrowed from French revue, literally 'review'. It parodied the events of the year.
hints: A show of comic sketches and songs.
Often mocks the news of the year.

definition: A large horned animal; short for rhinoceros.
note: A clipping of rhinoceros, from Greek words for 'nose' and 'horn'. In British slang the word has also meant money.
hints: A thick-skinned horned beast.
A threatened animal of Africa and Asia.

definition: Words that end in the same sound; or a short verse.
note: From Old French rime, with the spelling later influenced by Greek rhythmos. Nursery verses are called it.
hints: Cat and hat do it.
A nursery verse.

definition: A person who rides.
note: From Old English rideri, 'knight' or 'horseman'. It is also a clause added to a document.
hints: Sits on a horse or a bicycle.
Someone on a bike or horse.

definition: A long narrow raised strip of land.
note: From Old English hrycg, 'back' or 'spine'. The word started as the back of an animal.
hints: A narrow crest at the top of a hill.
The top line of a roof.

definition: A long gun fired from the shoulder.
note: Short for 'rifled gun', after the spiral grooves in the barrel. As a verb it also means to rummage through.
hints: A hunter's long gun.
To search roughly through a drawer.

definition: Correct; or the opposite of left.
note: From Old English riht, 'straight' or 'just'. It also names a legal entitlement.
hints: Opposite of wrong.
The side of the body opposite the left.

definition: Stiff and not bending.
note: From Latin rigidus, from rigere, 'to be stiff'. It also describes inflexible views.
hints: A steel bar is this.
A strict rule that cannot bend.

definition: Strictness; harsh exactness.
note: From Latin rigor, 'stiffness', from rigere, 'to be stiff'. It also shows in 'rigor mortis'.
hints: Hard, exact discipline.
The stiffness after death, in Latin.

definition: To wash with clean water.
note: From Old French rincier, 'to rinse'. It often removes soap.
hints: What you do after shampooing.
A quick wash that leaves no soap.

definition: To grow ready to eat.
note: From ripe plus -en, from Old English ripian. Fruit left in the sun does it.
hints: What a banana does on the counter.
To become fully mature, as fruit.

definition: Having gone up; the past participle of rise.
note: From Old English risen, past participle of risan. It is the word for dough that has done its job.
hints: What bread dough has done after proving.
The past participle of a word about going up.

definition: Something that goes up; or a step on stairs.
note: Built from rise plus -er. 'An early riser' is someone who wakes at dawn.
hints: Someone who is up at dawn.
The upright part of a stair.

definition: Likely to cause harm or loss.
note: From risk plus -y. Risk came into English from French, which took it from Italian risco.
hints: A gamble might be called this.
Describes a dangerous bet.

definition: A person or group competing against another.
note: From Latin rivalis, 'one who uses the same stream'. Neighbours who shared water were often in dispute.
hints: A competitor for the same prize.
A business that sells to the same customers.

definition: A large natural stream of water.
note: From Old French riviere, from Latin ripa, 'bank'. It flows to the sea.
hints: The Thames or the Nile.
Water flowing to the sea.

definition: A metal pin used to join sheets of metal.
note: From Old French rivet, from river, 'to fasten'. It is hammered flat at one end.
hints: Used to build ships and bridges.
A metal pin on a pair of jeans.

definition: A cockroach; or a freshwater fish.
note: The insect word is short for cockroach, from Spanish cucaracha. The fish is an older, different word from Old French.
hints: A pest in the kitchen.
A pest that survives anything.

definition: To cook in an oven; or to mock in good fun.
note: From Old French rostir, from a Frankish word. A comedy event named for it features jokes at the guest's expense.
hints: A Sunday dinner meat.
A comic event of friendly insults.

definition: A machine that carries out tasks automatically.
note: From Czech robota, 'forced labour', used in Karel Capek's 1920 play. It entered English soon after.
hints: A mechanical worker.
A machine from a Czech play of 1920.

definition: Full of rocks; or unsteady.
note: From rock plus -y. A relationship or a road can be this.
hints: A road of boulders and stones.
A shaky start to a project.

definition: A show of cowboy skills like bull riding.
note: From Spanish rodeo, from rodear, 'to surround', since it was a cattle roundup. It is now a sport.
hints: A show with bucking broncos.
Cowboys ride bulls in it.

definition: Radio word meaning 'message received'.
note: In 1940s military radio it stood for the letter R, short for 'received'. It was later replaced by 'romeo' in the spelling alphabet.
hints: What a pilot says to confirm.
Used in radio chat to say 'got it'.

definition: Having plenty of space.
note: From room plus -y. Room comes from Old English rum, 'space'.
hints: A big car interior.
Like a spacious closet.

definition: A perch where birds rest or sleep.
note: From Old English hrost, which meant 'perch' and also the framework of a roof. 'Rule the roost' means to be in charge.
hints: Where chickens sleep.
A perch where a hen settles for the night.

definition: The turning part of a machine.
note: From a clipping of rotator, coined by William Kingdon Clifford. A helicopter has blades on one.
hints: The spinning blades on a helicopter.
The turning part in a motor.

definition: A red powder for the cheeks.
note: Borrowed from French rouge, from Latin rubeus, 'red'. It means 'red' in French.
hints: Makeup applied for colour in the cheeks.
French for the colour red.

definition: Not smooth; or approximate.
note: From Old English ruh, 'rough' or 'hairy'. It is spelled with a gh but sounds like f.
hints: Sandpaper has a surface like this.
Like a draft that is not polished.

definition: Shaped like a circle or ball.
note: From Old French rond, from Latin rotundus, 'wheel-shaped'. It also names a turn in a game or a drinks order.
hints: Like a ball or a coin.
A turn in a boxing match.

definition: A wanderer; or a vehicle that explores a planet.
note: From rove plus -er. Spacecraft that explore planets are named after it.
hints: A vehicle that explores Mars.
A wanderer who never settles.

definition: Noisy and disorderly.
note: Possibly from row, in the sense of 'noisy argument'. It started in the United States for a rough person.
hints: A noisy crowd after a match.
Loud and out of control.

definition: A person who pulls oars.
note: From row plus -er. Oxford and Cambridge race each other each spring.
hints: Sits in a boat and pulls hard.
A person in a university boat race.

definition: Belonging to a king or queen.
note: From Old French roial, from Latin regalis, from rex, 'king'. It is a doublet of regal.
hints: A family with a crown.
A word for a monarch's household.

definition: Healthy reddish in colour.
note: From Old English rudu, 'redness', plus -y. In British speech it is also a mild swear word.
hints: A healthy red complexion.
The glow of a fire on a face.

definition: A team sport played with an oval ball.
note: Named for Rugby School in Warwickshire, where the game developed in the nineteenth century.
hints: A game of tries and scrums.
Played with an oval ball.

definition: A person who governs; or a straight measuring strip.
note: From rule plus -er. A schoolchild has one in a pencil case.
hints: A king or queen, or a strip for drawing straight lines.
Marked in centimetres.

definition: A Cuban ballroom dance with a slow rhythm.
note: Borrowed from Spanish rumba, of Cuban origin. It is danced in pairs.
hints: A Latin dance.
Cuban, and danced in pairs.

definition: An unproven story going from person to person.
note: An American spelling of rumour, from Latin rumor, 'common talk'. It spreads without proof.
hints: Gossip with no source.
What spreads in an office without proof.

definition: The currency of India and several nearby countries.
note: From Hindustani rupiya, a coin introduced by Sher Shah Suri in the sixteenth century. It is also used in Pakistan and Nepal.
hints: Money in India.
Currency in Nepal and Sri Lanka.

definition: Relating to the countryside.
note: From Latin ruralis, from rus, 'countryside'. It is the opposite of urban.
hints: Opposite of urban.
Farms and villages.

definition: In a sorrowful way; or unfortunately.
note: From sad plus -ly. 'Sad' once meant 'full' or 'satisfied' in Old English.
hints: How a person might say goodbye.
Used to introduce unwelcome news.

definition: A person recognised by a church as holy.
note: From Old English sanct and Old French saint, from Latin sanctus, 'holy'. Churches name many after them.
hints: A holy person with a feast day.
Patrick and George are two.

definition: A dish of raw vegetables, often with a dressing.
note: From Old French salade, from Latin sal, 'salt', because the greens were once dressed with salt. It reached English around the fifteenth century.
hints: A bowl of greens.
Lettuce, tomato and cucumber.

definition: A place where hairdressers or beauticians work; or a grand reception room.
note: Borrowed from French, which took it from Italian salone, 'large hall'. In the 1700s a salon was also a gathering for talk and ideas.
hints: A place for a haircut or a manicure.
A gathering of thinkers in an eighteenth-century drawing room.

definition: A spicy sauce; also a Latin dance and its music.
note: From Spanish salsa, 'sauce', from Latin salsus, 'salted'. The music style took the same word.
hints: A dip to go with tortilla chips.
A Latin dance with quick steps.

definition: A healing ointment.
note: From Old English sealf, from an old Germanic word for 'ointment'. It is also used for anything that soothes, such as a salve for guilt.
hints: A cream for a minor burn.
Anything that eases a conscience.

definition: A burst of gunfire; or a sudden round of applause or criticism.
note: From Latin salvo, 'safe' or 'reserved', first used in law for an exception. It later came to mean a volley of guns fired together.
hints: A volley of cannon fire.
An opening attack in a dispute.

definition: Too sentimental; or full of tree juice.
note: From Old English saepig, 'full of sap', built from sap plus -y. The sentimental sense is figurative, like something too sweet.
hints: A movie that is too soppy.
A tree full of sticky sugar.

definition: Bold, cheeky and lively.
note: An American alteration of saucy, first recorded in 1799. It describes a confident tongue.
hints: A cheeky answer to an elder.
A bold, spirited retort.

definition: A smooth fabric with a glossy surface.
note: From French satin, which may trace to the Arabic name of a Chinese port city. It reached Europe through trade.
hints: A glossy fabric for evening wear.
Sheets or gowns that feel silky.

definition: A half-man, half-goat spirit of Greek myth.
note: From Greek satyros, through Latin and French. In myth satyrs followed the god Dionysus.
hints: A creature from Greek myth with a goat's legs.
A woodland follower of the god of wine.

definition: A liquid served with food.
note: From Old French sauce, from Latin salsa, 'salted'. Salt was the original seasoning.
hints: What pasta is served with.
Tomato or soy, perhaps.

definition: Cheeky; or a little bit rude in a fun way.
note: From sauce plus -y. A sauce adds spice, so a saucy remark has a bit of spice.
hints: A cheeky remark with a bit of spice.
Slightly rude, but in a fun way.

definition: A small room heated to high temperatures for sweating.
note: Borrowed from Finnish sauna. Finland has a long tradition of them.
hints: A hot Finnish steam room.
A hot wooden room people sit in to sweat.

definition: Shrewd and well-informed.
note: Probably from creole forms of Portuguese sabe, 'he knows', from saber. It began as a pidgin word for 'to know'.
hints: What a tech-literate person is.
Streetwise and clever.

definition: To burn with hot liquid or steam.
note: From Old Northern French escalder, from Latin excaldare, 'to wash in hot water'. Milk is scalded by heating it almost to boiling.
hints: What boiling water does to skin.
A burn from steam.

definition: A set of marks for measuring; also a device for weighing; or a small plate on a fish.
note: From Latin scala, 'ladder', for the measuring sense, and from a separate Old French word for the plate on a fish.
hints: A bathroom device for weighing yourself.
A fish's armour plate.

definition: The skin on top of the head, under the hair.
note: From Middle English scalp, probably from a North Germanic word. It once meant the skull's crown.
hints: Where dandruff forms.
The skin under your hair.

definition: Covered with small flat plates.
note: From scale plus -y. Fish and snakes are covered with them.
hints: A lizard's skin.
What a fish's skin is covered in.

definition: A mischievous rascal.
note: From Middle Dutch schampen, 'to slip away', via Old French escamper, 'to run away'. It first meant a rogue and is now used affectionately of a naughty child.
hints: A cheeky child.
A little rascal.

definition: To frighten; or a fright.
note: From Middle English skerren, 'to frighten', from Old Norse. As a noun it names a sudden fright or public alarm.
hints: What a ghost story tries to do.
A sudden fright.

definition: A long strip of cloth worn around the neck.
note: Probably from Old Northern French escarpe, 'pilgrim's purse hung from the neck'. It then came to mean cloth worn around the neck.
hints: Worn around the neck in winter.
Keeps your neck warm.

definition: Causing fright.
note: From scare plus -y. It is the usual word for a horror film.
hints: A horror film is this.
Makes your heart race on a dark night.

definition: A smell, especially a pleasant one.
note: From Old French sentir, 'to feel or smell', from Latin sentire. Hounds follow a trail by it.
hints: A perfume's fragrance.
A trail a hound follows.

definition: A descendant of a notable family; also a cutting for grafting.
note: From Old French cion, from a Frankish word meaning 'shoot' or 'twig'. Gardeners graft one onto a rootstock.
hints: A young heir of a famous family.
A twig grafted onto a tree.

definition: To mock someone; or to eat greedily.
note: The mocking sense is from Middle English, probably of North Germanic origin. The eating sense is a separate British slang word.
hints: What a rude person does to a poor idea.
British slang for wolfing food down.

definition: To tell someone off angrily.
note: From Middle English scolde, first recorded around the twelfth or thirteenth century. It was once a noun for a quarrelsome person.
hints: What an angry parent does.
A telling-off for a child who misbehaved.

definition: A small baked quick bread eaten with jam and cream.
note: Originally Scots, possibly from a Dutch or Low German word for 'fine bread'. It is the centre of cream tea.
hints: Eaten with clotted cream and jam.
Part of an English afternoon tea.

definition: A tool for lifting loose material; also an exclusive news story.
note: From Middle Dutch schope, 'bucket for bailing water'. In journalism it is a story that a rival lacks.
hints: What you use to serve ice cream.
A reporter's exclusive news story.

definition: The extent of something; or an aiming device.
note: From Italian scopo, 'aim', from Greek skopos, 'target'. It is also a short form of words like microscope.
hints: How wide a project reaches.
A sight on a rifle.

definition: Deep contempt for someone or something.
note: From Old French escharnir, 'to mock'. To scorn something is to treat it as beneath you.
hints: A curl of the lip showing contempt.
What you may feel for a bad idea.

definition: To scrub hard; or to search thoroughly.
note: From Middle Dutch scuren, 'to polish'. The search sense comes from rough, hurried movement over an area.
hints: What you do to a burnt pan.
What a detective does to a crime scene.

definition: Someone sent ahead to gather information.
note: From Old French escoute, 'listening', from Latin auscultare, 'to listen'. It is also a young member of a youth movement.
hints: A soldier sent ahead of an army.
A talent-spotter at a football match.

definition: To frown angrily.
note: From Middle English scowlen, probably of North Germanic origin. It is used for dark, unfriendly looks.
hints: The face of a grumpy person.
A dark, angry frown.

definition: To go away quickly.
note: Possibly a clipping of scramble, or from German schramm. It is commonly shouted at someone unwelcome.
hints: What you tell a stray cat.
What you shout to shoo away a pest.

definition: A small piece left over; or to discard.
note: From Old Norse skrap, 'trifles'. It also means a minor fight, in British speech.
hints: A bit of leftover paper.
A bit of metal bound for the junkyard.

definition: A slope of loose stones on a hillside.
note: Probably from Old Norse skridha, 'landslide'. Climbers find it tiring because it slides underfoot.
hints: Stones sliding on a mountain.
Loose rock that slips under a climber.

definition: A threaded metal fastener you twist in.
note: From Old French escroue, 'nut'. It is driven in with a turn.
hints: What you drive with a driver.
A threaded fastener for wood.

definition: To rub hard to clean; or low bushes.
note: From Old English scrybb, a variant of shrub. The cleaning verb is separate.
hints: What you do to a dirty floor.
The low bushes of a dry plain.

definition: A tight huddle of players or people.
note: A shortening of scrummage, a variant of scrimmage. Rugby players push against each other in one.
hints: Packed forwards pushing in rugby.
A crush of reporters around a politician.

definition: Underwater breathing gear.
note: An acronym for 'self-contained underwater breathing apparatus'. It lets a diver breathe without a hose to the surface.
hints: What a diver wears to breathe.
Gear with an air tank.

definition: A closed car with a separate trunk.
note: The word first meant a covered chair carried by two men, from 1634. The car body style borrowed it.
hints: A four-door family car.
A chair carried by two porters.

definition: Shabby and a little disreputable.
note: From seed plus -y. The shabby sense dates to the 1700s and referred to worn-out appearance.
hints: A rundown bar in a bad district.
A squalid-looking hotel.

definition: To move smoothly from one thing to another.
note: From Italian segue, 'it follows', a musical direction. It now describes smooth transitions in talk.
hints: A smooth shift between topics.
Moving from one song to the next without a pause.

definition: To grab or take by force.
note: From Old French seisir, 'to take possession'. It is also used for grabbing a chance, as in 'seize the day'.
hints: What a customs officer does to contraband.
To grab hold of a chance.

definition: A way of perceiving, such as sight or smell; or good judgement.
note: From Latin sensus, 'feeling'. Humans have five of them, by tradition.
hints: Sight and smell are two of the five.
A word for good judgement.

definition: A reddish-brown colour of old photographs.
note: From Latin sepia, 'cuttlefish', whose ink gave the pigment. Old prints have this tint.
hints: The tint of a faded old photograph.
A pigment from a sea creature's ink.

definition: A small stroke at the end of a letter.
note: From earlier ceriph, of obscure origin. Times New Roman has them; Arial does not.
hints: A feature of Times New Roman.
A typeface style with tiny feet.

definition: The clear fluid part of blood; or a treatment made from it.
note: From Latin serum, 'whey'. It is now also a cosmetic liquid.
hints: A clear fluid from blood.
A face treatment in a small dropper bottle.

definition: To work for someone; or to put food on a plate.
note: From Old French servir, from Latin servire, 'to be a slave'. Tennis players do it to start a point.
hints: What a waiter does with food.
What you do to open a game of tennis.

definition: The way something is arranged or organised; or a trick arranged in advance.
note: A noun made from the verb phrase 'set up'. It names an arrangement of equipment, or a plot arranged to frame someone.
hints: How a desk and monitors are arranged.
A rigged situation meant to trap someone.

definition: The number after six.
note: From Old English seofon, shared by nearly all Indo-European languages. It was long regarded as a lucky number.
hints: One more than six.
The number of days in a week.

definition: To cut apart; to end a connection.
note: From Old French sevrer, from Latin separare, 'to separate'. It is a doublet of separate.
hints: What a surgeon or a quarrel can do to a tie.
To cut off completely.

definition: An underground channel that carries away waste water.
note: From Anglo-Norman sewere, 'water course', from Old French. It is the sort of place where alligators are said to live in urban legend.
hints: Below the street, carrying waste away.
Where city drainage ends up.

definition: A small, crude hut.
note: Its origin is unknown; some scholars suggest Mexican Spanish jacal, from Nahuatl. It is a roughly built shelter.
hints: A rickety hut by the shore.
Like a cabin that needs repair.

definition: A dark area out of the sun; or a variety of a colour.
note: From Old English sceadu. It also names a lampshade and a small variation of a colour.
hints: A cool spot under a tree.
Dark green or light green, as a variation.

definition: Giving shade; or suspicious and dishonest.
