note: Built from shade plus -y. A shady deal is one done out of sight.
hints: A park bench under a big tree.
A dodgy business deal.

definition: A long narrow rod or passage.
note: From Old English sceaft, 'pole' or 'spear shaft'. It is also a vertical passage in a mine or lift.
hints: The long body of an arrow.
A narrow vertical passage in a mine.

definition: To move quickly to and fro.
note: From Old English scacan, 'to shake'. It also names a drink made from milk and ice cream.
hints: What you do to a snow globe.
What a dog does after a bath.

definition: Trembling, or not firm.
note: Built from shake plus -y. A shaky voice or a shaky argument both lack steadiness.
hints: A voice that wavers when nervous.
An argument that might not hold.

definition: A soft, finely layered rock.
note: From Old English sceal, 'shell' or 'husk'. It splits into thin flakes and is a source of oil and gas.
hints: A rock that splits in thin layers.
A soft rock that gas is extracted from.

definition: A helping verb for the future or duty.
note: From Old English sceal, 'I must'. The earlier sense of obligation survives in 'thou shalt not'.
hints: Used with I and we in formal futures.
An old word of obligation in commandments.

definition: A painful feeling of having done something wrong.
note: From Old English scamu, 'shame' or 'disgrace'. It is also used for a pity, as in 'what a pity'.
hints: What a blush may show.
The feeling after doing something embarrassing.

definition: The part of the leg between knee and ankle.
note: From Old English sceanca, 'leg'. It also names the shaft of a tool and, in prison slang, a homemade blade.
hints: A cut of lamb from the lower leg.
The long part of a tool between handle and tip.

definition: The outer form of something.
note: From Old English gesceap and sceap, meaning 'creation' or 'form'. It also means condition, as in 'in good ___'.
hints: A circle or a square.
Fitness, as in 'in good form'.

definition: A broken fragment, usually of glass or pottery.
note: From Old English sceard, 'a gap' or 'broken piece'. Archaeologists find pottery ones.
hints: A sliver of broken pottery.
A sharp fragment of broken glass.

definition: A portion; or to give a part to others.
note: From Old English scearu, 'a cut' or 'division'. It also names a unit of ownership in a company.
hints: A slice of the pie.
A unit of stock in a company.

definition: A large predatory sea fish; or a cunning swindler.
note: From Middle English, first recorded in 1442 for the fish. Its origin is uncertain. A card shark is a swindler at cards.
hints: A big fish with a dorsal fin.
A cunning card-player who cheats.

definition: Having a fine cutting edge; or clever.
note: From Old English scearp, 'cutting'. It is also a musical note raised a half step.
hints: What a knife must be to cut well.
A music note raised a half step.

definition: To cut hair off the skin with a razor.
note: From Old English scafan, 'to scrape'. A narrow miss is a 'close one'.
hints: What you do with foam and a blade.
Done to a beard each morning.

definition: To cut off wool from a sheep.
note: From Old English sciran, 'to cut'. Sheep farmers do it each spring.
hints: What a farmer does to a flock in summer.
To clip a fleece.

definition: A gentle shine on a surface.
note: From Old English sciene, 'beautiful' or 'bright'. The adjective became a noun for a glossy brightness.
hints: The glow on polished wood.
A soft glossy shimmer.

definition: A woolly farm animal.
note: From Old English sceap. The plural is the same as the singular.
hints: What a shepherd tends.
A word whose plural looks identical.

definition: Complete; or very thin.
note: From Old English scire, 'bright' or 'clear'. It describes pure, unmixed things and also near-transparent cloth.
hints: A very thin curtain.
A cliff that drops straight down.

definition: A flat piece of cloth, paper or metal.
note: From Old English sciete, 'cloth'. A bed has one, and so does a printer tray.
hints: Linen on a bed.
A page in a printer tray.

definition: A hard outer covering.
note: From Old English sciell. Eggs, nuts and snails all have one.
hints: The covering of an egg or a snail.
A seaside find for a collector.

definition: To move or change position; or a period of work.
note: From Old English sciftan, 'to divide' or 'arrange'. It also names a work period, as in 'the night ___'.
hints: A change of position.
The hours someone works at a factory.

definition: To give out light.
note: From Old English scinan, 'to shine'. Shoes and the sun do it.
hints: What the sun does.
What polished shoes do.

definition: Bright and reflecting light.
note: From shine plus -y. New coins are this way.
hints: New coins and polished shoes.
What a polished car looks like.

definition: An English county.
note: From Old English scir, 'district'. It is the ending in county names such as Lancashire.
hints: Where Tolkien's hobbits lived.
The final part of several English county names.

definition: To avoid a duty.
note: First recorded around 1633, possibly linked to the verb shark. It describes dodging work.
hints: What a lazy worker may do with chores.
To avoid a responsibility.

definition: A garment for the upper body, with sleeves and a collar.
note: From Old English scyrte, from a Germanic root meaning 'short'. It is a cousin of skirt.
hints: Worn with a tie.
Buttoned up the front.

definition: A group of fish; or a shallow area of sea.
note: The fish sense is from Middle Dutch scole, 'troop'; the shallow-water sense is from Old English sceald, 'shallow'. The two words sound alike by accident.
hints: Fish swimming together.
A sandbank near a coast.

definition: A sudden upsetting surprise.
note: From Middle French choquer and Middle Dutch schokken, 'to jolt'. It also means an electric jolt.
hints: What bad news can be.
What an electric jolt delivers.

definition: To fire a weapon; or a new plant growth.
note: From Old English sceotan. It also covers filming a movie and a young plant sprout.
hints: What an archer does with an arrow.
A new plant growth.

definition: The land at the edge of a sea or lake.
note: From Middle English schore, perhaps from a Germanic word for a cliff. The beach lies on it.
hints: Where waves meet the land.
A coast in a sailor's view.

definition: Cut off; having had hair or wool clipped.
note: The old past participle of shear, from Old English scoren. Sheep farmers cut their wool in spring.
hints: A sheep after its spring cut.
Having lost one's locks.

definition: Not long or not tall.
note: From Old English sceort, from a Germanic root. It is cousin to skirt and shirt.
hints: The opposite of tall.
A kind of trousers worn in summer.

definition: To call out loudly.
note: From Middle English shouten, of uncertain origin. In Britain a 'shout' is also a round of drinks.
hints: What a fan does in a stadium.
To yell across a field.

definition: To push roughly.
note: From Old English scufan, 'to push'. It is a rougher form of a push.
hints: What you do in a crowded lift.
A rough push.

definition: Flashy and attention-seeking.
note: From show plus -y. A showy outfit is meant to be noticed.
hints: A peacock's feathers might be called this.
A loud, bright outfit.

definition: A tiny mouse-like animal; or a nagging woman.
note: From Old English screawa, 'shrew'. Shakespeare's play about taming one is a comedy.
hints: A tiny insect-eating mammal.
The Shakespeare play about one being tamed.

definition: A woody plant smaller than a tree.
note: From Old English scrybb, 'bushy plant'. It has several stems, unlike a tree.
hints: Smaller than a tree, bigger than a flower.
A bush in the garden.

definition: To raise the shoulders to show doubt or indifference.
note: From Middle English schruggen, probably from a Scandinavian word. A shrug can say 'I don't know'.
hints: A gesture meaning 'who cares'.
Raising both shoulders in doubt.

definition: To remove a husk or shell.
note: Its origin is unknown. It is what you do to corn and oysters.
hints: What you do to an ear of corn.
What you do to an oyster.

definition: To push aside or move elsewhere.
note: From Middle English schonten, 'to jerk or swerve'. A train is shunted onto another track.
hints: A train moved onto a side track.
Moving someone out of the way.

definition: To tell someone to be quiet.
note: Imitative of the hissing sound used to quiet someone. It resembles hush.
hints: What a librarian does.
The sound of a finger to the lips.

definition: In a timid, bashful way.
note: Built from shy plus -ly. Shy comes from Old English sceoh, 'timid'.
hints: How a child waves hello.
A way of smiling that avoids eyes.

definition: A long attack in which a place is surrounded.
note: From Old French sege, 'seat', from Latin sedere, 'to sit'. Besiegers sit down outside.
hints: An army camped around a castle.
Troy endured a famous one.

definition: A tool with small holes for separating fine from coarse bits.
note: From Old English sife. Flour is passed through one, and the phrase 'a memory like one' means forgetful.
hints: A kitchen tool with a mesh for flour.
Said of a poor memory that lets things fall through.

definition: The ability to see; or something seen.
note: From Old English gesihth, 'vision'. It also names the aiming device on a gun.
hints: One of the five senses.
What a tourist attraction is called.

definition: The eighteenth letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Greek sigma. In mathematics it stands for a sum, and in statistics for standard deviation.
hints: A Greek letter used for summing.
Written as an angular capital or a looping small letter.

definition: Soft and smooth, like fine fabric.
note: From silk plus -y. Silk was prized as a luxury import from China.
hints: A smooth, glossy hair or voice.
Soft as a fabric made by caterpillars.

definition: Foolish or playful.
note: From Old English saelig, 'happy' or 'blessed'. Its meaning slid from lucky to innocent to foolish over centuries.
hints: A clown's behaviour.
Once meant 'blessed' in Old English.

definition: From a past time up to now; or because.
note: From Middle English sithens, from Old English sith tham, 'after that'. It can start a time clause or a reason.
hints: A word used with dates, as in 'from then'.
Can also mean 'because'.

definition: To burn slightly at the surface.
note: From Old English sengan, 'to burn slightly'. Hair and fabric are easily scorched this way.
hints: What a match might do to hair.
A light scorch, not a full burn.

definition: A loud warning device; also a mythical sea singer.
note: From Greek Seiren, the sea women whose song lured sailors to their doom. The warning device took the name for its wail.
hints: Wails on an ambulance.
A mythical singer who lured sailors.

definition: Number six in a sequence.
note: From Old English siexta, built on six plus the ordinal ending. It follows the fifth.
hints: The one after the fifth.
A year of school in Britain, before university.

definition: The number after fifty-nine.
note: From Old English sixtig, 'six tens'. It marks the number of minutes in an hour.
hints: Minutes in an hour.
A ripe age for a retirement party.

definition: To glide on a blade or wheels; also a flat fish.
note: From Dutch schaats, from a word for a stilt. The fish is a separate word, from Old Norse.
hints: A blade fixed to a boot.
A flat ray-like fish.

definition: A person who glides down snow on long runners.
note: From ski plus -er. Ski is a Norwegian word meaning 'stick of wood'.
hints: Wears goggles on a mountain.
Moves down a slope on boards.

definition: A small light boat.
note: From Middle French esquif, from Italian schifo. It is the same root as the word ship.
hints: A small rowing boat.
A little boat for one or two.

definition: The ability to do something well.
note: From Old Norse skil, 'distinction' or 'discernment'. It is gained through practice.
hints: What practice builds.
Something an expert has and a beginner lacks.

definition: A garment that hangs from the waist.
note: From Old Norse skyrta, 'shirt'. It is a cousin of the word shirt.
hints: Worn at the waist, falling below.
Also to avoid a topic by going around it.

definition: To move around stealthily.
note: From Middle English sculken, from a North Germanic word. A group of foxes is also called one.
hints: To sneak around.
What a fox does in the dark.

definition: The bony frame of the head.
note: From Middle English sculle, probably of Scandinavian origin. A pirate flag shows one.
hints: The bone that shelters the brain.
The symbol on a pirate flag.

definition: A small black-and-white animal that sprays a foul-smelling fluid.
note: From an Algonquian word, from a root meaning 'one who squirts'. It reached English in the 1630s.
hints: An animal with a bad smell.
A black animal with a white stripe.

definition: Loose; not taut; or lazy.
note: From Old English slaec, 'lazy' or 'loose'. A rope can be this, and so can a worker.
hints: A rope that hangs loose.
Lazy in doing duties.

definition: Killed, especially in battle.
note: The past participle of slay, from Old English slean, 'to strike'. It belongs to epic poetry.
hints: What a dragon-killer's victim was.
A dragon, once the knight was done.

definition: Casual, informal language.
note: First recorded around 1756 for the special talk of thieves. Its origin is unknown.
hints: Words like 'cool' and 'bro'.
Casual words that dictionaries record later.

definition: A slope; or a point of view.
note: From Middle English, probably from a Scandinavian word. In news it can mean a particular bias in how a story is told.
hints: A tilt, like a roof.
A bias in a news story.

definition: To cut with a sweeping stroke; or the symbol /.
note: From Late Middle English, of uncertain origin. It is also the key above the Enter key.
hints: A sword stroke.
The key beside the full stop.

definition: A grey rock used for roofs; or a list of candidates.
note: From Old French esclate, 'splinter'. 'A clean slate' is a fresh start, from the writing tablets that were wiped.
hints: A grey roofing tile.
What you wipe clean to start over.

definition: A person owned by another and forced to work.
note: From Medieval Latin sclavus, from the name of the Slavic peoples, many of whom were enslaved in the Middle Ages. It is also used for a device controlled by another.
hints: A person held in bondage.
A device controlled by a master.

definition: Smooth and glossy.
note: A late variant of slick. It is used for hair, cars and designs.
hints: Describes a polished car or an otter's coat.
Smooth, shiny and elegant.

definition: To rest with your eyes closed.
note: From Old English slaepan. People do it for about a third of their lives.
hints: What you do at night.
What a dormouse does all winter.

definition: A thin piece cut from something.
note: From Old French esclice, 'splinter'. It is what you cut from a cake.
hints: A piece of bread.
A wedge of pizza.

definition: Smooth and slippery; or polished and clever.
note: From Old English slic, 'smooth'. An oil spill is one on water.
hints: Oil on water may make one.
A clever, too-polished salesman.

definition: To glide smoothly; or a playground structure.
note: From Old English slidan. It names a playground feature and a presentation page.
hints: Children go down one at the park.
A page in a presentation.

definition: A thick slippery goo.
note: From Old English slim, 'mud' or 'sticky stuff'. Snails leave a trail of it.
hints: What a snail leaves behind.
Green ooze in a children's show.

definition: Covered in slime; or repulsively insincere.
note: From slime plus -y. A slimy person is an oily flatterer.
hints: Like a wet frog.
A used-car salesman, in a rude description.

definition: To throw; or a strap for holding something.
note: From Middle English slyngen, probably from Old Norse slyngva, 'to hurl'. David used one against Goliath.
hints: What David used against Goliath.
A band that supports a broken arm.

definition: To move quietly and guiltily.
note: From Old English slincan, 'to creep'. A cat that has done wrong may do it.
hints: How a guilty dog leaves the room.
To creep away, ashamed.

definition: A single-masted sailing boat.
note: Borrowed from Dutch sloep. It is a doublet of chalupa and shallop.
hints: A one-masted sailboat.
A small ship in the age of sail.

definition: A surface that tilts upward or downward.
note: From the adjective aslope, 'at an angle'. A hill side or a ski run is one.
hints: A hillside that tilts, good for skiing.
Not flat; running at an angle.

definition: To splash noisily.
note: Imitative of the sound of liquid moving. Compare splash and splosh.
hints: What water in a bucket does when carried.
The noise of boots in puddles.

definition: Laziness; or a slow tree-dwelling animal.
note: From Middle English slouthe, 'laziness', built from slow. One of the seven deadly sins.
hints: One of the seven deadly sins.
An animal that hangs from branches.

definition: Past tense of slink.
note: The past tense of slink, from Old English slincan, 'to creep'. It is used for sneaking away.
hints: What a thief did on leaving.
What a cat did after being caught.

definition: To drink or eat noisily.
note: From Middle Dutch slurpen, 'to sip'. It is considered polite with noodles in Japan.
hints: The noise of soup eaten with relish.
What you do with a straw at the end of a drink.

definition: Half-melted snow.
note: Possibly a variant of sludge, or imitative of the sound. It makes city streets messy.
hints: Grey snow in a street.
Wet snow in thaw.

definition: In a sneaky or cunning way.
note: From Middle English sleighly, built from sly plus -ly. It suggests a secretive smile.
hints: A secretive smile, as of a fox.
Doing something while hoping no one notices.

definition: A sharp slap; or a slight taste.
note: The slap is imitative. The taste sense is from Old English smaec, 'taste'.
hints: A sharp blow with a flat hand.
A touch of flavour or trace of something.

definition: Little in size.
note: From Old English smael, 'narrow' or 'slender'. It is the opposite of large.
hints: The opposite of big.
Tiny, like a mouse.

definition: Clever; or to sting.
note: From Old English smeortan, 'to hurt'. The sense of clever evolved from being sharp or stinging.
hints: What a bright student is.
What a stinging cut does.

definition: To break violently; or a big hit.
note: Probably imitative of the sound. A tennis shot is named for it.
hints: What a hammer does to glass.
A hit show or film.

definition: To spread something messy across a surface.
note: From Old English smerian, 'to anoint with fat'. It also means to damage someone's name.
hints: What jam does on a cheek.
To blacken a rival's reputation.

definition: The sense that detects odours.
note: From Middle English smellen, of unknown earlier origin. It is the sense of the nose.
hints: What your nose picks up.
Fresh bread has a good one.

definition: To melt ore to extract metal; also a small silvery fish.
note: From Middle Low German smelten, 'to melt', and it is also the past tense of smell. The fish is a separate word in the same spelling.
hints: What a furnace does to ore.
A small fish in the same family as a salmon.

definition: To turn up the corners of the mouth in pleasure.
note: From Middle English smilen, probably from Middle Low German. It is a common show of happiness.
hints: What a joke or a greeting often brings.
A happy curve of the mouth.

definition: A self-satisfied, half-hidden smile.
note: From Old English smearcian, 'to smile'. It suggests smugness rather than warmth.
hints: A smug grin after winning.
The expression of someone who knows a secret.

definition: To strike hard; to punish severely.
note: From Old English smitan, 'to smear or daub'; the sense of striking came later. It appears in the Bible when God punishes.
hints: What a god or a hero might do to an enemy.
An old word for a heavy blow.

definition: A person who works metal; also a common surname.
note: From Old English smith, 'craftsman'. It survives in blacksmith and goldsmith.
hints: The one who shapes iron on an anvil.
The most common surname in England.

definition: A loose garment worn over clothes to protect them.
note: From Old English smocc, 'a garment slipped into'. Painters and children wear them.
hints: What a painter wears over clothes.
A loose protective shirt.

definition: The cloud given off by something burning.
note: From Old English smoca. It rises from chimneys and campfires.
hints: What billows from a chimney.
Where there is this, there may be fire.

definition: Filled with smoke, or tasting of it.
note: From smoke plus -y. Smoky bacon and whisky carry this flavour.
hints: A bar in the days before indoor bans.
A flavour of barbecue sauce or whisky.

definition: A small bit of food eaten between meals.
note: From Middle Dutch snacken, 'to snap at'. It is lighter than a meal.
hints: Crisps or fruit between meals.
What you grab when you are peckish.

definition: A slow animal with a spiral shell.
note: From Old English snegel. It carries its home on its back.
hints: A slow animal with a house on its back.
A creature that leaves a slimy trail.

definition: A long limbless reptile.
note: From Old English snaca. A person who betrays is also called one.
hints: A long, legless reptile that hisses.
A traitor, in a rude sense.

definition: Twisting like a snake; or sly.
note: From snake plus -y. A winding road can be this.
hints: A winding mountain road.
Twisting and treacherous.

definition: A trap; also a type of drum.
note: From Old English sneare, 'noose'. The drum takes its name from the wires stretched across the head.
hints: What a hunter sets with a loop of wire.
A drum with a rattling sound.

definition: To growl angrily; or a tangle.
note: The tangle is from Middle English snarlen, 'to trap', built on the word snare. The growl is a separate word.
hints: A dog baring its teeth.
A tangle in your hair.

definition: To move quietly and secretly.
note: From Old English snican, 'to creep or crawl'. A sneak preview is an early secret showing.
hints: What a burglar does through a house.
An early look at a film.

definition: To show scorn by curling the lip.
note: From Middle English sneren, 'to mock'. It is a scornful expression.
hints: A curled lip of scorn.
A look of contempt at a poor effort.

definition: Mockingly critical in a sly way.
note: Probably from a dialect word meaning 'sharp' or 'cutting'. A snide remark is a cheap shot.
hints: A sly, nasty comment.
A cheap jab from the back row.

definition: To breathe in through the nose in short, audible breaths.
note: From Middle English sniffen, imitative of the sound. A cold or a smell can make you do it.
hints: What a dog does at a lamp post.
What a person with a cold does.

definition: To shoot from hiding; also a wading bird.
note: From Old Norse snipa, the bird. Hunters who shot the elusive bird were 'snipers', and the verb followed.
hints: A hidden shooter's act.
A long-billed bird of the marsh.

definition: To pry into other people's affairs.
note: From Dutch snoepen, 'to eat in secret'. It now suggests prying.
hints: What a nosy neighbour does at a window.
To spy on a private matter.

definition: A loud rough breath through the nose.
note: From Middle English snorten, earlier fnorten. Pigs and bulls do it, and so do amused people.
hints: A pig's noise.
What a stifled laugh may turn into.

definition: The long nose of an animal such as a pig.
note: From Middle English snute. Pigs root in the ground with one.
hints: A pig's nose.
A part of a crocodile's face.

definition: To put out a candle; or powdered tobacco.
note: The tobacco sense is from Middle Dutch snuffen, 'to sniff'. A candle is put out by pinching its wick.
hints: What you do to a flame.
Ground tobacco taken through the nose.

definition: Covered in or like soap.
note: From soap plus -y. Bath water, bubbles and dishes may be this.
hints: Water full of bubbles.
How hands feel before the tap.

definition: Wet and heavy.
note: From dialect sog, 'soaked', plus -y. Neglected cereal and sandwiches often end up so.
hints: Cereal left in milk too long.
A sandwich left in the rain.

definition: Relating to the sun.
note: From Latin solaris, from sol, 'sun'. Panels turn sunlight into power.
hints: Panels on a roof turn sunlight into electricity.
Our system is named for this star.

definition: Firm and not liquid or gas.
note: From Latin solidus, 'firm'. Ice is one, but steam is not.
hints: What ice is, compared with water.
A state of matter that holds its shape.

definition: To find the answer to a problem.
note: From Latin solvere, 'to loosen or untie'. A mystery or puzzle can be settled by it.
hints: What you do with a puzzle.
What a detective does to a case.

definition: A way of finding objects underwater using sound.
note: An acronym for 'sound navigation and ranging'. Submarines and fishing boats rely on it.
hints: A submarine's ping.
How a ship finds the seabed.

definition: Relating to sound.
note: From Latin sonus, 'sound'. A sonic boom is made by an aircraft passing the speed of sound.
hints: A boom from a fast jet.
Having to do with noise.

definition: An old word for truth.
note: From Old English soth, 'true'. It survives in 'forsooth' and in 'soothsayer', one who tells the truth of the future.
hints: An archaic word for truth.
A person who foretells the future was named for it, with 'sayer'.

definition: Covered in soot.
note: From soot plus -y. A chimney sweep would be this.
hints: A chimney sweep's face.
A black smudge from a fire.

definition: Feeling regret; or poor and pitiful.
note: From Old English sarig, 'sore' or 'grieved', related to sore. It is not related to sorrow.
hints: What you say after stepping on a toe.
A word that begins an apology.

definition: Noise; also healthy or reliable.
note: The noise sense is from Latin sonus. The healthy sense comes from Old English gesund, 'healthy'.
hints: What an ear picks up.
As in 'safe and ___', in good shape.

definition: The direction opposite north.
note: From Old English suth. It is the way to Antarctica from the equator.
hints: Opposite of north.
The way swallows go in winter.

definition: A person who scatters seed.
note: From Old English sawere, built from sow plus -er. A famous parable features one.
hints: A farmer scattering grain.
The farmer in a famous parable.

definition: The area beyond Earth; or an empty area.
note: From Old French espace, from Latin spatium. It can also be a gap between words.
hints: Where the stars are.
The gap between words on a page.

definition: A digging tool with a flat blade; also a card suit.
note: From Old English spadu. The card suit is a different word, from Italian spada, 'sword'.
hints: What a gardener uses to dig.
A black card suit.

definition: A sudden involuntary muscle contraction.
note: From Greek spasmos, from spaein, 'to draw or pull'. It also means a sudden burst of activity.
hints: A twitch in a muscle.
A sudden painful clench.

definition: To talk.
note: From Old English specan, probably an altered form of an older word sprecan. It is what you do with your voice.
hints: What you do to give a talk.
What a person does at a podium.

definition: A long pointed weapon for thrusting or throwing.
note: From Old English spere. Hunters and soldiers carried them for thousands of years.
hints: A weapon thrown by hunters.
A long shaft with a sharp point.

definition: A tiny spot.
note: From Old English specca, 'small spot'. Dust leaves one.
hints: A tiny dot of dust.
A dot barely visible on a window.

definition: How fast something moves.
note: From Old English sped, which meant 'success' or 'prosperity'. 'Godspeed' wished a traveller good luck.
hints: What a gauge on a dashboard shows.
How fast a car goes.

definition: A magic formula; or a short period of time.
note: From Old English spel, 'story' or 'speech'. A word spoken with power became a charm.
hints: What a wizard casts.
A short stretch of weather.

definition: An ancient grain; or past tense of spell.
note: The grain is from Old English spelt, a kind of wheat. The past tense form is a British spelling of spelled.
hints: An old variety of wheat.
The British past of a word about letters.

definition: To pay out money; or to pass time.
note: From Old English, partly from Latin expendere, 'to weigh out'. You can do it with money or hours.
hints: What a shopper does.
What you do with a holiday week.

definition: A strong flavouring from a plant.
note: From Old French espice, from Latin species, 'kind'. Pepper and cinnamon are famous ones.
hints: Pepper and cinnamon.
What makes a curry hot.

definition: Hot with flavourings.
note: From spice plus -y. Chilli peppers make food this way.
hints: A hot curry.
A food with a kick.

definition: A long, practiced sales speech.
note: Borrowed from German Spiel, 'game' or 'play', perhaps via Yiddish. It describes a patter delivered with practice.
hints: A salesperson's patter.
A well-rehearsed pitch.

definition: A sharp pointed piece of metal; or a sudden sharp rise.
note: From Old Norse spik, 'nail'. Sprinters wear shoes with them, and a graph can show a sudden one.
hints: What a runner wears on shoes for grip.
A sudden jump on a chart.

definition: Covered with sharp points.
note: From spike plus -y. Hedgehogs and punk hair are this.
hints: A hedgehog's coat.
Hair styled with gel.

definition: To let liquid fall out by accident.
note: From Old English spillan, 'to destroy or waste'. The word shifted from killing to wasting to letting fall.
hints: What you do to a cup of tea.
Something to avoid crying over, in a proverb.

definition: Poured out accidentally; the past form of spill.
note: The past form of spill. A proverb warns not to cry over milk in this state.
hints: The state of milk in a proverb about regret.
A British past form of a word about accidents with drinks.

definition: Covered in sharp spines.
note: From spine plus -y. Cacti and sea urchins are this.
hints: A cactus or an urchin.
Prickly all over.

definition: A tall pointed tower on a church.
note: From Old English spir, 'stalk' or 'shoot'. A church steeple reaches skyward like one.
hints: The pointed top of a church tower.
Salisbury's is famously tall.

definition: The sound of a soft thing hitting a flat surface.
note: Imitative, related to an older verb meaning to spread flat. It is the noise of a tomato landing.
hints: A tomato hitting the floor.
A wet slap of a dropped pie.

definition: To divide; or to break along a line.
note: From Middle Dutch splitten, recorded since about 1567. You can do it to a log, a bill, or a banana dessert.
hints: What you do to a bill among friends.
What an axe does to a log.

definition: To ruin; or to pamper.
note: From Latin spolium, 'plunder'. Food goes off, and children can be overindulged by it.
hints: What happens to milk left out.
What you do to a grandchild with sweets.

definition: Past of speak; also a rod in a wheel.
note: The verb is the past tense of speak. The wheel part is from Old English spaca, a different word.
hints: Joins the hub of a bicycle wheel to the rim.
What a person did at a podium.

definition: A light-hearted parody; or a trick.
note: Coined in 1884 by the English comedian Arthur Roberts as the name of a card game of trickery. It then came to mean a hoax.
hints: A comic imitation of a film.
A hoax played for laughs.

definition: A ghost; or to frighten.
note: Borrowed from Dutch spook, 'ghost'. It can also name a secret agent.
hints: What a ghost story might feature.
To startle a horse.

definition: A tiny reproductive cell of a fungus or plant.
note: From Greek spora, 'seed'. Mushrooms and ferns release them.
hints: What a mushroom scatters to reproduce.
A tiny seed-like particle from a fern.

definition: A competitive physical activity.
note: Short for disport, from Old French, 'to amuse oneself'. It originally meant any pastime.
hints: Football or tennis.
What the Olympics celebrates.

definition: A tube from which liquid pours.
note: From Middle English spouten, from Middle Dutch. A kettle has one, and so does a whale.
hints: The part of a teapot for pouring.
What a whale blows through its blowhole.

definition: A fine mist of liquid.
note: From Middle Dutch spraeyen, 'to sprinkle'. It also names a bunch of flowers.
hints: What an aerosol can does.
A cluster of flowers in a bouquet.

definition: A short period of unrestrained activity, especially shopping.
note: Of uncertain origin; it was first recorded in the early nineteenth century. It suggests wild abandon.
hints: A shopping binge.
An outing of reckless indulgence.

definition: A small twig or shoot.
note: From Middle English sprigge, of uncertain origin. A cook adds a small one of parsley.
hints: A small piece of parsley.
A little twig used to garnish a dish.

definition: To gush out suddenly; or a short burst of effort.
note: From earlier spirt, 'to sprout'. A runner makes one to overtake near the finish.
hints: What water does from a cut hose.
A final dash near the finish line.

definition: A small group working together.
note: From French escouade, from Spanish escuadra, 'square'. It first named a troop drawn up in a square.
hints: A football team's group of players.
A group of soldiers or police.

definition: To crouch low; or short and wide.
note: From Old French esquatir, 'to crush or flatten'. It also names a gym exercise and settling in an empty building.
hints: A deep knee bend at the gym.
What a short, stocky shape is called.

definition: A small firework that fizzes; or a short satire.
note: Possibly imitative of a small explosion. A damp one fizzles without going off, which gave the word its sense of a weak joke.
hints: A firework that fizzles.
A short, witty satirical piece.

definition: A tidy pile.
note: From Old Norse stakkr, 'haystack'. Pancakes and plates are piled in them.
hints: A pile of pancakes.
A tall pile of books.

definition: The employees of a business; or a long stick.
note: From Old English staef, 'stick' or 'letter'. It also names the lines on which music is written.
hints: The workers at a shop.
A stick used by a wizard.

definition: Serious, steady and rather dull.
note: An old spelling of 'stayed', the past participle of stay. It describes someone settled in their ways.
hints: A sober, conventional person.
The opposite of wild.

definition: A step in a flight.
note: From Old English staeger, 'step', from a word meaning 'to climb'. You go up a flight of them.
hints: One step in a flight.
What you climb in a house.

definition: No longer fresh.
note: From Old French estale, 'in place', as in standing too long. Bread and jokes both go this way.
hints: Bread left out for days.
A joke told too many times.

definition: The stem of a plant; or to follow someone secretly.
note: From Middle English stalke, of uncertain earlier origin. The following sense is a different word, from Old English.
hints: The stem of celery.
What a predator does to its prey.

definition: A market table; or to delay.
note: From Old English steall, 'standing place'. A car engine can do it, and so can a speaker buying time.
hints: A table in a market.
What an engine does when it cuts out.

definition: To be upright on your feet.
note: From Old English standan. It also names a stall, a position, or a platform.
hints: What you do when the anthem plays.
A position taken on an issue.

definition: Past tense of stink.
note: From Old English stanc, the past of stincan, 'to smell'. It describes a foul smell.
hints: What rotten eggs did in the fridge.
A past form of a word about foul smells.

definition: To look fixedly.
note: From Old English starian, 'to gaze'. It is considered rude when done at strangers.
hints: What you do at an eclipse you should not look at.
To gaze rudely.

definition: Severe or plain; or complete.
note: From Old English stearc, 'stiff' or 'strong'. A bare room or a sharp contrast can be this.
hints: A bare white room.
An obvious, harsh contrast.

definition: To begin.
note: From Old English styrtan, 'to leap up'. A sudden jump gave the word its sense of beginning.
hints: What you do at the line of a race.
The opposite of finish.

definition: A hidden supply.
note: Of unknown origin. It may blend 'stow' and 'cache'. People keep one of treats or cash.
hints: A hidden hoard of sweets.
A secret store.

definition: A condition; or a country's government and territory.
note: From Latin status, 'condition'. It can also mean to say something formally.
hints: What a nation is called politically.
The condition something is in.

definition: A narrow strip of wood; or to fend off.
note: A back-formation from staves, the plural of staff. 'Stave off' means to hold danger at a distance.
hints: A strip of wood in a barrel.
To keep hunger or danger away for a while.

definition: The place or role of another.
note: From Old English stede, 'place'. It survives in 'in his stead' and in 'homestead'.
hints: A word in an old phrase about taking another's place.
The tail end of the word for a farm and its buildings.

definition: A thick slice of meat.
note: From Old Norse steik, 'roast on a stick'. Beef is the best known.
hints: A thick cut of beef on a plate.
What a grill sizzles.

definition: To take something that is not yours.
note: From Old English stelan. In baseball, a runner can do it to a base.
hints: What a thief does.
What a runner does to a base.

definition: Hot water vapour.
note: From Old English steam, 'vapour'. Engines once ran on it.
hints: What rises from a kettle.
What drove old trains.

definition: A strong alloy of iron.
note: From Old English stiele. It builds bridges and skyscrapers.
hints: A strong alloy for bridges.
Iron mixed with carbon.

definition: Rising sharply; or to soak in a liquid.
note: From Old English steap, 'high' or 'lofty'. Tea leaves are soaked, and a high price is also called it.
hints: A hill hard to climb.
What tea does in a pot.

definition: To guide a vehicle; or a young bull.
note: From Old English steoran, 'to guide'. The animal sense is separate, from Old English steor.
hints: What you do with a wheel.
A young bull raised for beef.

definition: A large beer mug.
note: From German Stein, 'stone', short for stoneware jug. It is associated with Oktoberfest.
hints: Raised at Oktoberfest.
A mug for beer.

definition: Strict and severe; or the back of a ship.
note: The strict sense is from Old English styrne. The ship sense is a separate word, from Old Norse.
hints: A teacher who allows no nonsense.
The rear of a boat.

definition: A thin piece of wood; or to attach.
note: From Old English sticca, 'twig'. As a verb, it describes glue doing its work.
hints: A twig from a tree.
What glue does.

definition: Rigid and hard to bend.
note: From Old English stif. A neck after a long drive can be so.
hints: How your neck feels after a long drive.
Not flexible.

definition: Not moving; or even so.
note: From Old English stille, 'quiet' or 'motionless'. It is also a distilling apparatus.
hints: Motionless, like a pond.
A word meaning 'nevertheless'.

definition: A tall pole with a footrest for walking high off the ground; or a post holding up a building.
note: From Middle English stilte. Circus performers walk on them, and some houses stand over water on them.
hints: What a circus performer walks on to look tall.
A post that raises a house above a flood.

definition: To pierce skin with a sharp point, as a bee does; or a police trap.
note: From Old English sting, 'a piercing'. A sting can also mean a police operation to catch criminals.
hints: What a bee or a nettle does.
A police trick to catch a crook.

definition: To give off a strong foul smell.
note: From Old English stincan, which originally meant just 'to smell', pleasant or not. Only later did it turn bad.
hints: What rotten eggs do.
A bad smell.

definition: A fixed period of work.
note: From Old English styntan, 'to make blunt', which led to the sense of limiting. You may do a stint abroad.
hints: A short spell in a job.
A spell on duty, like a tour.

definition: A supply of goods; or a share in a company; or a flavoured broth.
note: From Old English stocc, 'tree trunk' or 'post'. It has many senses, from shop inventory to soup base.
hints: Goods on a shop's shelves.
Soup is built on a good one.

definition: A person who endures pain without complaint.
note: From Greek Stoikos, after the Painted Porch in Athens where the philosophers taught. They preached calm acceptance of fate.
hints: Someone who bears hardship without complaint.
A philosopher like Marcus Aurelius.

definition: To tend a fire by adding fuel.
note: From Middle Dutch stoken, 'to poke'. You can also stir up feelings with it.
hints: What you do to a furnace with coal.
To fuel a fire or an argument.

definition: Past tense of steal; also a long wrap worn over the shoulders.
note: The past tense is from Old English stal. The garment is from Latin stola, a different word.
hints: What the thief did to the jewels.
A fur wrap for a lady's shoulders.

definition: To step down heavily.
note: A variant of stamp, first recorded in 1803. A foot pounding the floor does it.
hints: What an angry child does.
A heavy walk that shakes the floor.

definition: A hard piece of rock.
note: From Old English stan. It is also a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds.
hints: A pebble on a beach.
A British measure of weight.

definition: Full of rocks; or cold and unfeeling.
note: From stone plus -y. A stare can be this way as can a field.
hints: A field full of rocks.
An unfriendly, cold silence.

definition: A seat with no back.
note: From Old English stol, 'seat' or 'throne'. A bar often has high ones.
hints: A seat in a bar.
What a milkmaid sat on.

definition: To bend forward and down; also the steps at a building's front door.
note: The verb is from Old English stupian. The porch sense is American, from Dutch stoep.
hints: What you do to pick up a coin.
The steps at a New York brownstone.

definition: A place where goods are sold; or to put away for later.
note: From Old French estorer, 'to build or furnish'. It is both a shop and a verb for saving.
hints: Where you buy groceries.
What a squirrel does with nuts.

definition: A large wading bird with long legs and bill.
note: From Old English storc. Folklore says it brings babies.
hints: A bird said to deliver babies.
A tall bird nesting on chimney tops.

definition: A violent disturbance of the weather.
note: From Old English storm. It describes wind, rain, snow and thunder.
hints: Thunder and lightning.
A hurricane or a blizzard.

definition: A tale told for entertainment; or a floor of a building.
note: From Old French estoire, from Latin historia, the same source as history. The meaning of a floor in a building is a separate sense of uncertain origin.
hints: A tale before bedtime.
One level of a skyscraper.

definition: A device for cooking or heating.
note: From Middle Dutch stove, 'heated room'. It first meant a hot room before the cooking sense.
hints: A cooker with burners.
What you boil a pot on.

definition: A narrow band of leather or cloth.
note: From strop, a variant of an old word for a loop on a harness. It holds a watch or a bag.
hints: What holds a watch on your wrist.
A band that holds a rucksack on a shoulder.

definition: Dried stalks of grain; or a thin tube for drinking.
note: From Old English streaw. The tube was first made of actual stalks.
hints: What a scarecrow is stuffed with.
What you sip a milkshake through.

definition: To wander off; or a lost animal.
note: From Old French estraier, 'to roam'. A lost dog or cat is called one.
hints: A lost cat without a home.
A dog roaming without an owner.

definition: A long narrow piece; or to remove clothing or covering.
note: From Middle Low German strippe, 'strap', of uncertain origin. It names a comic page, an airfield, and the act of undressing.
hints: A long, thin piece of paper.
A runway for aircraft.

definition: To walk proudly; or a supporting bar.
note: From Middle English strouten, 'to bulge'. A peacock does it. The bar sense is related.
hints: A peacock's walk.
A brace in a roof.

definition: Unable to move or progress.
note: The past tense of stick, from Old English stician. A cork can be this, and so can a crossword solver.
hints: What a car may be in mud.
How a puzzler feels without ideas.

definition: To learn about a subject.
note: From Old French estudier, from Latin studium, 'zeal'. It also names a room for reading.
hints: What a student does before an exam.
A room with a desk and books.

definition: Things or material; or to fill tightly.
note: From Old French estoffe, 'material'. It also means to cram a turkey with a filling.
hints: Odds and ends.
What you do to a turkey before roasting.

definition: What remains of a cut tree.
note: From Middle English stumpe. A politician's campaign speech is a 'stump speech'.
hints: What is left of a felled tree.
A short, thick remainder of something.

definition: A daring feat; or to hold back growth.
note: Its origin is unknown. It first appeared in American slang in the late nineteenth century for a feat of skill. A separate verb sense means to hold back growth.
hints: A dangerous move in a film.
What a lack of food can do to growth.

definition: A manner of doing things; or fashion.
note: From Latin stilus, 'pointed writing tool'. The writing tool gave its name to a way of writing, and then to any manner.
hints: How someone dresses or writes.
A fashionable quality.

definition: Smooth and charming in manner.
note: From Latin suavis, 'sweet'. It is a doublet of sweet.
hints: A debonair, polished gentleman.
Charming, like a film spy.

definition: A sweet crystalline food.
note: Ultimately from Sanskrit sarkara, 'gravel' or 'grit', through Arabic and Italian. Cane and beets are the main sources.
hints: What goes in tea.
A sweet crystal from cane.

definition: A set of rooms; or a set of musical pieces.
note: From French suite, 'following'. It is a doublet of suit.
hints: A fancy hotel room set.
A set of musical movements.

definition: Silent and moody after being upset.
note: From sulk plus -y. A sulky is also a light cart for harness racing that seats just one rider.
hints: A child quietly pouting.
A one-seat racing cart.

definition: To stain or spoil.
note: From Old English sylian, 'to soil'. It is most often used of reputations.
hints: What a scandal does to a good name.
To tarnish something clean.

definition: A shrub, and the tangy red spice made from its berries.
note: From Middle English sumac, from Arabic summaq, from a word meaning 'red'. It is used in Middle Eastern cooking.
hints: A tangy red spice.
A shrub whose leaves turn red in autumn.

definition: Bright with sunshine.
note: From Old English sunnig, built from sun plus -y. It also describes a cheerful nature.
hints: A clear, bright day.
A cheerful disposition.

definition: Excellent; or above and beyond.
note: From Latin super, 'above'. It is used as a prefix and on its own as slang.
hints: A slangy word for great.
The word before 'man' for a flying hero.

definition: Rude and bad-tempered.
note: A sixteenth-century alteration of sirly, 'lordly', from sir plus -ly. It once meant haughty before it meant gruff.
hints: A grumpy waiter.
Unfriendly and short-tempered.

definition: A Japanese dish of vinegared rice with fish or other toppings.
note: Borrowed from Japanese. The word originally referred to the sourness of the rice.
hints: Raw fish on rice.
Rolled with seaweed and eaten with soy sauce.

definition: A Hindu religious teacher.
note: From Hindi svami, from Sanskrit svamin, 'master' or 'lord'. It is used as a title of respect.
hints: A Hindu teacher.
A title meaning 'master'.

definition: Wet, spongy land with trees.
note: Early records from 1624 are from North America, with uncertain earlier roots. Alligators live in them.
hints: Wet land where alligators live.
A soggy, muddy marsh.

definition: A large flying or moving group of insects.
note: From Old English swearm. Bees and locusts do it, and so do crowds.
hints: Bees leaving a hive.
A large crowd moving together.

definition: The rush of water up a beach after a wave breaks.
note: Of Scandinavian origin; compare Swedish and Norwegian dialect words for splashing. It is the opposite of backwash.
hints: Water running up a beach.
Where the surf spreads out on the sand.

definition: A broad strip or sweep.
note: From Old English swaeth, 'track'. A farmer cuts a wide one with a scythe.
hints: A wide strip of cut grass.
A broad band of land.

definition: To make a solemn promise; or to use rude words.
note: From Old English swerian, 'to take an oath'. Both senses grew from the idea of invoking something sacred.
hints: What a witness does in court.
To curse when angry.

definition: To clean with a brush; or a long arc.
note: From Middle English swepen. It also names a chimney cleaner and a clean win in a series.
hints: What you do to a floor with a broom.
A win of every game in a series.

definition: Tasting like sugar; or pleasant and kind.
note: From Old English swete. It also names a candy in British speech.
hints: What honey tastes like.
A kind, endearing nature.

definition: To grow larger; or a rolling wave.
note: From Old English swellan. An ankle can do it, and so can the ocean.
hints: What a sprained ankle does.
A long wave out at sea.

definition: Past tense of sweep.
note: The past tense of sweep, from Middle English swepen. It describes a floor cleared with a broom, or someone carried away.
hints: What a broom did to the floor.
How a romantic hero treats someone off their feet.

definition: Fast; or a type of bird.
note: From Old English swift, 'quick'. The bird is named for its fast, darting flight.
hints: Quick and rapid.
A fast bird with sickle-shaped wings.

definition: Liquid kitchen scraps fed to pigs; or to drink greedily.
note: From Old English swillan, 'to wash'. It also means cheap, poor-quality drink.
hints: What a farmer pours into the pig trough.
To gulp down drink in large amounts.

definition: A pig; or a contemptible person.
note: From Old English swin. It is an old plural-looking word that is also singular.
hints: An old word for hogs.
A rude name for an awful person.

definition: To move back and forth; or a seat on ropes.
note: From Old English swingan, 'to beat or whip'. It also names a playground seat and a jazz style.
hints: A seat on chains at the playground.
What a golfer does with a club.

definition: To twist round and round.
note: From Middle English swirlen, probably from a Scandinavian word. Water in a drain does it.
hints: What milk does when stirred into tea.
The spiral of water in a plughole.

definition: A soft rustling sound; or smart and fashionable.
note: Imitative of a sound like a brush or a skirt. In British slang it means stylish.
hints: The sound of a basketball through the net.
A silk skirt's soft rustle.

definition: To dive down suddenly.
note: From Old English swapan, 'to sweep'. Eagles do it onto prey.
hints: What a hawk does to catch a mouse.
A sudden dive from above.

definition: A long blade for fighting.
note: From Old English sweord. Knights carried them.
hints: A knight's weapon.
A long blade with a hilt.

definition: Declared under oath.
note: The past participle of swear, from Old English sworen. An enemy may be one of these.
hints: What a witness's statement is.
Bound by an oath, as an enemy.

definition: A church council.
note: From Greek sunodos, 'meeting', from sun, 'together', and hodos, 'way'. It is a gathering of church leaders.
hints: A gathering of bishops.
A formal church meeting.

definition: A thick sweet liquid.
note: From Old French sirop, from Arabic sharab, 'drink'. Pancakes are often poured with maple.
hints: What goes on pancakes.
Maple is a sweet tree one.

definition: A cat with striped or mottled fur.
note: From French tabis, 'striped silk', named from a district in Baghdad where it was made. The cat took the name from the pattern.
hints: A striped house cat.
A cat with dark swirls on grey fur.

definition: A piece of furniture with a flat top.
note: From Latin tabula, 'board'. It is also a grid of data.
hints: Where you eat dinner.
A grid of rows and columns.

definition: Something forbidden by social custom.
note: Borrowed from Tongan tapu, 'sacred' or 'prohibited'. Captain Cook introduced it to English in the 1770s.
hints: A subject you do not raise at dinner.
A word from the Pacific meaning forbidden.

definition: Sticky; or cheap and in poor taste.
note: From tack plus -y. Wet paint is the first kind.
hints: Wet glue or paint.
A garish, cheap decoration.

definition: A chewy candy.
note: Probably related to tafia, a kind of rum. It is pulled until it is soft.
hints: A sweet pulled at the seaside.
A candy that sticks to your teeth.

definition: To spoil or contaminate.
note: From Old French teint, 'dyed', through the idea of tinging with something. A scandal may do it to a name.
hints: What a scandal does to a reputation.
Rotten food has this kind of spoil.

definition: The past participle of take; also in a romantic relationship.
note: From Old Norse tekinn. It can mean seized, or, in casual speech, no longer single.
hints: What a seat is if someone else is in it.
Describes someone who has a partner.

definition: One who accepts or grabs something.
note: From take plus -er. It is the opposite of a giver.
hints: Opposite of a giver.
Someone who accepts the bet.

definition: A running count.
note: From Latin talea, 'stick', for the notched stick used to keep records. Votes are counted by it.
hints: A running count of votes.
To add up scores.

definition: A sharp claw of a bird of prey.
note: From Old French talon, 'heel'. Eagles grip with them.
hints: An eagle's claw.
What an owl grips a mouse with.

definition: A person who trains wild animals.
note: From tame plus -er. A circus lion one is a familiar figure.
hints: Someone in a circus who trains lions.
A person who calms wild creatures.

definition: A passionate dance from Argentina; or the letter T in radio code.
note: Borrowed from Rioplatense Spanish. The dance began in Buenos Aires in the late nineteenth century.
hints: A dance of sharp steps and close hold.
The word for T in the spelling alphabet.

definition: Sharp and zesty in flavour.
note: From tang plus -y. Lemon and vinegar are this way.
hints: A sharp, citrus flavour.
Describes yoghurt or barbecue sauce.

definition: To narrow to a point; or a thin candle.
note: From Old English tapor, 'candle', of uncertain origin. Candles narrow towards the top.
hints: A thin candle.
To grow gradually narrower.

definition: A pig-like animal with a short trunk.
note: From Tupi tapi'ira, through French. It lives in forests of South America and Asia.
hints: A hoofed animal with a flexible snout.
A relative of the rhinoceros and horse.

definition: A deck of cards used for fortune-telling.
note: From French tarot, from Italian tarocchi. The deck was first used for a card game.
hints: Cards read by a fortune teller.
A deck with 'The Fool' and 'The Tower'.

definition: The sense of flavour; or to try food.
note: From Old French taster, 'to touch or try'. It is the sense used by the tongue.
hints: What a chef samples.
What the tongue does.

definition: Pleasant to eat.
note: From taste plus -y. It is a casual word for delicious.
hints: Delicious, in a casual word.
Another word for yummy.

definition: Worn out and shabby.
note: A British word of uncertain origin, in use since the 1500s; it may be linked to tatters. A different, dialect word clips potato.
hints: A scruffy old coat.
Faded and frayed.

definition: Yellowish-brown in colour.
note: From Old French tane, 'tanned'. A kind of owl shares the name.
hints: A lion's coat colour.
A brown owl is named after it.

definition: To pass on knowledge.
note: From Old English taecan, 'to show'. It is what a professor does.
hints: What a professor does.
To instruct a class.

definition: Filled with tears.
note: From tear plus -y. A farewell may leave you so.
hints: Eyes at a sad goodbye.
About to cry.

definition: To mock playfully; or to comb out fibres.
note: From Old English taesan, 'to pluck apart'. A friend does it with gentle jokes.
hints: What siblings do to one another.
To make fun lightly.

definition: The plural of tooth.
note: From Old English teth, an irregular plural. Dentists look after them.
hints: Brushed twice a day.
What a dentist inspects.

definition: A principle that a group believes.
note: Latin for 'he holds'. A core belief is something held.
hints: A guiding principle.
A core belief of a faith.

definition: A high male singing voice; or the general sense of something.
note: From Old French tenour, from Latin tenere, 'to hold'. In music it held the main melody in early choral works.
hints: A singer like Pavarotti.
The overall tone of a speech.

definition: Stretched tight; or the form of a verb showing time.
note: The grammar sense is from Latin tempus, 'time'. The tight sense is from Latin tensus, 'stretched'.
hints: What nerves feel before an exam.
Past, present or future.

definition: Number ten in order.
note: From Middle English tenth. Old English used teotha, which gave 'tithe'.
hints: The one after the ninth.
One part in ten.

definition: Barely warm.
note: From Latin tepidus, 'lukewarm'. A bath left too long gets this way.
hints: Water that has cooled down.
An unenthusiastic reception.

definition: Earth or land, in Latin.
note: Borrowed from Latin terra, 'earth'. It shows up in words like terrace and terrain.
hints: A Latin word for soil.
Think of the 'firma' that follows it.

definition: Brief and abrupt.
note: From Latin tersus, 'wiped clean', used of neat and polished style. It now suggests curtness.
hints: A one-word reply.
A short, curt message.

definition: Easily annoyed.
note: From Old French testu, 'headstrong', from teste, 'head'. Someone who is short of sleep may be this way.
hints: Short-tempered and snappish.
Describes someone about to snap.

definition: To show gratitude.
note: From Old English thancian. It is related to the word think, from the idea of a thought of kindness.
hints: What you say after a gift.
To express appreciation.

definition: The act of stealing.
note: From Old English thiefth, related to thief. It is a crime of taking someone's property.
hints: What a burglar commits.
A crime against property.

definition: Belonging to them.
note: From Old Norse their(r)a. It replaced the older English word hira.
hints: A word for what belongs to more than one person.
Often confused with a place word.

definition: The main subject or idea.
note: From Old French teme, from Greek thema, 'something laid down'. A story, a party or a piece of music has one.
hints: The central idea of a story.
A party's chosen topic for costumes.

definition: In or at that place.
note: From Old English thaer. It is the opposite of here.
hints: The opposite of here.
A word that points to a place.

definition: The eighth letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Greek theta. Mathematicians use it for an angle.
hints: A Greek letter used for angles.
Written with a horizontal bar in an oval.

definition: Having great depth; or dense.
note: From Old English thicce. Soup and fog can be this way.
hints: Opposite of thin.
A fog you can barely see through.

definition: A person who steals.
note: From Old English theof, shared across the Germanic languages. A shoplifter or burglar is one.
hints: A burglar by another name.
Takes what belongs to someone else.

definition: The part of the leg above the knee.
note: From Old English theoh. A drumstick on a chicken is the lower part, but this is above.
hints: The upper leg.
A cut of meat between hip and knee.

definition: To use your mind to reason.
note: From Old English thencan. It is related to the word for 'thank', both from an old sense of 'thought'.
hints: What you do before answering.
What a brain does.

definition: Number three in order.
note: From Old English thridda. It follows the second.
hints: The bronze medal place.
What comes after second.

definition: A narrow strip of leather; or a sandal held by a strap.
note: From Old English thwong, 'strip of leather'. It was used for binding and for whips.
hints: A leather strip for tying.
A beach sandal held on by a strap.

definition: A sharp spike on a plant.
note: From Old English thorn. Roses have them.
hints: What a rose has along its stem.
A prickle on a bush.

definition: The number after two.
note: From Old English thri, shared across Indo-European languages. It is a number of many sayings.
hints: One more than two.
A crowd, they say, when added to two.

definition: To beat with a strong pulse.
note: From Middle English throbben, possibly imitative. A bruised thumb does it.
hints: What a headache does.
A beat of pain, in time with the heart.

definition: To hurl through the air.
note: From Old English thrawan, 'to twist or turn'. A pitcher does it from a mound.
hints: What a pitcher does with a ball.
To toss a ball.

definition: A low, steady humming sound.
note: Imitative of a continuous vibration. A guitar string or an engine can do it.
hints: The sound of a purring engine.
A low, steady strumming.

definition: The short, thick digit on the hand.
note: From Old English thuma. The word has a silent b, added later in spelling.
hints: What a hitchhiker sticks out.
The finger that gets an upturn for approval.

definition: A heavy dull blow or its sound.
note: Probably imitative, from the mid sixteenth century. A dropped book makes one.
hints: The sound of a book dropped on a floor.
A dull knock on a door.

definition: A small herb used in cooking.
note: From Old French thym, from Greek thymon. It sounds like 'time'.
hints: A herb sounding like a clock's word.
Often paired with parsley and sage.

definition: A small jewelled crown.
note: From Latin tiara, 'Persian headdress', from Greek. A beauty queen or a bride might wear one.
hints: A jewelled headpiece for a princess.
What a pageant winner is crowned with.

definition: The shin bone.
note: From Latin tibia, 'shinbone' or 'flute'. It is the larger bone in the lower leg.
hints: The bone below the knee.
The shinbone.

definition: Relating to the ebb and flow of the sea.
note: From tide plus -al. A wave of this kind is caused by the moon's pull.
hints: Water that comes and goes twice a day.
A wave named for the ocean's rise and fall.

definition: A large cat with orange fur and black stripes.
note: From Greek tigris, through Latin and Old French. It is native to Asia.
hints: A striped big cat.
What Tony the Frosted Flakes mascot is.

definition: Firmly fixed; not loose.
note: From Middle English tight, a variant of thight, 'dense'. A rope or a schedule can be this.
hints: A rope pulled firm.
A close-fitting pair of jeans.

definition: The wavy line over a letter, as in n with a wave.
note: From Spanish tilde, from Latin titulus, 'inscription'. It marks Spanish letters and Portuguese vowels.
hints: A wavy mark over a letter.
The squiggle on a Spanish n.

definition: A device that counts down time.
note: From time plus -er. Ovens and eggs often need one.
hints: What you set when baking.
A kitchen device that rings.

definition: Shy and lacking confidence.
note: From Latin timidus, from timere, 'to fear'. A mouse is a classic example.
hints: Describes a nervous mouse.
Not bold; easily scared.

definition: Slightly drunk.
note: From tips, an old word, plus -y. It describes the unsteady stage before outright drunkenness.
hints: A little unsteady after a glass or two.
Slightly drunk.

definition: A giant; or someone of huge power.
note: From the Titans of Greek myth, the giants who ruled before the Olympian gods. It now describes a person of great power.
hints: A giant of industry.
One of the old gods overthrown by Zeus.

definition: This present day.
note: From Old English to daege, 'on this day'. It is the opposite of tomorrow or yesterday.
hints: Not yesterday, not tomorrow.
The current date.

definition: A hot sweetened drink with whisky.
note: From Hindi tari, the fermented palm sap, brought to Britain through India. The British drink took the name.
hints: A hot drink for a cold.
Whisky with honey and hot water.

definition: Relating to tone or pitch.
note: From tone plus -al. It can describe music or the overall mood of a piece.
hints: About the pitch of music.
How colours or sounds are balanced.

definition: A restorative; or fizzy water flavoured with quinine.
note: From Greek tonikos, 'of stretching'. Gin is often mixed with it.
hints: What goes with gin.
A medicine that refreshes.

definition: One of the hard white structures in the mouth.
note: From Old English toth. A saw has them as well.
hints: What a dentist fills.
A bit of the cutting edge of a saw.

definition: A yellowish gemstone.
note: From Old French topace, from Greek topazos. It is the birthstone for November.
hints: A golden-yellow jewel.
A November birthstone.

definition: A subject of conversation or writing.
note: From Greek topika, 'matters of place', the title of a work by Aristotle. It now means a subject.
hints: The subject of a talk.
What an essay is about.

definition: A handheld light; or a burning stick.
note: From Old French torche, 'twisted', since the first ones were twisted straw or rope. In British English it also means a flashlight.
hints: What an Olympic runner carries.
What you use in a power cut.

definition: The trunk of the body.
note: From Italian torso, 'stump', from Latin thyrsus. A statue without limbs is often called this.
hints: A statue with no head or limbs.
The body between neck and hips.

definition: A doughnut shape in geometry.
note: Latin for 'swelling' or 'cushion'. Mathematically it is a ring made by spinning a circle.
hints: A shape like a ring doughnut.
A tyre-like geometrical form.

definition: The whole amount; or complete.
note: From Medieval Latin totalis, from totus, 'whole'. You reach it by adding.
hints: The sum of all the parts.
What a bill adds up to.

definition: A natural object that represents a family or clan.
note: Borrowed from Ojibwe, from a word for a clan relative. Totem poles carved by Pacific Northwest peoples display them.
hints: A carved pole with animal faces.
An emblem of a clan.

definition: To make contact with the hand.
note: From Old French touchier, of Germanic origin. It is also one of the five senses.
hints: One of the five senses.
What a fingertip does.

definition: Strong and hard to damage; or difficult.
note: From Old English toh, 'tenacious'. Both steak and a hard problem can be this way.
hints: A chewy steak.
A hard problem to solve.

definition: A cloth for drying.
note: From Old French toaille. You use one after a bath.
hints: What you use after a shower.
Thrown in to give up in boxing.

definition: A tall narrow building or structure.
note: From Old English torr and Old French tur, from Latin turris. Churches and castles often have them.
hints: The Eiffel one is famous.
A tall part of a castle.

definition: Poisonous.
note: From Greek toxikon, 'poison for arrows', from toxon, 'bow'. It now describes harmful chemicals or behaviour.
hints: Describes a poisonous chemical.
A harmful, bad relationship.

definition: A poison made by a living thing.
note: From the same Greek root as toxic. Snake venom and bacteria produce them.
hints: A poison made by a snake.
What bacteria can produce to harm the body.

definition: A small sign of something; or to follow.
note: From Old French trace, 'track'. You can follow one, or draw over a picture.
hints: A tiny amount left behind.
To copy a drawing through thin paper.

definition: An area of land; or a short pamphlet.
note: From Latin tractus, 'a drawing out'. A digestive passage is called by it too.
hints: A large expanse of land.
A short religious pamphlet.

definition: To buy and sell; or a skilled craft.
note: From Middle Low German trade, 'track' or 'course'. A carpenter has one, and so does a merchant.
hints: What merchants do.
A skilled job such as plumbing.

definition: A line of linked railway carriages; or to teach.
note: From Old French trainer, 'to drag', from Latin trahere. It also names the long trailing part of a gown.
hints: What runs on rails.
What a coach does with athletes.

definition: A distinguishing characteristic.
note: From French trait, 'line' or 'feature', from Latin tractus. Eye colour is inherited this way.
hints: Something like generosity or bravery.
A feature passed in genes.

definition: To walk heavily; or a vagabond.
note: From Middle Low German trampen, 'to stamp'. It names a wanderer who walks long distances.
hints: A long, heavy walk through mud.
A wanderer without a home.

definition: Rubbish.
note: From Middle English trasch, probably a dialect word for broken twigs. It is what you put in a bin.
hints: What goes in a bin.
Waste to be thrown out.

definition: To fish by dragging a large net.
note: From Dutch tragelen, 'to drag'. It also means to search through a large amount of material.
hints: What a fishing boat does with a big net.
To search through a mass of records.

definition: To walk on; or the pattern on a tyre.
note: From Old English tredan, 'to step'. A tyre has a grooved one for grip.
hints: What you do carefully on thin ice.
The grooves on the sole of a boot.

definition: To behave towards someone; or a special pleasure.
note: From Old French tretier, 'to handle', from Latin tractare. It covers medicine, behaviour, and a small gift.
hints: What a child gets at Halloween.
What a doctor does for an illness.

definition: A general direction of change.
note: From Middle English trenden, 'to roll about'. It now names what is fashionable or on the rise.
hints: What goes viral for a while.
A line that slopes upward on a graph.

definition: A group of three.
note: From Greek trias, 'three'. In music it is a chord of three notes.
hints: Three things grouped together.
A chord made of three notes.

definition: A test; or a legal hearing.
note: From Old French trier, 'to try'. A new medicine goes through one, and a defendant faces one.
hints: What a defendant faces in court.
A test of a new medicine.

definition: A social group sharing ancestry and customs.
note: From Latin tribus, which originally meant one of three divisions of Rome's early people.
hints: A group with a shared chief and customs.
A Native community, or an ancient Hebrew clan.

definition: A very short moment.
note: From Middle English trisen, 'to pull sharply'. In the phrase 'in a trice' it means in an instant, as quickly as a tug.
hints: A moment, in the phrase 'in a'.
A blink of time.

definition: A cunning act meant to fool someone.
note: From Old Northern French trique, 'deceit'. A magician performs them.
hints: What a magician performs.
A cheeky deceit at Halloween.

definition: Past tense of try.
note: From Middle English, built from try plus -ed. It can also mean tested, as in 'tried and true'.
hints: What you did when you attempted.
A word that goes with 'true'.

definition: The stomach lining of a cow, eaten as food; or nonsense.
note: From Old French tripe, 'entrails'. Calling an idea this means it is rubbish.
hints: A Lancashire dish from a cow's stomach.
A word for nonsense.

definition: Overused and unoriginal.
note: From Latin tritus, 'worn out'. A cliche is this.
hints: A cliche is this.
A phrase worn out from overuse.

definition: A group of soldiers; or to move in a group.
note: From French troupe, recorded in English since 1545. It can also name a group of scouts or monkeys.
hints: A unit of soldiers.
A group of monkeys.

definition: A recurring theme or device.
note: From Greek tropos, 'turn'. A familiar figure of speech or storytelling pattern is called one.
hints: A familiar plot device in films.
A cliche of a genre.

definition: A freshwater fish related to the salmon.
note: From Old English truht. Anglers prize them.
hints: A fish caught by fly fishers.
Spotted and found in cold streams.

definition: A valuable collection of things found.
note: From Anglo-Norman tresor trouve, 'found treasure'. It is most often used in 'treasure ___'.
hints: A hoard of valuables found.
A hidden store of valuable things.

definition: An agreement to stop fighting.
note: From Middle English trewes, 'pledges', from Old English treow, 'faith'. Soldiers in 1914 held a famous one at Christmas.
hints: A pause in a war.
A white flag signals a wish for one.

definition: A large road vehicle for goods.
note: Perhaps from Greek trochos, 'wheel'. It was first a small wheel, then a cart.
hints: A big lorry.
A vehicle that carries cargo.

definition: Really; genuinely.
note: From Old English treowlice, 'faithfully'. It is used at the end of a letter.
hints: The word before a signature in 'yours ___'.
Said when you mean it sincerely.

definition: A winning card suit; or to beat.
note: Possibly from French triomphe, 'triumph'. A trump beats the other suits.
hints: A card that beats the rest.
To outdo a rival's play.

definition: The main stem of a tree; or an elephant's nose; or a car's boot.
note: From Old French tronc, 'alms box' or 'tree trunk'. Travellers also pack their belongings in a large box of the same name.
hints: An elephant's long nose.
The back storage area of an American car.

definition: A framework of beams; or to tie up tightly.
note: From Old French trousse, 'bundle'. Bridges and roofs use them, and cooks tie up a bird with string.
hints: A triangle framework in a roof.
To tie up a chicken before roasting.

definition: Belief that someone is reliable.
note: From Old Norse traust, 'confidence'. It also names a legal arrangement for managing assets.
hints: What a bridge of friendship needs.
What you put in a reliable friend.

definition: What is true.
note: From Old English triewth, 'faithfulness'. It is related to the word true.
hints: The opposite of a lie.
What a witness swears to tell.

definition: Relating to a tube.
note: From tube plus -al. It is a medical word, as in tubes of the body.
hints: A medical word about a duct.
Describes a passage like a tube in the body.

definition: A thick underground stem of a plant, like a potato.
note: From Latin tuber, 'swelling'. Potatoes and yams are examples.
hints: A potato is one.
A fleshy root vegetable.

definition: A cup-shaped spring flower.
note: From Middle French tulipe, from Turkish tulbent, 'turban', since the flower looks like a turban. The Dutch grew a mania for them in the 1600s.
hints: A flower tied to the Netherlands.
A spring bulb in many colours.

definition: A fine netting used for veils and ballet skirts.
note: Named after the French town of Tulle, where it was made. Bridal veils use it.
hints: The airy fabric of a tutu.
A fine net for a bride's veil.

definition: An abnormal lump of tissue.
note: From Latin tumor, 'a swelling'. It is the American spelling of tumour.
hints: A medical growth that a scan can show.
A lump a doctor may remove.

definition: A long loose garment worn over the body.
note: From Latin tunica. Roman soldiers wore one under their armour.
hints: A Roman soldier's garment.
A long shirt reaching to the thighs.

definition: A turbine; or a booster in an engine.
note: Short for turbine or turbocharger, from Latin turbo, 'whirl'. It forces extra air into an engine.
hints: A booster for a car engine.
A fast speed setting.

definition: A private teacher.
note: From Latin tutor, 'guardian'. Students hire one for extra help.
hints: Someone hired to help with homework.
A university teacher guiding a few students.

definition: A sharp ringing sound; or a nasal accent.
note: Imitative of a string being plucked. A banjo string and a country voice both have one.
hints: The sound of a guitar string plucked.
A nasal accent in a country song.

definition: To adjust slightly.
note: From Old English twiccian, 'to pluck'. It started as a pinch and became a small adjustment.
hints: A small adjustment.
What you do to settings.

definition: The short chirp of a bird; or a post on a social network.
note: Imitative of a bird's call. It also names a short social media post.
hints: A bird's short call.
A short online post.

definition: Two times.
note: From Old English twiges, from twi, 'two'. It is the adverb for doing something once more.
hints: One more time than once.
Said of doing it double.

definition: Strong string made of twisted threads; or to wind.
note: From Old English twin, 'double thread'. A gardener ties plants with it.
hints: String for tying a parcel.
What a vine does round a post.

definition: To spin round and round.
note: Of Scandinavian origin. A dancer or baton does it.
hints: What a ballerina does.
A fast spin.

definition: To turn round; or an unexpected turn in a story.
note: From Middle English twist, from Old English, a pair of things. A story or a rope can have one.
hints: What you do to open a jar.
A surprise at the end of a film.

definition: An old word meaning 'between'.
note: A shortened form of betwixt, from Old English. It is found in the phrase 'twixt and between'.
hints: An old poetic word for in between.
A short version of a longer old preposition.

definition: The act of fastening with a knot.
note: From tie plus -ing, from Old English tigan. A shoelace or a knot can be involved.
hints: What you do to shoelaces.
Fastening with a knot.

definition: The milk gland of a cow.
note: From Old English uder. It hangs below the cow.
hints: What a farmer milks.
The bag under a cow.

definition: An open sore.
note: From Latin ulcus, 'sore'. Stomach ones were once thought to be caused by stress.
hints: A sore in the stomach lining.
An open sore on the skin.

definition: Extreme; beyond the usual.
note: From Latin ultra, 'beyond'. It is used as a prefix, as in ultrasound.
hints: A prefix meaning beyond.
A race longer than a marathon is named with it.

definition: A brother of one's parent.
note: From Old French oncle, from Latin avunculus, 'little grandfather'. It is a family member on one side.
hints: A parent's brother.
Said to be what Bob is, in a saying.

definition: Not cut; or not edited.
note: From un- plus cut. A rough gemstone or a film not trimmed may be it.
hints: A rough diamond.
A film with nothing removed.

definition: Below or beneath.
note: From Old English under. It is the opposite of over.
hints: The opposite of over.
Found beneath a bed or a bridge.

definition: Excessive or unwarranted.
note: From un- plus due. It describes something beyond what is right.
hints: Beyond what is called for.
Needless, as in worry.

definition: Not suitable; or out of shape.
note: From un- plus fit. A person who rarely exercises may be it.
hints: Not up to the standard.
Out of condition.

definition: To make into one.
note: From Late Latin unificare, 'to make one'. A nation or group can be brought together this way.
hints: What a leader does for a divided country.
To bring parts into a whole.

definition: A joining together; or a group of workers.
note: From Late Latin unio, from unus, 'one'. A marriage is one, and so is a trade body.
hints: A workers' association.
A marriage, in a formal word.

definition: To join together as one.
note: From Latin unire, 'to make one', from unus, 'one'. Countries and teams do it.
hints: What a common cause does to people.
To bring separate things together.

definition: The state of being as one.
note: From Old French unite, from Latin unitas, 'oneness'. It is what a team strives for.
hints: Agreement and togetherness.
What 'strength in numbers' relies on.

definition: Not lit.
note: From un- plus lit. A dark path or a fire never lit is this.
hints: A dark street at night.
A candle before the match.

definition: Not fulfilled or not yet encountered.
note: From un- plus met. Needs and conditions can be this.
hints: A condition that has not been satisfied.
A goal not reached.

definition: Not fixed or not yet placed.
note: From un- plus set. Jelly that has not firmed up is this.
hints: Jelly that is still runny.
A gem not yet put in a ring.

definition: To loosen a knot.
