note: From Middle English untien, from un- plus tie. A shoelace or a rope can be loosened this way.
hints: What you do to a shoelace.
To free a rope from its knot.

definition: Up to the time of.
note: From Middle English until, probably a northern variant built from Old Norse und, 'up to'. It marks a limit in time.
hints: A word marking an end point in time.
Up to the moment when.

definition: Not married.
note: From un- plus wed. It is a bit formal for single.
hints: Not yet married.
Said of an unmarried person.

definition: To open a fastener with teeth.
note: From un- plus zip. A jacket or a file can be this way opened.
hints: What you do to a jacket.
To open a compressed computer file.

definition: Higher in position.
note: From Middle English, the comparative of up. It is the opposite of lower.
hints: Opposite of lower.
The top deck of a bus.

definition: To disturb or overturn; or unhappy.
note: From Middle English upsetten, 'to set up'. A stomach, a cart and a person can all be this.
hints: A tipped glass of water.
Distressed after bad news.

definition: Relating to a city.
note: From Latin urbanus, from urbs, 'city'. It is the opposite of rural.
hints: Opposite of rural.
Of a big town.

definition: Liquid waste from the kidneys.
note: From Latin urina. A medical sample for a test is often of it.
hints: A sample a doctor may test.
Waste water made by the kidneys.

definition: The way something is used.
note: From Old French usage, from user, 'to use'. A dictionary records it.
hints: How a word is commonly employed.
The amount of data or power consumed.

definition: A person who shows people to their seats.
note: From Old French ussier, 'doorkeeper', from Latin ostiarius. It also means to guide someone in.
hints: Works at a wedding or cinema.
To guide in, as to show guests in.

definition: Normal; as expected.
note: From Latin usualis, 'of use'. It is what happens most of the time.
hints: The standard order at a cafe.
What is customary.

definition: To seize power wrongfully.
note: From Latin usurpare, 'to take over'. A rebel might do it to a throne.
hints: What a pretender does to a king.
To take a throne with no right.

definition: Useful.
note: From Latin utilis, 'useful'. It is an old, learned word.
hints: An old word for useful.
A cousin of the word utility.

definition: To say aloud; or complete.
note: From Middle English utteren, 'to speak out', and as an adjective, 'outermost'. 'Utter nonsense' is total nonsense.
hints: To say a word aloud.
Total, as in nonsense.

definition: A person who parks cars or attends to a man's clothes.
note: From Old French vaslet, 'young man'. It now describes a car-parking service.
hints: Takes your car at the hotel door.
A gentleman's personal servant.

definition: Great courage, especially in battle.
note: The American spelling of valour, from Latin valere, 'to be strong'. It is awarded in medals.
hints: Bravery on the battlefield.
What a medal may honour.

definition: How much something is worth.
note: From Old French value, 'worth'. It can be money or principles.
hints: What a price shows.
What you hold dear.

definition: A device that controls the flow of liquid or gas.
note: From Latin valva, 'leaf of a door'. The heart has four.
hints: A tap-like part in a pipe.
A part of the heart that controls flow.

definition: Dull and lacking interest.
note: From Latin vapidus, 'flat' or 'stale', used of wine. Conversation can be this way.
hints: A dull conversation.
Lacking spark.

definition: A mist or gas from a liquid.
note: The American spelling of vapour, from Latin vapor, 'steam'. It rises from a kettle.
hints: What rises from a hot bath.
The gas form of a liquid.

definition: An arched ceiling; or a strong room; or to leap.
note: From Old French volte, 'turned'. It names a bank room, a church ceiling, and a pole jump.
hints: A bank's secure room.
To leap over using a pole.

definition: To boast.
note: From Old French vanter, from Latin vanus, 'vain'. It survives in 'much vaunted'.
hints: To brag about something.
What a boastful person does with achievements.

definition: Someone who avoids all animal products.
note: Coined in 1944 from the first and last letters of vegetarian. It excludes dairy and eggs.
hints: Eats no meat, dairy or eggs.
Stricter than a vegetarian.

definition: The place where an event happens.
note: From Old French venue, 'a coming'. A concert is held at one.
hints: Where a concert is held.
A place booked for a wedding.

definition: The edge of something; or to be close to.
note: From Old French verge, 'rod'. It also names the grass at the road's edge.
hints: The grass at a road's edge.
Close to tears, on the brink.

definition: Energy and enthusiasm.
note: From French verve, 'caprice' or 'rapture'. A performer can play with it.
hints: Liveliness in a performance.
A burst of spirited energy.

definition: A parish priest in the Church of England.
note: From Old French vicaire, from Latin vicarius, 'substitute'. He stood in for a bishop or rector.
hints: A priest in an English village.
A church leader in a parish.

definition: A recording of moving images.
note: From Latin video, 'I see'. It also names a recorded film.
hints: What a camera records.
A clip on a phone.

definition: A large house in the country or by the sea.
note: From Latin villa, 'country house'. Holiday ones are rented abroad.
hints: A holiday home in the sun.
A Roman country house.

definition: A stringed instrument slightly larger than a violin.
note: From Italian viola, from a Latin word for fiddle. It is played under the chin.
hints: An instrument a bit bigger than a violin.
A flower, a cousin of the pansy.

definition: A venomous snake.
note: From Latin vipera, 'snake that gives birth to live young'. An adder is one.
hints: A poisonous snake.
The adder is a British one.

definition: Relating to a virus; or spreading quickly online.
note: From virus plus -al. A video can be called it if shared widely.
hints: A video shared by millions.
Caused by a germ.

definition: A tiny infectious agent; or a harmful computer program.
note: From Latin virus, 'poison'. It is smaller than bacteria.
hints: A cause of colds and flu.
Harmful code on a computer.

definition: To go and see someone.
note: From Latin visitare, 'to go to see'. You can pay one to a friend or a museum.
hints: What you do to see a friend.
A trip to a place.

definition: A front part of a helmet or cap that shades the eyes.
note: From Anglo-Norman viser, from Old French vis, 'face'. A knight's one lifted to show the face.
hints: A knight's face guard.
A cap's brim that shades the eyes.

definition: A long view, especially a scenic one.
note: From Italian vista, 'sight'. A mountain top offers one.
hints: A scenic outlook.
A wide view over a valley.

definition: Essential; or full of life.
note: From Latin vitalis, from vita, 'life'. Vital signs show life.
hints: Essential for life.
Pulse and breathing are called this sign.

definition: Bright and clear.
note: From Latin vividus, 'lively'. A dream or a colour can be this.
hints: A bright colour.
A memory so clear it feels real.

definition: A female fox.
note: From Old English fyxen, 'she-fox'. It is also an old insult for a bad-tempered woman.
hints: A she-fox in the wild.
A reindeer in the Christmas song.

definition: Relating to the voice; or speaking out.
note: From Latin vocalis, from vox, 'voice'. A singer has them, and a campaigner can be this.
hints: A singer's part of a song.
Someone who speaks out loudly.

definition: A clear strong spirit, usually from grain or potato.
note: From Russian vodka, a diminutive of voda, 'water'. It means 'little water'.
hints: A clear spirit from Russia.
Used in a Moscow mule.

definition: To throw up the contents of the stomach.
note: From Latin vomere. It is a medical and a plain word.
hints: What seasickness may cause.
What a queasy stomach may lead to.

definition: A person who casts a ballot.
note: From vote plus -er. In many countries you must register to be one.
hints: Someone at the polls.
Casts a ballot in an election.

definition: To confirm that someone or something is reliable.
note: From Middle English vouchen, 'to summon as a witness', from Old French. A friend can do it for your character.
hints: What a reference does for a job seeker.
To speak up for someone's honesty.

definition: A speech sound made without blocking the breath; or the letter for it.
note: From Old French vouel, from Latin vocalis, 'sounding'. In English they are a, e, i, o and u.
hints: A, E, I, O or U.
What a consonant is not.

definition: Competing for something.
note: The present participle of vie, from Old French envier, 'to challenge'. Rivals are said to be doing it for a prize.
hints: Two rivals competing for a title.
Competing eagerly for first place.

definition: Funny in a crazy way.
note: From whack plus -y. It describes zany people and ideas.
hints: A zany, eccentric idea.
Like a comedy full of bizarre antics.

definition: A thin crisp biscuit; or a thin disc of bread used in communion.
note: From Anglo-Norman wafre, from a Germanic word for 'honeycomb', because of the pattern. Ice cream is often served between them.
hints: A thin crisp biscuit for ice cream.
A thin disc of bread in church.

definition: A four-wheeled cart for goods.
note: Borrowed from Dutch wagen. Settlers crossed America in covered ones.
hints: What settlers rode across the prairie.
A child's pull-along toy cart.

definition: The narrow part of the body between ribs and hips.
note: From Middle English wast, probably from Old English. A belt goes round it.
hints: Where a belt sits.
The narrow part of an hourglass figure.

definition: To give up a right or a claim.
note: From Middle English weyven, 'to abandon'. A bank might do it to a fee.
hints: What a landlord may do to a late fee.
To choose not to enforce a rule.

definition: A ballroom dance in three-beat time.
note: From German Walzer, from walzen, 'to roll or turn'. Vienna made it famous.
hints: A ballroom dance with a one-two-three beat.
Strauss wrote famous ones.

definition: Covered in small hard growths.
note: From wart plus -y. A toad's skin is this way.
hints: A toad's skin.
Lumpy and rough.

definition: To use carelessly; or rubbish.
note: From Old French guast, from Latin vastus, 'empty'. It names both throwing things away and what is thrown away.
hints: What you do with money you squander.
Rubbish thrown out.

definition: To look at carefully; or a timepiece on the wrist.
note: From Old English waecce, 'wakefulness'. A guard keeps one at night.
hints: What you wear on your wrist.
What a lifeguard does at the beach.

definition: The clear liquid that falls as rain.
note: From Old English waeter. Rivers, rain and oceans are made of it.
hints: What you drink when thirsty.
A chemical made of hydrogen and oxygen.

definition: To be unsteady or unsure.
note: From Middle English waveren, 'to move unsteadily'. A flame or a decision can do it.
hints: What a voice does when nervous.
To be torn between choices.

definition: Made of wax; or pale like wax.
note: From Old English weaxen, 'of wax'. A pale face may be called it.
hints: A pale, smooth face like a candle.
Made of the stuff candles are formed from.

definition: To make cloth by crossing threads.
note: From Old English wefan. A loom is used.
hints: What a loom does.
What a spider does with a web.

definition: A tapering piece of material used to split or hold.
note: From Old English wecg. A door may be held open by one.
hints: What keeps a door open.
A piece of cheese cut like a triangle.

definition: Full of weeds; or thin and weak.
note: From weed plus -y. A neglected garden is this way.
hints: An overgrown flowerbed.
A puny, thin person.

definition: To find how heavy something is.
note: From Old English wegan, 'to carry or lift'. A scale does it.
hints: What a scale does.
To consider options before choosing.

definition: Strange or unusual.
note: From Old English wyrd, 'fate'. The word first meant destiny, then something uncanny.
hints: Odd and unsettling.
Once meant fate in Old English.

definition: To hit sharply.
note: Uncertain in origin; it is probably imitative of the sound of a blow. 'Out of whack' means out of order.
hints: A hard blow with a stick.
The sound of a bat hitting a ball.

definition: A huge sea mammal.
note: From Old English hwael. Blue ones are the largest animals ever.
hints: The largest animal in the sea.
A mammal that sings in the ocean.

definition: A structure where ships dock.
note: From Old English hwearf, 'bank' or 'shore'. Boats load and unload at one.
hints: A place for ships to tie up.
A landing stage beside the water.

definition: A cereal grain from which flour is made.
note: From Old English haete, probably related to white. Bread is baked from it.
hints: What bread is made from.
A golden field crop.

definition: A round part that turns on an axle.
note: From Old English hweol. Bicycles and cars roll on them.
hints: A round part on a bicycle.
What you turn to steer a ship.

definition: A puppy; or a cheeky young man.
note: From Old English hwelp. Dogs and wolves have them.
hints: A baby dog or wolf.
A rude word for a young upstart.

definition: At what place.
note: From Old English hwaer. It starts a question about location.
hints: A question about a location.
What a map answers.

definition: What one of several.
note: From Old English hwylc, 'of what kind'. It asks a choice.
hints: A question word for choosing.
A word to pick between two.

definition: A faint smell.
note: Imitative, first recorded for a puff of air. A bit of perfume or smoke is one.
hints: A hint of cooking in the air.
A faint trace of perfume.

definition: A period of time; or during the time that.
note: From Old English hwil, 'time'. It can also mean 'although'.
hints: A short period of time.
A word meaning 'although' or 'during'.

definition: To complain in a high, drawn-out tone.
note: From Old English hwinan, 'to whistle through the air'. A dog or a child may do it.
hints: What a puppy does at the door.
A child's long complaint.

definition: Complaining in a fretful tone.
note: From whine plus -y. It describes a child who keeps grumbling.
hints: A child grumbling in the back of a car.
Constantly moaning.

definition: To spin rapidly.
note: From Middle English whirlen, from a Scandinavian word. A dancer or a tornado can do it.
hints: What a dancer does.
A spinning motion.

definition: The colour of snow or milk.
note: From Old English hwit. It is the colour of clean paper.
hints: The colour of fresh snow.
The opposite of black.

definition: Complete; not divided.
note: From Old English hal, 'healthy', also source of hale and heal. A loaf or a number may be this.
hints: Every bit of it, not in parts.
The opposite of a fraction.

definition: A loud cry of joy.
note: From Middle English whopen, imitative. It is a sound of excitement.
hints: A shout of excitement.
What a crowd gives at a win.

definition: Of which person.
note: From Old English hwaes, the genitive of who. It asks about ownership.
hints: A word asking who owns it.
The possessive of who.

definition: To make or become wider.
note: From wide plus -en. A road or a gap can be this way.
hints: What a road project does.
What your eyes do in surprise.

definition: A woman whose husband has died.
note: From Old English widuwe. It is the same word in many Indo-European languages.
hints: A woman who has lost her husband.
A spider with a famous black name.

definition: How wide something is.
note: From wide plus -th, on the pattern of length. A ruler can measure it.
hints: Side to side measure.
What a door's frame has.

definition: To hold and use a tool or weapon.
note: From Old English wealdan, 'to rule'. A king can do it to power, and a knight to a sword.
hints: What a knight does with a sword.
To exercise power over others.

definition: An old word for a living creature.
note: From Old English wiht, 'creature'. It also names ghostly beings in fantasy.
hints: An archaic word for a being.
A ghostly figure in fantasy.

definition: Weak or cowardly.
note: From wimp, of uncertain origin, plus -y. It describes feeble people or things.
hints: The opposite of brave.
A weak, timid manner.

definition: To flinch in pain.
note: From Anglo-Norman wincier, 'to bend aside'. A sharp pain makes you do it.
hints: What you do at a sharp pain.
To flinch at a sudden sting.

definition: A machine that hauls with a drum and cable.
note: From Old English wince, 'reel'. A tow truck often has one.
hints: A tow truck's cable drum.
A crank for hauling a heavy load.

definition: With a lot of wind.
note: From Old English windig, built from wind plus -y. A kite flies best on such a day.
hints: A day for flying a kite.
Chicago is nicknamed the city of this.

definition: Thin and light, like a wisp.
note: From wisp plus -y. Hair or cloud can be this.
hints: Fine, thin hair.
A cloud thin and light.
